## **Foreword by Thomas M. Coughlin**

Consumer electronic (CE) devices are a ubiquitous part of our everyday lives. These devices are increasingly connected to the Internet and depend upon web-based services. Because these devices capture and contain a lot of personal data and can be used to monitor and track consumers, the security of these devices (from both hardware and data perspectives) has become of paramount importance. As the growth in what is often called Internet of things (IoT), including several smart hardware devices as the backbone, creates loopholes for hardware threats as well as an increasing number of targets for consumer data and privacy invasion, we need strong hardware and data protection and intellectual property (IP) core ownership security built into these devices at the most basic level.

At the same time that consumer content must be protected, IP cores in these devices as well as the authenticity of the supply chain used to manufacture and distribute consumer products have become a major concern and are intimately tied to hardware and content security. Older techniques for protecting hardware security using today’s commoditized system-on-chip (SoC) network connected devices with IP cores from multiple sources are insufficient to meet the needs of modern consumer products and copyrighted content on these devices.

**IP core protection and hardware-assisted security for consumer electronics** address the general issue of protecting hardware (especially DSP cores) of CE as well as data on CE, including new demands created by IoT enabled products. The book also addresses the potential threats from intervention in the CE design supply chain and how these threats can be circumvented. These supply chain security solutions may include hardware watermarking, hardware fingerprinting, symmetrical IP core protection, hardware metering, computational forensic engineering for IP core protection, and various forms of hardware obfuscation.

The book explores and addresses many different types of security attacks that can be launched against CE products, including power and timing “side channel” attacks, as well as backdoor and brute-force attacks. Methods are discussed for defeating/blocking Trojan horse attacks as well as reverse engineering attacks.

The book discusses the latest methods for active and passive IP core security of DSP cores used in CE device and protection mechanisms for the buyers of ICs and incorporated IP that includes “watermarking” and “fingerprinting” as well as structural obfuscation, functional obfuscation, hardware AES, watermarked AES, and physically unclonable functions (PUFs). The book also explores the use of forensic engineering for resolving ownership issues for reusable digital signal processing (DSP) IP cores. In addition to these direct security concerns, the book discusses the trade-offs of energy consumption, security and performance for CE hardware.

The first of its kind on CE security, this book should be read by designers, programmers, or engineers involved in the design of CE devices as well as for services using these devices.

Thomas M. Coughlin  
IEEE Fellow,  
Chair, IEEE Consumer Electronics Future Directions Committee

## **Foreword by Pradipta Patra**

We are delimited by consumer electronics (CE) in our everyday life. It is hard to envision a smart life without smart devices currently. However, a smart CE device is valuable as long as its security is intact. Security is integral to the successful deployment of a smart CE product. The term “security” encompasses hardware security, hardware assisted security, data security, media security, etc. At the heart of every security protocol is the underlying hardware which is the lifeline of every application. In the current world of cybersecurity, securing and protecting hardware (and intellectual property (IP) cores) as well as securing data/information are paramount.

For the first time authors in this book present an all-inclusive comprehensive book that encompasses **security of CE devices from hardware security perspective as well as data/media perspective**. The book covers a wide spectrum of modern security topic ranging from fundamentals of IP core protection and hardware-assisted security, Trojan security of DSP cores used in CE hardware, hardware watermarking of DSP /IP cores/IC, symmetrical DSP/IP core protection using watermarking and fingerprinting, computational forensic engineering, structural obfuscation of DSP cores, including a case study on JPEG CODEC, functional obfuscation of DSP cores, hardware AES, watermarking, IoT security, PUF, and media protection.

To the best of my knowledge, there is no book that presents the details of **multiple hardware-assisted security topics** under one umbrella. The book covers various state-of-the-art security attack details possible on DSP IP core as well as recommends interesting solution to them, which have industry applicability. The attack and solutions described in the book can be deployed for hardware security and IP core protection of DSP cores used in CE devices such as digital camera, camcorder, smart phone, smart watch, etc. The book can be extremely interesting for industry practitioners, researchers (both beginners and advanced level), graduate students/scholars, and any academicians.

The book also provides conceptual questions and exercise for each chapter. This book provides a great opportunity to challenge the understanding for each security topic and refine a reader’s understanding level. The book can also be easily adopted in for any graduate-level course (master’s and Ph.D.) at an institute/university. Additionally, it can also serve as designer’s handbook who is eager to learn designing secured DSP hardware core. The book provides several examples of industry-level practical design procedure on secured DSP cores such as digital filters, JPEG, DCT, and FFT. End-to-end design flow for devising secured DSP IP cores is described in each chapter, in the context of different threat models.

To my knowledge, this is the first book ever on CE device IP core protection and hardware-assisted security. It is a must-read book for a hardware designers, FPGA programmers, or CAD tool designers, as well as researchers and academicians involved in the design of CE devices.

Pradipta Patra, Ph.D.  
Power Innovation Lab, Frontier Research Team  
Samsung Research,  
Samsung Electronics, Seoul, South Korea

## **Foreword by Swarup Bhunia**

Digital signal processing (DSP) and multimedia applications affect every spheres of modern society. These applications work on discrete physical signals (e.g., image, video, speech, and physiological signals), analyze their behavior, and recognize the patterns of significance. Over the years, they have made pervasive and profound impact in the consumer electronics (CE) and other industrial sectors. With unprecedented growth of smart and sensor-enriched Internet of things (IoT) edge devices, which interface with the physical world through sensors and actuators, the role of DSP to analyze signals and extract meaningful information from them has become ever more significant. We observe a growing trend of incorporating autonomy and smartness in IoT devices as well as in complex system of systems (e.g., autonomous vehicles). In this context, we expect to see the increasing role of DSP and its integration with artificial intelligence to make complex reliable decisions without or with little human intervention.

Implementation of DSP and multimedia algorithms has taken various paths, ranging from purely software implementation to implementation in a domain-specific processor, i.e., DSP, a reconfigurable platform (e.g., FPGA), to purely custom hardware implementation (e.g., ASIC), and any combination of these. In all possible implementation platforms, traditionally, designers have aimed at optimizing the power-performance-area to achieve target quality of service (QoS). Security issues associated with these implementations and ways to address them have not been at the forefront of efficient realization of wide variety of DSP and multimedia algorithms. However, security for DSP/multimedia applications has emerged as a key design parameter as variety of security issues involving the hardware itself or the content being processed have surfaced. These issues include tampering and piracy of DSP/multimedia cores, while the protection approaches include fingerprinting, watermarking, and secure hardware design.

The book, for the first time to my knowledge, provides a compendium of chapters covering, rather comprehensively, the security issues and protection approaches in hardware/software implementation of DSP/multimedia functions, and touches on both current practices and recent innovations. The comprehensive coverage of DSP and hardware security concepts with relevant background material and description of current industrial practices are the key distinctive features of this textbook.

Some of the salient features of the book include the following:

*   The book encompasses hardware-assisted security approaches for DSP/multimedia cores with comprehensive coverage for today’s CE devices.
*   It includes emerging attack vectors such as Trojan attacks in DSP/multimedia core.
*   It covers promising countermeasures for various attacks, e.g., robust watermarking for DSP/multimedia cores, symmetrical protection for DSP/multimedia cores that combine fingerprinting with watermarking and structural and functional obfuscation for DSP/multimedia cores.
*   It presents forensic analysis techniques on DSP/multimedia cores to examine and provide proof of ownership with case studies on JPEG CODEC.
*   It includes chapters which focus on the protection of digital media and the role of secure hardware design in IoT security.
*   It provides several examples of practical design procedure in industry for secured DSP cores, such as digital filters, JPEG, DCT, and FFT.
*   It depicts an end-to-end design flow for devising secured DSP IP cores.

The book can serve a valuable resource for a wide readership consisting of students, researchers, and practitioners. It can be an essential read for a hardware designers, FPGA programmers, CAD tool designers, as well as researchers and academicians involved in the design of secure CE devices. It can be easily adopted in as a graduate-level elective course at an institute. Additionally, it can also serve as a handbook for a designer, who needs to understand the security issues and realize secure hardware while implementing DSP/multimedia functions. I believe the book would greatly help the readers to gain knowledge on this topic, motivate them for advanced research, and effectively do the security analysis and security design.

It is my great pleasure to see the book getting published. I wish it all the success in fulfilling the authors’ mission.

Dr. Swarup Bhunia,  
Preeminence Professor and Steven Yatauro Faculty Fellow,  
University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA,  
ACM Distinguished Speaker

## **Foreword by Peter Corcoran**

We live in a time of continual change and nowhere is this more evident than in the consumer electronics (CE) industry. Nearly 6 years ago, I wrote an editorial for *IEEE Consumer Electronics Magazine* entitled “Change and the Consumer Electronics Industry” ([http://bit.ly/CEchange](http://bit.ly/CEchange)). A key point of this article is that if you want to work in this industry you have to embrace change and go with it. Technology is constantly adapting to the market and the needs of the consumer and this was never truer than it is today.

Today, we live in a world of shortening product cycles, increasing NRE costs, and, unless your organization owns a global technology platform or manufactures’ high-value consumer device platforms, there are enormous challenges in building sustainable revenue from our engineering works. Add to these day-to-day concerns the constant struggle to keep up with an ever-changing technology landscape and new technical challenges.

Among these challenges we now find that hardware design is the “new” software are now being built in the same way that complex software products like operating systems were built in the 1990s—constructed from the work and contributions of different engineering teams with specialized skills and integrated onto a single platform—these increasingly complex “system-on-chip” designs that are the mainstay of today’s advanced CE products, from smartphones, to TVs, from autonomous vehicles to immersive AR/VR headsets.

With this growth in system complexity, it becomes challenging for smaller engineering companies to build their own integrated circuits and for many of our business model becomes that of the fabless IP supplier. We painstakingly build specialized hardware designs to license into larger SoC platforms owned by global corporations. And we face the same challenges faced by smaller software vendors in the 1990s—how can we prevent the theft of our engineering designs by copying from one IC design to another? After all they are just patterns of registers and transistors, albeit highly complex and sophisticated ones embodying many thousands of hours of engineering effort.

In this context, I am delighted to introduce this new book addressing the increasingly important topic of *IP Core Protection and Hardware-Assisted Security for Consumer Electronics*. This textbook is targeted to this increasingly important design challenge for today’s CE engineers.

This text starts with the fundamentals of IP core protection and proceeds to develop a number of alternative and complimentary approaches including a number of detailed case studies. The text examines Trojan security approaches, robust watermarking and symmetrical approaches that combine fingerprinting with watermarking. Forensic analysis techniques are presented to examine and provide proof of ownership, and several advanced techniques based on design and functional obfuscation methodologies are presented together with case studies on JPEG CODEC and DSP cores. Additional chapters consider the protection of digital media and the role of secure hardware design in IoT security.

This text appears at a very timely juncture when CE engineers are facing increasing challenges. It provides a detailed and comprehensive coverage of this increasingly important field and will be of great benefit to both practicing engineers looking to update their knowledge in this field and equally to graduate students working on advanced hardware R&D projects.

Dr. Peter Corcoran  
IEEE Fellow and Emeritus Editor-in-Chief,  
IEEE Consumer Electronics Magazine  
National Inventors Hall of Fame, Ireland

## **Preface**

The recent rapid proliferation of smart city and Internet of things (IoT) framework has only become a reality owing to the expansive developments in the field of consumer electronics (CE), cloud computing, and high-speed networking infrastructure. CE include smart mobile devices that are responsible for combining multiple functions into one device, providing a phone, camera, video recorder, alarm clock, personal music player, paging system, TV remote control, etc. It also acts as gateway for some other devices. It provides user interface to access, manage, and control our things. It is a disruptive technology. Cloud computing has evolved a set of sophisticated infrastructure for storage, messaging, security, content, and connectivity. In terms of connectivity technology, we now have more sophisticated and reliable Wi-Fi connections due to the tremendous growth in computing infrastructure and computing power augmented with the exponential growth of network data for next few years.

However, each of these modules as part of IoT or smart city is solely dependent on the security and protection of the underlying hardware system. For example, smart mobile devices in CE, hardware infrastructure in cloud computing, and system framework for reliable and trusted connectivity technology would need built-in hardware security technologies to protect against unauthorized access to personal information, detect/correct malicious hardware, data integrity, etc. There could be several types of cyber attackers depending on the probability of occurrence and potential damage caused, such as (1) amateur attackers whose probability of occurrence is high but potential damage caused is low, (2) petty criminals whose probability of occurrence is not as high but its potential damage could be higher than amateur attackers, and (3) terrorists activists/state-sponsored attackers whose probability of occurrence is low but potential damage caused could be extremely severe. Thus, in the world of CE and IoT, security, privacy, and protection of hardware and its information are critically imperative. It is universally acknowledged that for IoT, security of underneath hardware is pivotal for reliable functioning. The underlying hardware may have been affected by several threat factors. An adversary may generate secret exist that leaks crucial data such as encryption key employed in secure transmission line, the maker could intervene the design by implanting hardware Trojans, or implant artifacts with recognized dependability susceptibilities. Current generation designs assimilate intellectual property (IP) blocks from manifold vendors, mass-produced and verified by diverse companies worldwide. Accordingly, numerous access points exist for hardware to be attacked. For a trusted or secured hardware design, defense of intellectual property cores is of ultimate significance.

Electronics design industry in future is heading for a paradigm shift toward secured, reliable, and low-cost CE hardware from the conventional ones. Reading this book will enable the readers to push their boundaries of knowledge to dive into the some emerging hardware-assisted security and IP core protection aspect of CE devices. In this book, we present for the first time “intellectual property core protection and hardware-assisted security” for CE. We define “hardware-assisted security” as the security/protection of hardware cores. Intellectual property cores of CE systems and hardware are designed to secure/protect the information processed by CE systems. The term “security” encapsulates a broad theme that covers many aspects including hardware security, protection, privacy, trustworthiness, and intellectual property protection and information security. The system security may refer to the security of the system (e.g., a specific CE device) that handles the data or information. Though there have been textbooks focusing on system security, hardware defense against malicious Trojan, however no textbook encompasses details of wide-spectrum hardware threats/attacks and its hardware-assisted defense mechanism. In this book, explicit focus has been made on hardware (IP core) Trojan, IoT security, hardware watermarking, hardware structural obfuscation, hardware functional obfuscation, hardware encryption, watermarking encryption hardware, forensic engineering, JPEG core, memory attacks, security, privacy, IP right in IoT and CE systems obfuscation, IP core fingerprinting, PUF, and several others.

Broadly, the theme of this book includes the following:

1.  Security aspects in IoT
    
2.  Hardware security/protection against Trojans
    
3.  Hardware security/IP core protection against reverse engineering attacks
    
4.  Symmetrical IP core protection of CE hardware
    
5.  Active and passive IP core protection by functional and structural obfuscation
    
6.  Forensic engineering-based protection of CE hardware
    
7.  Protection mechanisms of IC/IP buyer
    
8.  Protection mechanisms of IC/IP seller by watermarking and fingerprinting
    
9.  Hardware-assisted approaches for media and information security
    
10.  PUF-based security and protection methods of CE hardware
     

Chapter 1 presents an “Introduction to IP core protection and hardware-assisted security of consumer electronics.” The salient features of this chapter include providing a security perspective, defining hardware-assisted security, providing background on IP cores and its significance, necessity of security and protection of DSP kernels—with details on high-level synthesis framework and finally ending with hardware-assisted media protection.

Chapter 2 presents “Security in consumer electronics and Internet of things.” The salient features of this chapter include IoT architecture, challenges, and its applications; the big picture on security, privacy, IP right in IoT and CE systems; memory security, radio frequency identification (RFID) security; near field communications (NFC) security; smart healthcare and transportation security, firmware security, and finally ending with blockchain technology.

Chapter 3 presents “Trojan security-aware DSP IP core and integrated circuits.” The salient features of this chapter include types of hardware Trojan, hardware Trojan in a 3PIP module, Trojan security approaches, Trojan security-aware DSP kernel/IP core design process, and finally ending with analysis on case studies.

Chapter 4 presents “IP core and integrated circuit protection using robust watermarking.” The salient features of this chapter include introduction to hardware (IP core) watermarking, description of selected IP core watermarking approaches, design process of a watermarked IP core, properties of a hardware watermarking, and finally ending with analysis on case studies.

Chapter 5 presents “Symmetrical protection of DSP IP core/IC using fingerprinting and watermarking.” The salient features of this chapter include background on watermark and fingerprint, its associated threat model, fundamentals of IP core protection, symmetrical IP cores protection for DSP kernels, case study on symmetrical IP core protection, and finally ending with analysis on different DSP kernel test cases.

Chapter 6 presents “Computational forensic engineering (CFE) for resolving ownership conflict of DSP IP core.” The salient features of this chapter include overview on CFE for IP core protection, IP core feature extraction algorithms, important characteristics of customized CFE, and finally ending with analysis on case studies.

Chapter 7 presents “Structural obfuscation of DSP cores used in CE devices.” The salient features of this chapter include introduction to structural obfuscation, its associated threat model, relative perspective of logic, code, and structural obfuscation techniques, compiler transformation-driven structural obfuscation, design process of low-cost structurally obfuscated IP core, case study on multistage structural obfuscation, and finally ending with case studies on DSP kernels.

Chapter 8 presents “Functional obfuscation of DSP cores used in CE devices.” The salient features of this chapter include attack scenarios and threat model, selected functional obfuscation approaches for DSP IP core, design of functional obfuscated DSP IP core, security of functionally obfuscated DSP core design, optimization engine for functional obfuscation of DSP kernels, and finally concluding with analysis on DSP kernel case studies.

Chapter 9 presents “Obfuscation of JPEG CODEC IP core for CE devices.” The salient features of this chapter include the overview of JPEG compression and decompression process, design process of structurally obfuscated JPEG IP core, its associated threat model, formulation, optimization framework, implementation of JPEG CODEC IP core, and finally concluding with design analysis.

Chapter 10 presents “Advanced encryption standard (AES) and its hardware watermarking for ownership protection.” The salient features of this chapter include introduction to the AES algorithm, its description and custom hardware design, AES digital watermarking, process of embedding watermark in AES hardware, and finally ending with the design analysis.

Chapter 11 presents “Hardware approaches for media and information protection and authentication.” The salient features of this chapter include introduction to digital rights management (DRM), copyright protection of multimedia, hardware versus media protection, general framework for copyright protection, types of digital watermarks, applications of digital watermarks, desired characteristics of watermarks, hardware-based approaches for watermarking, dynamic watermarking in smart car, side-channel information leakage attacks and countermeasures, attacks on watermarks and watermarking systems, and finally ending with the limitations of watermarking.

Chapter 12 presents “Physical unclonable functions (PUFs).” The salient features of this chapter include principles of PUFs, properties or characteristics of PUFs, classification of PUFs, description of different types of PUFs such as ring oscillator based, static random access memory based, memristor based, diode based, magnetic based, practical implementations of PUF, case study of PUF, and finally ends with discussion on its issues and challenges.

This book aims to present novel solutions for any security/protection problems related to hardware used in CE. Authors believe that there is no book that presents details of numerous hardware-assisted security topics under one canopy. The theme is important for researchers and graduate students in different areas of specialization, as it encompasses overlapping contents of EDA-CAD, hardware design security, VLSI design (high-level synthesis, RTL, gate-level synthesis, etc.), IP core protection, optimization using evolutionary computing, system-on-chip design, and finally application-specific processor/hardware accelerator design for CE applications. All the aforesaid topics are encapsulated in the proposed theme where researchers, practitioners, industry experts, CAD/design engineers, system architects, and students are expected to show interest in reading.

The book offers theoretical exercise for each chapter. This presents abundant prospect to test the understanding for each security topic and hone readers understanding. The book is prepared keeping in mind that can be easily integrated to any master’s and Ph.D. level course as well as senior bachelor’s course. The book provides materials to train senior-level engineering students on hardware-assisted security topics. Furthermore, it also serves as designer’s handbook for a designer who is eager to learn designing secured hardware, especially IP core for DSP kernels. Each chapter also includes end-to-end design flow for secured IP core architecture from the perspective of different threat/attack models.

## *Chapter 1*  
**Introduction to IP core protection and hardware-assisted security of consumer electronics**

This chapter presents an overview of the book and discussions on topics that could serve as an introductory part toward the overall content of the book. It is assumed that the readers will have some subject knowledge on topics such as very large scale integration (VLSI), embedded systems, hardware design flow, etc., before adopting the section of this book.

### 1.1 Consumer electronics and security perspectives

Consumer electronics (CE), embracing high-end devices ranging from digital camera, multi-spectral camera, IP TV, smart tablets, night vision camera to smart meter, accompanied by data and communication know-how makes emerging smart cities and internet-of-things (IoT) a reality. In today’s world of CE and IoT, security, privacy, and protection of hardware and its information are increasingly becoming critically imperative. It is universally accepted that for IoT, security of underneath hardware is pivotal for its correct operation. The underlying hardware is affected by several threat factors. An adversary may generate secret exist that leaks crucial data such as encryption key employed in secure transmission line, the maker could meddle the design by implanting ‘hardware Trojans,’ or inserting artifacts with recognized dependable susceptibilities. Current generation designs and assimilates intellectual property (IP) blocks from manifold vendors, which are mass-produced and verified by diverse companies worldwide. Accordingly, numerous access points exist for any typical hardware and are prone to be attacked. For a trusted hardware design, defense of IP cores is of utmost importance and significance ([Sengupta and Kundu, 2017](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib26); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib27)).

A typical CE system ([Figure 1.1)](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig1) has digital signal processing (DSP), embedded processor, memory, system software, and application software. Significantly, various forms of attacks can occur to this CE system, i.e.: system security, information security, system privacy, information privacy, network security, firmware security, system trustworthiness, hardware IP rights, and information copyrights. The origins of all these attacks vary and are different, for example, they can be remote or local. They can be either attacked by software or hardware. They can attack either software or hardware components of the CE system. Thus, it is a quite challenging and difficult task for any system design engineer to ensure that the CE system that is being designed is completely full-proof. There is no single solution that can work for (1) overall system for all types of attacks and (2) for all types of hardware (e.g., digital, analog, and radio-frequency components). Thus, the protections from intellectual property rights (IPR) of both the hardware components and the information (including media) that a CE system processes needs different solutions. The chapter corresponding to this section will discuss the details of these attacks and explore the corresponding possible solutions for their mitigation. Moreover, many of these attacks and solutions will be discussed throughout the different chapters of this book. The hardware-assisted security is defined as the ‘security provided by hardware’ for: (1) information being processed, (2) hardware itself, and (3) overall system ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib27); [Mohanty 2018a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib10), [2018b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib14)). The hardware-assisted security solutions may be in different forms such as: (1) additional hardware components used for security, (2) hardware design modification performed, and (3) system design modifications performed ([Mohanty, 2018a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib10), [2018b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib14)). Overall, a system can be considered as trustworthy, if it incorporates security, privacy, and IP protection solutions during the design phase while obtaining the components from trusted vendors and trusted manufacturing units.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f01.jpg)

Figure 1.1 Consumer electronics components and security vulnerability

It is a well-known fact that the CE system is a heterogeneous combination of various types of hardware, software, and firmware and can be conceptualized as analog/mixed-signal system on a chip (AMS-SoC) ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib13)). CEs or CE system are essentially AMS-SoCs, and it includes almost everything, e.g., smart watch, smart camera, smart phone, smart car, smart healthcare device, etc. (see [Figure 1.1)](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig1). In the hardware-digital-hardware, analog hardware, RF hardware, and mixed-signal hardware are needed for various signal processing and communications that happens in the CE system. Memory is needed for buffer processing and storage. The software are system software, application software, and middleware. The security vulnerability can arise from any of these components of a typical CE system ([Mohanty, 2018a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib10), [2018b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib14)). This section will present a brief overview, and detailed discussions are presented in the corresponding chapters. The following sections discuss about hardware design flow and more specifically at the architecture level.

### 1.2 Hardware-assisted security and IP core protection

Currently, design age of CE devices comprises complex data/control intensive hardware such as DSP cores in the form of IP cores which depend on the integrated circuit (IC) supply chains globally. To enhance the design efficiency and improve the design speed, the use of IP cores for DSP applications in CE devices, normally provided by a third-party vendor, has turned into a typical exercise in the CE industry. Nonetheless, surging threats to security is prevalent and rising piracy concerns make global supply chains vulnerable ([Sengupta, 2015](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib20), [2016](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib19)). [Figure 1.2](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig2) shows the hardware threats in a typical system-on-chip design cycle comprising third-party IP (3PIP) cores. The first location is during the process of importing 3PIP cores from outside vendors and second location is at the foundry where copying of design netlist is performed. Thus, security is mandatory in these two locations. Furthermore, [Figure 1.3](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig3) shows the various elements in a chip design cycle which are trustworthy and untrustworthy by nature. Other forms of hardware threats such as infringement of IP core ownership, IP core buyer ownership, etc., are also possible which will be discussed in the latter half of this chapter and other chapters.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f02.jpg)

Figure 1.2 SoC design and fabrication including 3PIP cores indicating possible hardware vulnerabilities (Sengupta, 2017)

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f03.jpg)

Figure 1.3 Chip design flow used in CE devices indicating trustworthy and untrustworthy elements ([Sengupta, 2017a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib21), [2017b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib22))

In this book, we define ‘hardware-assisted security’ as the security/protection of hardware/IP core for DSP and multimedia applications in CE devices or information by a hardware/system of CE devices. The term ‘security’ encapsulates a broad theme that covers many aspects including hardware security, protection, privacy, trustworthiness, and IP core protection and information security. The terms ‘security’ depicts the security of a system (such as CE device) that handles the data or information. In a CE-based structure, defense of its hardware and IP cores is very essential. Therefore, the practice of using secured IPs becomes significant. In this age of smart cities, growing CE hardware design complexity is outpacing the designer yield, thus, resulting into bigger undertakings. Additionally, the present group of CE designs is enormously reliant on global IP supply chains. To upsurge the design productivity and to reduce the design time, the usage of IP cores often supplied by a third-party vendor has turned into a vital and *de-facto* practice in the industry. It is estimated that top counterfeits could have an impact of $300B on the semiconductor market. However, increasing threats to security and swelling piracy concerns do affect the global supply chains. Thus, information security that covers the security of data, information, and multimedia which are handled all the time by CE devices becomes important ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib27); [Mohanty 2018a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib10), [2018b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib14)).

### 1.3 Intellectual property (IP) cores/hardware

#### 1.3.1 Utility of IP cores in CE devices

The express intensification of silicon technology resulted into terrific upsurge in design complexity of CEs devices. In the realistic operation of multi-billion dollar foundries, more and more applications are unified on a single silicon die. Synchronously, demands of market have directed bigger design start-ups, reduced design time, and growing time-to-market burden. To defy these difficulties, IP cores, especially for complex DSP and multimedia applications, have become a pragmatic solution. An IP core once corroborated in a design with a specific process technology can be employed to other designs that use the identical process technology. In turn, this eradicates the necessity to embrace such a core in most of the system-level simulation testing, which in turn, decreases the intricacy of inclusive system design and verification. To provide a simple illustration, once a JPEG CODEC core or wavelet transformation core used in image compression is validated for a specific silicon process, it can be assimilated into SoC designs of other CE devices easily ([Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib19)).

#### 1.3.2 Why security and protection of hardware/IP cores?

Demands of sophisticated CE devices, including complex DSP/multimedia cores, have led to extensive usage of reusable IP cores. The swelling reuse of such complex IP cores inexorably uncovers them to perils of counterfeiting. Since an IP core can represent several years of design, R&D, and validation, a critical concern is how to safeguard this asset? and how can a counterfeit of a core be identified/prevented?

To the best of our knowledge, it is a fact that the privileges of the actual IP owner can be battered both deliberately and inadvertently. This can be conceivable by an abuse of the license treaty by deploying the IP core in numerous devices, when a solo license has been obtained. There can be a high enticement for a foundry or even to other IP-core makers to integrate a high-quality design into other system components where the actual licensing rule can prevents this. As the systems grow composite, there is a rising trend for IP core makers to sub-license other IP cores for including that in their designs, and once a design process has been finished, it is alluring to reuse it in other supplementary products that may not encompass the actual licensing. Another impending threat to IP cores is that of piracy, where by dishonest means or reverse engineering, direct stealing/copying of the IP for reuse without authorization are done. As a result of the IP theft, the attacker possibly may even claim the entitlement of the IP. Thus, a method of annulling dishonest claims of IP ownership is highly desirable. For the makers of the IP core or a whole-chip design, it is both problematic and costlier to demonstrate that their IP in the product has been employed unlawfully. In case of silicon chips, one of the realistic methods of identifying an IP core is to acquire an example of the product under test for sending to a professional laboratory for analysis. Furthermore, injection of any form from the third-party invasion in the hardware-design process may cultivate and result in serious security apprehension for CE hardware. Thus, safeguarding CE/IoT hardware can be realized as a protection of IP cores against dishonest entitlement of ownership. Another version of threat called ‘hardware Trojan’ is an act of intentionally injecting malicious logic into a design (such as IP core hardware) by an adversary in the vendor house, which will target detection/correction policies affecting security protocol. Both the hardware vulnerabilities, mentioned above, may occur in any of the design abstract levels. Pre-processing or post-processing style approach is defined based on the level at which security is employed, which is often driven by complexity of the DSP core. For example, in case of complex DSP/multimedia cores comprising gates in the order of 15K–50K, security approach during architectural (high-level) synthesis is more beneficial and fruitful ([Sengupta and Kundu, 2017](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib26)).

#### 1.3.3 Traditional forms of IP protection not enough?

For the last several years, various methodologies for the protection of such cores through patents, copyrights, trademarking, etc., have been employed. Yet, these approaches are not established adequately to shield the worth of IP cores used in CEs devices. The primary reason is the design costs of implementation; in addition, liability of proof to exhibit infringement is also too expensive. Besides, when it comes to the protection of reusable IP cores in CE industry, most of the IP core vendors trust on a combination of communal conviction of their business collaborators and privacy during operation.

### 1.4 IP core protection and hardware-assisted security of CE device—DSP core

As discussed earlier, at the core of a CE device, several DSP cores used for data intensive or control intensive functions are present. These DSP cores are IP cores in the form of SoC platform which are responsible for data processing of large chunks of data. For example, digital video cameras almost always have a second built-in microprocessor, dedicated to video calculations. This process is called as digital signal processor (DSP)—its role is to perform repetitive mathematical tasks in real time. In simpler terms, while our smart phone’s main microprocessor is checking to see if we have any incoming calls, second processor will simultaneously run the email in the background, manage Wi-Fi signal, check when video is coming through the lens, etc., and all such calculations are taken care by second dedicated processor, DSP core. A thematic example is shown in [Figure 1.4](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig4). As evident from this figure, the multimedia/DSP core (JPEG compression/decompression IP core) plays a significant role in the successful operation of a CE device. Similarly, other DSP cores such as discrete cosine transformation (DCT) core, fast Fourier transform (FFT), digital filters, etc., also play a critical role in CE device design. For example, FIR filter helps to improve the audio quality and the cellular infrastructure in the CE device. Protection of such complex DSP/multimedia cores relies on the high-level synthesis (i.e., architectural synthesis) as backbone design framework. This is because such complex DSP cores that comprise 15K–60K gates never initiates the design process from lower abstraction level. Furthermore, selecting/controlling the architecture of these DSP cores is seamlessly possible through high-level synthesis framework as it includes design space exploration (DSE) module (driven through intelligent evolutionary algorithms). This is not possible if these designs have to start from register-transfer (RT)/gate-level/lower levels.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f04.jpg)

Figure 1.4 DSP/multimedia core in CE device: digital camera

A protection/security mechanism of such complex cores is thus intertwined with the high-level synthesis design process. For such hardware, protection is mostly applied during higher levels of abstraction (i.e., during high-level synthesis). On the contrary, security/protection mechanism of less complex hardware such as adder, encoder, decoder, etc., can be performed at lower levels such as RT level/gate level, etc. [Figure 1.5](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig5) shows the classification of different hardware-assisted securities and IP core protection mechanisms at higher and lower levels of abstraction. As discussed, for DSP/multimedia cores such as infinite impulse response (IIR) filter, FIR, JPEG, etc., protection/security algorithms are applied at higher levels of abstraction which enables the constraints of the security algorithms to propagate to the lower levels also through RT level/gate level synthesis.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f05.jpg)

Figure 1.5. Hardware protection mechanisms

#### 1.4.1 Security and protection methodologies available for IP core/hardware

Some of the recognized protection mechanisms used extensively for DSP IP cores of CE designs that depend on the threat model/vulnerability are watermarking, fingerprinting, hardware metering, computational forensic engineering, Trojan security, structural obfuscation, functional obfuscation, physically unclonable functions (PUF), and patents/copyrights ([Alkabani *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib1); [Castillo *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib3); Christof and Jan, 2009; [Hong and Potkonjak, 1999](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib6); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib8); [Marvel, 2005](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib9); [Ni *et al.*, 2006](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib16); [Sengupta and Roy, 2018a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib24), [2018b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib25)). [Figure 1.6](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig6) shows an overview of threat models along with its hardware security countermeasures for CE device.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f06.jpg)

Figure 1.6 Overview of some common hardware threats and its countermeasures

**(i) IP core/hardware watermarking**: This hardware protection mechanism is employed when the hardware threat anticipated to be false claim of ownership. This threat model is basically because of ownership abuse or false claim of IP core ownership or piracy. Although watermarking protects against the aforesaid threats, it can only detect and not prevent the threats. In other words, watermarking approach is capable of providing passive form of protection to an IP core. More details on this protection mechanism are presented in Chapter 4.

**(ii) Computational forensic engineering (digital forensics) for IP cores**: This hardware protection mechanism is employed when the hardware threat under question is ownership abuse or false claim of IP core ownership or piracy. It has the same threat model as watermarking and provides the detection of the legal owner in case of ownership conflicts. The objective of computational forensic engineering (CFE) is to recognize the individual that produced the IP. It examines certain properties of a given IP and measures the probability that a particular individual has produced it. The CFE method identifies from a group of synthesis tool, the one which is employed to make a specific IP design. It is to be noted that this approach is also capable of providing passive forms of protection to an IP core. More details on this protection mechanism are presented in Chapter 6.

**(iii) Hardware metering**: This is the method of monitoring an IC. Some of the effective methods are to physically identify serial numbers on chips or storing unique identifiers in its memory ([Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib2); [Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib18)). The taxonomy of hardware metering is shown in [Figure 1.7](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig7). Hardware metering can be broadly classified into two categories: non-functional and functional. In non-functional identification method, a unique ID is created that is separate from the chip functionality. However, it can have the following drawbacks:

1.  Vulnerability to cloning and/or removal;
    
2.  Once chip is tagged, foundry can copy same tag on other chips or simply remove tag so chip cannot be traced;
    
3.  Possibility to overproduction;
    
4.  Foundry can produce multiple chips with same tag;
    
5.  Out of millions of chips, probability of finding two matching tags is small.
    

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f07.jpg)

Figure 1.7 Taxonomy of hardware metering methods

Non-functional identifiers in hardware metering are sub-classified into two types: (1) reproducible and (2) unclonable. Reproducible identifiers are a unique ID stored inside a chip package, die, or a chip memory. They can be in the form of indented serial number or digitally stored serial number. Its advantages are that it does not depend on randomness and are easy to track/identify. Disadvantages are that it is easy to clone/modify and easy to overproduce. On the other hand, unclonable non-functional identifiers can use extrinsic or intrinsic methods for metering. For example, intrinsic method may use IC leakage, power, timing, path signatures, etc., which are all unique due to process variations. This method does not need any additional logic and can be used as such on existing designs. On the contrary, extrinsically unclonable non-functional identifiers uses additional logic such as PUF which is a structure comprising ring of oscillators (RO) capable of generating random values due to process variations. PUFs are impacted by power supply noise, temperature, delay, etc.; therefore, the values will keep on changing constantly. The other class of metering method is functional identifier-based metering. This method links identifiers to chip’s internal functional details during the synthesis process. Some of the properties are:

*   Each chip’s function gets a unique signature;
    
*   Additional states added generate same output;
    
*   Function unchanged from input to output;
    
*   Internal transactions unique to each chip.
    

The above methods discussed so far in the context of hardware metering are all passive metering methods. There exists an active metering method which uses external-locking techniques to lock IC. Some of the properties of active metering methods are:

*   This technique tries to allow IP owner to have control over;
    
*   Uses key encryption to lock correct functionality of a chip;
    
*   At the gate level, XOR gates are placed on selected non-critical paths;
    
*   Requires that every chip be activated with an external key. Only IP owner can generate key ([Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib2); [Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib18)).
    

**(iv) IP core/hardware fingerprinting**: This hardware protection mechanism is employed when the hardware threat anticipated is false claim of ownership by the IP seller/vendor or illegal redistribution of extra copies without the knowledge of the IP buyer. The threat model is unlawful redistribution/resell of IP core copies in the market by a dishonest IP seller ([Hong and Potkonjak, 1999](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib6)). Thus, IP core fingerprinting protects against the ownership abuse of IP buyer. Although fingerprinting protects against the aforesaid threats, it can only detect and not prevent the threats. In other words, fingerprinting approach is capable of providing passive forms of protection to an IP core. More details on this protection mechanism are presented in Chapter 5.

**(v) IP core/hardware obfuscation and encryption:** This hardware protection mechanism is employed when the hardware threat anticipated is IP netlist theft/counterfeit/piracy through reverse engineering. There are two types of hardware obfuscation methodologies: (1) structural obfuscation and (2) functional obfuscation. In structural obfuscation, the goal is to enhance the reverse engineering complexity to make it more challenging for an attacker to discover the actual functionality of an IP core from its transformed structure. On the contrary, in functional obfuscation, the goal is to disable the IP core through ‘keys’ such that normal functionality of the obfuscated design can only be enabled by the successful application of a single pre-determined key or a series of covert keys at the input; otherwise, an IP core design will operate in a mode, which will exhibit incorrect functionality. Both these types of obfuscation methods aim to provide protection against IP infringement and Trojan insertion. Structural obfuscation is regarded as a ‘passive’ form of obfuscation as it does not affect the functionality of the IP core, while only making syntactic changes, i.e., modifying the circuit description in a soft form such that it becomes challenging for an attacker to understand the internal working of an IP core. A major shortcoming of the passive approach is that it does not change the black-box functionality of a design, and hence unable to avert potential usage of an IP as black-box in a design. However, since it does not add extra-locking circuitry to the IP core, the chances of design overhead is lower than active approaches which makes it an equally attractive choice in CE industry. More detail on this protection mechanism is presented in Chapters 7 and 8.

**(vi) Trojan security/detection of an IP core:** Hardware Trojan in the context of IP cores is a malicious alteration of logic inside IP core that causes to change its functionality such that under rare event condition, the IP core produces wrong output. This hardware protection mechanism is employed to safeguard against hardware Trojan secretly hidden inside a 3PIP cores used in SoC integration. Due to globalization of IC design chain, involvement of third-party IP cores play a crucial role in the mass production of CE devices in stricter time to market pressure. Trojan security of DSP IP cores can be achieved through dual modular redundancy technique during system-on-chip integration running concurrently with an optimization framework. This enables detection of hardware Trojan that causes functional change. More detail on this protection mechanism is presented in Chapter 3.

**(vii) Physically unclonable functions**: PUF is a ‘digital fingerprint’ that serves as a unique identity for the hardware. It acts as hardware security primitive due to its complexity and the unpredictability between its outputs and the applied inputs. PUFs are based on physical variations which occur naturally during semiconductor manufacturing and which make it possible to differentiate between otherwise identical hardware. Because of the random process variations, no two ICs even with same layout are identical. There are various types of PUFs, such as: (1) *Latch PUFs* where the output changes due to intrinsic property of the latch; (2) *SRAM PUF* where the initial power up values of the SRAM cells are random; (3) *Ring of oscillator (RO) delay-based PUF* where the path delay is unpredictable due to manufacturing variation; and (4) *Arbiter PUF* where the path delay is unpredictable due to physical randomness. In arbiter PUF, each challenge selects a unique pair of delay gates. Random process variation determines which path is faster ([Potkonjak and Goudar, 2014](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib17)). More detail on this protection mechanism is presented in Chapter 12.

**(viii) Hardware**\-**based encryption:** Another hardware protection mechanism for securing classified data used in CE device is hardware-based encryptions. Hardware-based encryption process can be used for securing data storage and transfer, as well as for DSP IP core protection in the context of CE devices. Advanced encryption standard (AES) ([Paar and Pelzl, 2009](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib4)) is the most robust encryption process that can be used as the hardware-based encryption of classified data as well as in DSP IP core protection from external attacks. More detail on this protection mechanism is presented in Chapter 10.

**(ix) Patent and copyright**: A patent is an authorized privilege sanctioned by the government of a specific dominion which on submission safeguards the IP of the maker and thus can only be sold and used by the approval of the owner. More explicitly, the owner is given the constitutional privilege to thwart others from commercially abusing the invention. It is the owner’s right to report the case of any contravention under civil law ([Sengupta, 2015](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib20)).

IP protection that relates to printed publications as well as in any form of public communication such as TV broadcasting, and hardware systems for storing, is called ‘Copyright.’ It shields the maker in terms of privileges in creative works against fraud who aim to plagiarize ([Sengupta, 2015](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib20)).

#### 1.4.2 Different IP core protection and hardware-assisted security mechanisms: advantages and disadvantages

##### 1.4.2.1 Hardware metering vs. hardware watermarking

In hardware watermarking, a secret signature is chosen which is implanted on the original design. In IP metering, a distinctive identifier (ID) is injected into the product for validating any unlicensed copy made. In case of watermarking, a design-inspection step is required during signature detection process. IP metering also includes a design-inspection step as the ID is accessible by reading some registers or trivial I/O access. Furthermore, implanting a watermark is certainly secure for cases of false claim of ownership or IP piracy as only the owner can evidently validate the enactment of a secret watermark. Similarly, IP metering is also effective for identifying the IP piracy and for reckoning the likely measure of piracy, which makes it extremely significant in court proceedings to endorse assessments of compensations.

Design-overhead may follow due to implanting a concealed signature in the original IP core, in case of hardware watermarking. This also depends on the type of signature selected and its size. But, in case of IP metering, the design-overhead is non-existent or nominal, as a trivial area of the IP-core is re-configured for each designed/manufactured hardware. IP metering only comprises modification in configuration in a tiny segment of the design.

In the context of DSP IP cores, watermarking techniques are mostly implanted before the RT level synthesis, i.e., as a pre-processing or during in-synthesis, i.e., signature is implanted during the execution of the high-level synthesis process. On the contrary, IP metering is generally executed post-layout or during manufacturing, through memory programming or indenting serial number on device body. During watermark, care should be exercised so that the signature insertion does not damage the functionality of the design and hampers its quality. There is a clear tradeoff in case of watermarking with respect to robustness vs. design overhead. In other words, larger size watermark is certainly more robust but may incur more design overhead. None of these parameters are present for metering ([Sengupta, 2015](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib20)).

##### 1.4.2.2 Hardware obfuscation vs. hardware watermarking

Hardware obfuscation is completely different than hardware watermarking of IP core. In hardware obfuscation, the circuit description of the IP core is deliberately obscured either through encryption or by introducing unreadability in the circuit structure, so that the reverse engineering process becomes significantly harder. On the contrary, hardware watermarking introduces ownership information in a concealed manner within the IP core design itself, so that when required, legal ownership of the rightful owner can be proved. Although the threat models of both these protection mechanisms are slightly different, hardware watermarking can be used in unification with hardware obfuscation. In an obfuscated design, watermarking can be effective in providing a next line of defense against unlicensed copying efforts. Both these protection methods may incur design overhead, if not properly implanted/performed.

##### 1.4.2.3 Computational forensic engineering vs. hardware watermarking

Computational forensic engineering for IP core protection employs a set of digital forensic evidences to infer the rightful owner. It is a signature-free approach, unlike hardware watermarking for IP core protection. Furthermore, as CFE does not employ signature for resolving IP ownership conflicts, it has zero chance of quality degradation on the original design. Additionally, no extra care is needed for CFE as it does not disturb the functionality of the design. Yet, the general process to execute CFE is more composite than watermarking as it warrants cognizance on the various phases of statistics collection, feature extraction, clustering, and validation. Thus, CFE incurs more time complexity when compared with watermarking in case of DSP IP cores.

#### 1.4.3 HLS (architectural synthesis) as design backbone for implementing security algorithms for DSP IP cores

As DSP/multimedia IP cores depend on high level synthesis (HLS) design framework as its backbone, the security/protection algorithms are mostly in-synthesis by nature, i.e., the security constraints/techniques are performed during the high-level synthesis itself. Before reading the subsequent chapters that deal with the details of the security methodologies for DSP cores, it is important to review and study the high-level synthesis design process in this chapter itself. This sub-section will present an overview of the generic HLS design/tool flow for DSP/multimedia cores. The design flow shown in [Figure 1.8](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig8) is broadly applicable to any modern HLS methodology/HLS tool such as Vivado HLS (Vivado User Guide, 2018; [Xilinx, 2018](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib29)). The HLS flow can be used to design and secure any complex IP core such as FIR filter, IIR Butterworth filter, high/low-pass digital filter, DCT, inverse DCT, decimation in time, FFT, Haar wavelet transformation, JPEG compression, JPEG decompression, band pass filter, MPEG motion vectors, H.264, etc.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f08.jpg)

Figure 1.8 Overview of generic HLS design/tool flow

A typical HLS design flow accepts a DSP application in the form of C-code and converts it into a graphical representation called control data flow graph through parsing. Along with this application, HLS also accepts the technology library of modules based on which the design evaluation is performed. The technology library information is based on a particular technology scale and comprises details of silicon area, delay, power, etc., of a unit module. Once a control data flow graph (CDFG) is obtained after parsing the C-code, it then undergoes a series of transformations to convert it into an optimized form. These series of transformations can be compiler driven or Boolean function driven by nature. This optimized CDFG accepts HLS pragmas/directives to pass the information to the DSE system in HLS. The first step of DSE system is operation scheduled, which also accepts its own set of HLS pragmas/directives as well as scheduled configuration to assign time (cycle) stamp to each operation. Examples of directives at this step include chaining, multi-cycling, data pipelining, functional pipelining, loop unrolling, etc. This is followed by resource allocation and binding phase which also accepts its own set of directive for executing spatial constraint to functional resources. Binding enables sharing/reuse of functional hardware resources for multiple operations. Subsequently, register allocation is performed through its own set of HLS directive to obtain an optimal number of register sets required for implementing the application in hardware. Once these phases are over, then the determination of datapath is performed by analyzing the I/O connectivity, multiplexers, demultiplexers, etc., based on the datapath obtained, and the timing sequence for the generation of control path is determined. This yields cycle-by-cycle execution details of each hardware resource. Both the datapath and controller are described in hardware description language (HDL) and finally integrated to form the RTL system schematic/HDL description of the DSP/multimedia application. As the security algorithms/features of DSP IP cores are integrated during one or more HLS synthesis steps, hence understanding the HLS design framework is crucial. More details on HLS design process are available in [Sengupta and Mohanty (2016)](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib23).

### 1.5 Hardware-assisted media protection

The idea of ownership right, copyright, or IPR that a CE system can be subjected to is depicted in [Figure 1.9](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig9). As far as ownership right is concerned, the common factor of hardware, software, overall CE system, or media piracy is the loss of revenue of the actual or legal owner. But, these ownership issues/attacks are diverse, and correspondingly solutions to be deployed may differ. The hardware IP core protection aspects which are results of hardware piracy have been discussed in previous sections. Overall, system piracy or cloning is also a problem in the CE area, due to which multiple fake CE systems such as cameras, USB drives, hardware components for smart cars, fake batteries, are available in black market. These may be cheap, and user may think that he/she got a good deal, without having a knowledge that these would have lots of wrong implications. For example, a cloned/fake hardware may be providing a backdoor entry to the CE system that uses such hardware. Imagine, the case of a smart car, a hacker through this back door can get access to the smart car and take control of it. This can lead to fatal consequences, e.g., an attacker/hacker can create accidents. Similarly, a fake/cloned battery can be a safety hazard for the CE system as a bad battery can explode and catch fire, examples of all such several case scenarios are available in the Internet. Use of pirated software also can have potential backdoor for the hackers to take control over the system. Every CE system processes data, information, video, audio, and game in every second of its active state ([Mohanty, 2017a](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib11), [2017b](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib12)). It is estimated that the sensors, social networks, web pages, image and video applications, and mobile devices generate more than 2.5 quintillion bytes (i.e., 10^(18) bytes) data per day ([Mohanty *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib15)). This will be further complicated as smart cities initiatives around the world take momentum in which IoT with billions of connective devices process data throughout the day and night. It is rightly said that ***it is not oil rather it is data that is the new gold***. In terms of media piracy video, audio have impact on the entertainment industry, online streaming companies, and various-related industry in terms of revenue loss. In the chapter corresponding to this ownership matters, discussions will be presented on the hardware-assisted solutions for media protection. Both software-based and hardware-based solutions are possible, but hardware provides advantages in terms of real-time performance and protection right from the source-end to consumer-end.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f09.jpg)

Figure 1.9 Concept of ownership right, copyright, or intellectual property (IP) rights

### 1.6 Physical unclonable functions

It is a fact that most of the security, privacy, and IP rights solutions are based on some forms of encryption, scrambling, hashing, and watermarking. These mechanisms rely on some form of random number or pseudorandom number. It is a fact that a general-purpose processor, which is a deterministic machine, computes the next instruction based on a program counter that cannot generate true random numbers. Also, the keys random/pseudorandom numbers typically are stored in the memory or drives for possible use in future. Hacking a system is a matter of time only, and it is possible for a hacker to get access to it and consequently access to the system and information that it contains. Primitive PUF hardware generates a random number on the fly as shown in [Figure 1.10](#Chapter1.html#c01_fig10) and completely eliminate the need of storing keys on a hard-drive, thus making it secure ([Yanambaka *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib30), [2018](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib31); [Joshi *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter1.html#c01_bib7)). A PUF relies on the variations at the physical level of the IC which is originated due to the nanoscale semiconductor manufacturing. Thus, PUF makes good use of the process variations instead of a designer trying to reduce the impact of the process variations on the IC. The output generated by a particular PUF is unique to it, and hence serves like a signature of it. The PUF chapter will discuss on topics such as PUF principles, various types of PUFs, and applications of PUFs.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-01-f10.jpg)

Figure 1.10 Concept of physical unclonable function (PUF)

### 1.7 Organization of the book

This section summarizes the roadmap of the book in terms of overview of the organization of the expected content.

**Chapter 2** presents the broad overview as well as some specifics on security, privacy, and ownership protection in the context of CEs and IoT. It presents a broad perspective of IoT and CE including its driving technology and challenges. It further discusses about security and privacy in IoT/CE systems with an emphasis on the attacks and its countermeasure, memory security, radio frequency identification (RFID) security, smart healthcare, and smart transportation security.

**Chapter 3** presents the details on hardware Trojan security aware DSP IP core/IC. The chapter includes introduction to the concepts, followed by features of the Trojan-secured methodology—that includes threat model, description of features, and advantages of performing Trojan security at higher abstraction level. The next sections of this chapter comprises an example of hardware Trojan inside 3PIP module, discussion on selected Trojan security approaches, goal/models/problem formulation of a Trojan security aware DSP IP core, and the detailed description of its design process. Subsequently, the implementation and results are presented, followed by conclusion and questions and exercise for the learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 4** presents the details on how to protect a DSP IP core/IC using robust watermarking. The chapter includes introduction to watermarking, description of selected watermarking approaches, design process of watermarked IP core/hardware—including threat model, explanation on single-phase and multi-phase watermarks, followed by discussion on desirable properties of a watermark and threat scenarios. Subsequently, details on implementation and results are provided—that includes security analysis and design cost/overhead analysis. The chapter end with a conclusion of the concepts learnt and some exercise for the learners/practitioners.

**Chapter 5** presents the details on symmetrical protection of DSP IP core/IC using fingerprinting and watermarking. The chapter includes introduction to the problem and concepts on symmetrical protection, description of background on fingerprinting and watermarking, followed by threat models and benefits of providing symmetrical protection at higher design abstraction level. The next sub-sections focus on the fundamentals of IP core protection, process of implanting symmetrical IP core protection, and finally finishing with a motivation example of this approach. Subsequently, implementation and results are presented, followed by conclusion and exercise questions for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 6** presents the forensic engineering for resolving IP core ownership problem. The chapter includes introduction to the concept, followed by the description of the customized CFE approach for IP core protection. The next sub-sections focus on IP core feature extraction algorithms, followed by implementation and results. Finally, the chapter concludes with an inference, followed by exercise questions for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 7** presents the structural obfuscation of DSP IP cores used in CE devices. The chapter includes the introduction to the concept, followed by the description of its threat model and benefits of obfuscation at higher abstraction layer. The next sub-sections focus on the fundamentals of obfuscation for IP core protection, process of structural obfuscation, and generation of low-cost obfuscated IP core design. Subsequently, a motivational example is presented, followed by the details of implementation and results. The chapter ends with a conclusion and exercise questions for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 8** presents the description of functional obfuscation of DSP cores used in CE devices. The chapter encompasses the following—introduction to the concepts, discussion on selected functional obfuscation approaches, followed by the explanation of the design process of the functionally obfuscated DSP core and security view point—analysis and attack scenarios—of the functionally obfuscated DSP core. The next sections of this chapter presents optimization engine for deriving the low-cost/optimal functionally obfuscated DSP core architecture, implementation and results, and finally ending with the conclusion and questions and exercise for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 9** presents the details on a real-world complex application—obfuscation of JPEG CODEC IP core for CE devices. The chapter includes introduction to the concepts, overview of JPEG compression/decompression process, followed by design process of an obfuscated JPEG IP core design—including threat models and detailed design steps. The next sub-sections focus on the implementation of the design, presentation of the results and conclusion. Finally, the chapter ends with exercise questions for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 10** presents the details on AES and its hardware watermarking for ownership protection. The chapter starts with the introduction to the concepts, followed by the description of AES algorithm—encompassing overview of AES, custom hardware design, and its digital watermarking. Next, results are presented for watermarked AES hardware, followed by conclusion and exercise questions for learners and practitioners.

**Chapter 11** presents the details on the protection and authentication of media content with emphasis on the hardware vs. media protection, digital rights management (DRM), copyright protection of multimedia as well as general framework of multimedia watermarking, its applications, challenges, attacks, and countermeasures.

**Chapter 12** presents the details on the PUF with an emphasis on its properties, classification, and discussion on different types of PUF based on security, structure, and fabrication. It also presents the details on the implementations of PUF, challenges, and other issues on PUF.

### 1.8 Conclusions

This chapter introduced ‘hardware-assisted security and IP core protection’ in the context of CE systems. Various types of security threats are briefly summarized from an overall system point of view. It also presented an overview of different IP core protection and hardware-assisted security techniques, with its pros and cons. Through the help of a real-life CE design, the significance of DSP core was explained along with the different hardware threats possible on DSP IP cores. The chapter also summarized the roadmap of this book—including the expected contents of each chapter from a reader’s perspective.

## *Chapter 2*  
**Security in consumer electronics and internet of things (IoT)**

In a typical consumer electronics generation, diverse forms of attacks exist, e.g., system security, information security, information privacy, system trustworthiness, hardware IP protection, information copyright protection. Each of the attacks have their own threats and serve different purposes. Objective of this chapter is to differentiate each of these attacks in the context of internet of things (IoT). IoT is a very hot, trending topic of research, where different devices, sensors, and computers are connected to a network, collect data, and process for different purposes. A network of devices and sensors connected to the cloud can complete many unimaginable tasks, and without the existence of cloud, almost all task would have been very difficult to achieve and complete. Since, most connectivity occurs in cloud, there is always a probability of security and privacy threats. Because all types of the different devices are connected to the internet, attackers pose a huge threat to the system. For example, if any electronic system that is responsible for home care, healthcare, running an entire city, etc., are attacked, then the consequence of this threat will be a major catastrophe.

This chapter is organized as follows: Section 2.1 presents an introduction and broad overview of IoT; Section 2.2 presents a broad view of security, energy, and cost trade-offs in consumer electronic systems; Section 2.3 presents different security threats and solutions to the memory modules of the system; Section 2.4 provides different threats and solutions to the radio-frequency identification (RFID) modules; Section 2.5 provides security flaws and how to mitigate them in an near-field communication (NFC) module of the system; Section 2.6 discusses different security flaws in the smart vehicles, the autonomous cars, and the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs); Section 2.7 discusses different ways on how an attacker can attack a healthcare device and provides solutions for some of the attacks; Section 2.8 discusses the threats on firmware of the devices; and Section 2.9 discusses the emerging technology of blockchain, its advantages, and issues. The conclusion and future directions are presented in Section 2.10.

### 2.1 Internet of things (IoT) – a broad overview

Communication has evolved in the world at a very fast and rapid pace. Several solutions have been proposed for communications, short or long distance. Technological growth also helped this in developing high-performance computing devices, making it a necessity to look for newer inventions. One of the such major creation is ‘internet of things’ and this has become an integral part of everyday life. There are many definitions for IoT that differs depending upon the individual’s perspective. In an IoT environment, all the devices or ‘THINGS’ are connected to a network and exchange data among themselves or send to the cloud ([Mohanty *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter2.html#c02_bib57)). The concept of ‘3-I’ in the context of IoT is shown in [Figure 2.1](#Chapter2.html#c02_fig1), which includes. ‘Interconnection,’ ‘Intelligence,’ and ‘Instrumentation.’ These three are the important aspects of an IoT environment, as illustrated in the figure pertaining to the smart city environment. Interconnection is the communication platform that provides the network for the devices and Internet connection that helps in transmitting the data among themselves or to the cloud services, where post-processing take place. Intelligence is the brain of the entire environment, and Instrumentation refers to various devices and sensors that are present in the environment. There are various devices present in an IoT environment such as microcontrollers, single board computers, and sensors. Each of them should have a unique IP address to be considered as a THING for the IoT ([Mohanty, 2018](#Chapter2.html#c02_bib55)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-02-f01.jpg)

Figure 2.1 Smart cities 3 ‘I’s

An IoT can be defined as Any TIME connection, Any THING connection, and Any PLACE Connection as shown in [Figure 2.2](#Chapter2.html#c02_fig2) ([IEEE, 2015](#Chapter2.html#c02_bib35)). IoT is not localized to one location, but it is omnipresent and can be felt anywhere. Some of the IoT devices can be deployed in places where they are not monitored continuously. Its role is to monitor a parameter and transmit the data over the air ([Yanambaka *et al.*, 2016a](#Chapter2.html#c02_bib111)). In such cases, it should be continuously connected to the internet which needs ‘Any PLACE Connection,’ ‘Any TIME Connection,’ and ‘Any THING Connection.’ With the technological advancements, various devices and board are attaining communication capabilities which can help in implementing an IoT environment at a very low cost.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-02-f02.jpg)

Figure 2.2 Definition of internet of things

#### 2.1.1 IoT – architecture

The structure of an IoT solution is described in its architecture. It includes various aspects including physical, the THINGS and virtual, the communication protocols. The IoT architecture is shown in [Figure 2.3](#Chapter2.html#c02_fig3). As shown in the figure, the IoT architecture contains three different aspects which are connected to each-other by Internet.
