## *Chapter 4*  
**IP core and integrated circuit protection using robust watermarking**

This chapter discusses robust watermarking approaches for the ownership protection of hardware cores \[a.k.a. intellectual property (IP) cores\]. Watermarking ensures some additional attributes inserted in the hardware core such a way that it can be used to verify ownership of the hardware core when required. Robust watermarking approaches have been discussed as these are resilient to various attacks that happen in global supply chain for various reasons. The remaining chapter is structured as follows: Section 4.2 provides an overview on selected hardware/IP core watermarking approaches; Section 4.3 discusses design process of watermarked IP core; Section 4.4 analyses the hardware watermarking approaches on case studies/test cases; and finally, Section 4.5 draws the conclusion.

### 4.1 Introduction

A watermark is a secret mark implanted into an entity such as official documents, currency notes, postal stamps, audio/video files, etc., to protect ownership right of an owner. Usually, a watermark embedded into an entity is expected to preserve its quality and functionality. However, for the domains in which watermarking is applied such as audio/video, documents, etc., slight degradation of the quality is usually noticed. Given the advantages of a watermark, it may be considered an extremely useful tool for protecting hardware \[e.g., digital signal processor (DSP) core\] ownership as well. However, the prime difference from watermarking in other domains is zero tolerance toward modification of quality/functionality of the hardware design. This makes hardware watermarking challenging but extremely useful for protecting legal rights of an IP vendor/owner. It is widely acknowledged that complex consumer electronics (CE) system design relies heavily on DSP IP cores realized as system-on-chip (SoC). Thus, hardware watermarking plays an integral role in IP core protection of CE devices ([Mohanty *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib11); [Voyatzis and Pitas, 1999](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib23); [Cox *et al.*, 2006](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib4); [Roy *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib13); [Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib16); Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011; Sengupta *et al*., 2013).

In the modern era of CE, use of DSP IP cores in global supply chains become an inexorable part of complex SoC design process. IP cores not only speedup the design productivity massively but also decreases the design period immensely. Importing these IP cores from third-party IP vendors by the system integrator or SoC designer has become a common industry practice. Previously, IP vendors have mainly focused on IP performance and IP functionality but have neglected IP security. As evidence it can be observed that in a typical IP design flow, measurement of performance and functionality is only included in the IP specification. However, prevailing usage of IP cores in SoC design process increases the rivalry between multiple IP core vendors, which invites security threats like IP core forgery, dishonest claim of ownership, etc., which can be tackled by hardware watermarking. Thus, the threat model can be defined as:

*Threat model*: The targeted threat models for watermark-based IP core protection mechanism are: (i) false claim of ownership, (ii) ownership conflict, and (iii) IP piracy/forgery in IP cores.

The designing process of an IP core involves many man-hours of research, investment, and substantiation; therefore, this effort must be protected. As IP core can be copied easily, IP piracy and ownership abuse is a rising security concern now. Hence, protecting the ownership of an original IP owner is very crucial. For example, after importing an IP core from a third-party IP vendor, a SoC integrator may claim himself as the original owner of the IP or may reuse the IP core without acknowledging the original IP owner. Thus, nullifying false claim of ownership or detecting the illegal misuse of an IP core is essential and complex for an original IP owner. One popular way to safeguard an IP core against aforementioned potential threats is embedding vendor signature in the IP core during its design process in the vendor house itself ([Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2008](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib1); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8); [Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib15); [Guajardo *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib7); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib21); Sengupta and Roy, 2017).

### 4.2 Selected watermarking approaches

This section discusses few selected watermarking mechanisms for IP core protection. Ziener and Teich ([2008](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib24)) devised an IP core watermarking methodology for field programmable gate array (FPGA) architecture. The IP owner signature as a watermark is embedded in the netlist and the bit-stream file of the IP core. The watermarking algorithm embeds the signature into the functional part of the IP core in such a way that it becomes challenging to remove the watermark without destroying the IP core. The signature is identified from the power supply pins of the watermarked FPGA. More specifically, the authors have devised a signature detection algorithm that decodes the watermark through voltage trace with high reliability. Additionally, two robustness enhancement algorithms are also devised so that the signature can be decoded correctly in the presence of significant noise. The overview of Ziener and Teich ([2008](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib24)) approach is shown in [Figure 4.1](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig1). Two in-synthesis IP core watermarking methodology: a low-cost watermark and a costless watermark are possible ([Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib9)). The vendor signature in the form of a watermark is embedded based on the ‘temporally free’ IP output slot. In low-cost watermarking approach, the watermark is characterized by a set of arbitrarily selected internal computation values of the IP which get transferred through a ‘temporally free’ output slot. In costless watermarking approach, the watermark uses dynamic transient outputs unit to drive selected data to the output ports when the slots are temporarily free which can be achieved by modifying the IP control. As high level synthesis (HLS) tools design a control unit using a finite state machine, therefore, the costless watermarking approach only influences the finite state machine of an IP core. The desired mathematic relations used to generate watermarked IP core can be validated using equality-checking tests of the ‘temporally free’ IP output slots. A watermark can be represented as ([Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib9)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c04_eqn1.gif)

where *M*[*i*](*n*) indicates *i*th sub-mark or mathematical function and *C*[*i*] indicates the clock cycle number during which the sub-mark is sent to a ‘temporally free’ IP output port. Different DSP applications are used as the benchmark to embed this watermarking approach and the result is compared with the approach ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) in terms of area and timing overhead. The overview of Le Gal and Bossuet ([2012](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib9)) approach is shown in [Figure 4.2](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig2).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f01.jpg)

Figure 4.1 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Ziener and Teich ([2008](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib24))

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f02.jpg)

Figure 4.2 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Le Gal and Bossuet ([2012](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib9))

Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) devised a dynamic watermarking process to shield a DSP IP core ([Coussy *et al.*, 2009](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib3)). A set of design and timing constraints in the form of vendor watermark is embedded in the IP core. In this approach, a vendor’s signature is transformed into its equivalent binary form where each digit (0 or 1) indicates a watermarking constraint. More specifically, these watermarking constraints are embedded in register allocation and binding phase. This is achieved by adding additional edges in the equivalent colored interval graph (CIG) of the IP design. In a CIG, each node indicates a storage variable. The lifetime of a storage variable lies between the time it is created (value written into it) and the last use (value read from it). An edge between two nodes indicates there is an overlap in lifetime between those storage variables. The color of the node indicates the allocated register of that corresponding storage variable. Therefore, two storage variables whose lifetimes overlap cannot be stored in the same register. In other words, two nodes having a common edge between them cannot have same node color. Thus, adding additional edges in the CIG as watermarking constraints will force to execute two storage variables in two different registers. The overview of Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) approach is shown in [Figure 4.3](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig3).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f03.jpg)

Figure 4.3 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Koushanfar et al. ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8))

Unlike dual variable (0 and 1) signature encoding rule in Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)), Sengupta and Bhadauria (2016) devised a single phase multi-variable (combination of four) watermarking methodology to protect a reusable IP core. Each variable which carries a unique encoding rule (unknown to an attacker) adds an additional edge between two node pair in the CIG. Thus, Sengupta *et al.* (2016) embed a more robust and tamper-proof watermark compared with Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)). Due to insertion of watermarking constraints in both Sengupta *et al.* (2016) and Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) area overhead may occur. Therefore, to minimize the design cost, a low-cost design solution is explored through particle swarm optimization in Sengupta *et al.* (2016). The embedded signature can be detected by inspecting the datapath hardware description language (HDL) file of the watermarked IP. As the encoding rules are hidden to an attacker, it is almost impossible to identify the watermarking constraints from its datapath. The overview of Sengupta *et al.* (2016) approach is shown in [Figure 4.4](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig4).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f04.jpg)

Figure 4.4 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Sengupta et al. (2016)

Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) devised a triple-phase watermarking process to secure a DSP IP core (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011). In this approach, vendor signature consists of 7-variables. The IP owner signature as watermarking constraints is embedded in three dissimilar (but interconnected) phases of HLS, i.e., scheduling phase, hardware allocation phase, and register allocation phase. Due to insertion of watermarking constraints in three different phases, vendor signature is distributed throughout the IP core design. Thus, complete removal or malicious alteration of the watermark is extremely difficult. Besides, embedding 7-variable encoding makes this approach tremendously strong. Additionally, the watermark in scheduling phase is independent of the watermark in hardware allocation and register allocation phase. Similarly, the watermark in register allocation phase is independent of both scheduling and hardware allocation phase watermarks. Due to these benefits, the triple-phase watermarking approach is tremendously robust as well as tamper resistant. The embedded signature can be detected by inspecting the datapath and controller HDL file of the watermarked IP. As the watermarking constraints are well dispersed in the IP design and the encoding rules are hidden to an attacker, it is extremely difficult to identify the watermarking constraints from its datapath and controller by an adversary. The overview of Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) approach is shown in [Figure 4.5](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig5).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f05.jpg)

Figure 4.5 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Sengupta et al. ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22))

### 4.3 Design process of watermarked IP core/hardware

As mentioned earlier, IP/hardware watermarking is a process of embedding owner’s signature covertly in the design of an IP/hardware to proof his/her ownership in case of any conflict ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib21)). In this section, we discuss problem formulation and design process of two (i.e., single-phase and triple-phase) IP core watermarking processes in detail. Both the approaches are demonstrated through a motivational example.

#### 4.3.1 Problem formulation

**Inputs:** (i) DSP application, (ii) resource configuration, (iii) module library, and (iv) vendor signature.

**Output:** Watermarked IP core design.

Sengupta *et al.* (2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) accepted DSP application in the form of data flow graph (DFG), module library in the form of NanGate 15-nm technology ([NanGate Open Cell Library, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib12)) or 90-nm library/other library, and user-specified resource configuration (*R*). Here, *R* is represented as: *N(X*[1])*, N*(*X*[2])*, …, N*(*X*[*D*]), and *N*(*X*[*D*]) indicating the number of resources of type *X*[*D*]. Sengupta *et al.* (2016) proposed a vendor signature that contains four encoding variables used for generating watermarking constraints. These watermarking constraints are embedded in a single HLS phase of a DSP IP core design process. On the other hand, [Sengupta *et al.* (2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) proposed a vendor signature that contains seven encoding variables. These watermarking constraints are embedded in three different HLS design phases of a DSP IP core design process. [Figure 4.6](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig6) depicts the inputs and output of an IP core watermarking process.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-04-f06.jpg)

Figure 4.6 Inputs and output for watermarked IP core

**Target platform:** The targeted platform for Sengupta *et al.* (2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) watermarking approach is any modern computer-aided design (CAD) tool. Both watermarking approaches generate the final watermarked DSP IP core design in HDL; therefore, any HDL-based CAD tool used for generating IP core can easily adopt these watermarking algorithms.

#### 4.3.2 Design process of single-phase watermarked IP core/hardware

In this section, we describe the design of a watermarked DSP IP core/hardware (especially for DSP/multimedia applications).

##### 4.3.2.2 Watermarking process for DSP IP core

As an example, we have used single-phase watermarking approach presented in Sengupta *et al.* (2016) to demonstrate the design process. Watermark in DSP IP core can be embedded as additional design constraints in one of the HLS design phases. Sengupta *et al.* (2016) embed watermarking constraints in the register allocation phase of HLS. To embed additional constraints, a register allocation table is generated using the aid of CIG. In CIG, the nodes indicates the storage variables of the scheduled design, the edges indicates existence of overlapping of lifetime between two storage variables, and the color of the node indicates allocated register of that corresponding node. Therefore, if there is an edge between two storage variables (nodes) then the same register cannot be assigned between them. In other words, if there is an edge between two nodes, then the color of them must be different.

In Sengupta *et al.* (2016) and Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)), watermarking constraints are added as supplementary edges between the nodes of a CIG. The color of the nodes are adjusted after embedding additional edges and the register allocation table of an IP core is generated from the final modified CIG. More specifically, inserting each edge as watermarking constraints, force two storage variables of a CIG to execute through distinct registers. Thus, embedding additional edges in a CIG affect the allocation of the register of a design. However, these additional edges should be derived from a vendor’s hidden signature. This mandates designer to design a strong signature encoding process. Sengupta *et al.* (2016) devised a multi-variable signature encoding scheme to embeds a robust watermark. Compared with the authors in Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)), who have used two variables signature encoding scheme, a more robust and stronger signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta *et al.* (2016). The signature encoding scheme of Sengupta *et al.* (2016) is discussed in the rest of this section.

##### 4.3.2.3 Signature encoding scheme

A four variables signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta *et al.* (2016) where each variable indicates an encoded watermarking constraint. More specifically, each decoded signature digit inserts an additional edge between two nodes of a CIG as a watermarking constraint. An IP core owner can select his desired signature using any random combination of four variables, i.e., ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’. The encoded rule of each variable is as follows:

*   ‘i’ = Add an additional edge between (prime, prime) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘I’ = Add an additional edge between (even, even) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘T’ = Add an additional edge between (odd, even) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘!’ = Add an additional edge between (0, any integer) node pair of CIG.
    

In Sengupta *et al.* (2016), as IP sellers signature is embedded based on multi-variable signature encoding scheme and distributed throughout the DSP design, it is harder for an adversary to detect and remove the complete watermark. Thus, provides significant robustness and stronger encoding.

##### 4.3.2.4 Watermark embedding process for DSP IP core

In the previous sub-section, we have discussed the signature encoding rule using four variables. Here, we discuss how to embed an IP seller’s signature into an original (non-watermarked) IP design. As mentioned earlier, all the aforesaid encoding variables embed watermarking constraints in the register allocation phase of HLS; the phases of HLS appearing before register allocation phase, is described as the pre-processing steps of watermark. Therefore, watermark embedding process is divided into two parts, viz., pre-processing steps and watermark embedding steps. Detailed steps of the complete watermarking process (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016) are as follows:

*   A. **Pre-processing steps**
    
    1.  Accept an original/non-watermarked DSP application in the form of CDFG with resource configuration as input.
        
    2.  Schedule the CDFG of DSP application based on the resource configuration (constraint).
        
    3.  Assign storage variable for each operation of the scheduled CDFG.
        
    4.  Construct the CIG to identify the minimal registers essential for register allocation.
        
    5.  Generate the register allocation table from the constructed CIG.
        
    6.  Sort storage variables in ascending order according to their number.
        
    7.  Accept an *n*\-digit vendor’s signature as a combination of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ variables.
        
*   B. **Watermark embedding steps**
    
    1.  Extract the decoded meaning of each signature digit based on encoded rule of each variable.
        
    2.  Construct a list of additional edge from the decoded value of vendor’s signature by traversing the sorted nodes.
        
    3.  Insert those additional edges in the CIG (constructed in pre-processing step 4) one by one as watermarking constraints and adjust the CIG if required.
        
    4.  After embedding all the additional edges in the CIG, modify the register allocation table (constructed in pre-processing step 5) based on the updated CIG.
        

After following the above steps, IP owner’s watermark gets embedded into the DSP IP core. The watermarking constraints are embedded into the register allocation phase of HLS. Each constraint forces two storage variables to be executed through a distinctive register. Thus, manipulates the register sharing which creates an impact on the final datapath of the IP core and its corresponding gate-level structure (netlist). Therefore, embedding this watermark retains the correctness and functionality of a DSP IP core.

##### 4.3.2.5 Didactic example of single-phase watermarking process

In this sub-section, we demonstrate end-to-end single-phase watermark embedding process through a representative example. The CDFG of FIR-2 filter adopted from DSP Benchmark Suite ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib6)) shown in [Figure 4.12](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig12).

[Figure 4.11](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig11) is taken as input (according to step A.1). The accepted CDFG is then scheduled based on two adders and two multipliers (according to step A.2). Storage variables (V0–V30) are assigned to each operation of the scheduled DFG (according to step A.3). A CIG is constructed (according to step A.4) with 31 nodes, i.e., V0–V30 and eight registers, i.e., register purple (Reg\_P), register dark\_blue (Reg\_DB), register light\_blue (Reg\_LB), register green (Reg\_G), register yellow (Reg\_Y), register red (Reg\_R), register orange (Reg\_O), and register black (Reg\_B). The corresponding CIG is shown in [Figure 4.12](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig12). The scheduled CDFG after performing storage variable assignment and register allocation is shown in [Figure 4.13](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig13). The number of control steps (cs) required to schedule the FIR-2 CDFG is 9. The register allocation table corresponding to the constructed CIG (shown in [Figure 4.12](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig12)) is reported in [Table 4.1](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl1) (according to step A.5). All the storage variables (V0–V30) are sorted in ascending order according to variable number and a list is generated (according to step A.6). As an example, a 14-digits vendor signature: ‘**i I I T I TT I IT ! TTT’** is selected which is a combination of four aforementioned signature variables (according to step A.7). All the pre-processing steps to embed single-phase watermark is performed now. The next step is to decode the 14-digits signature, based on aforementioned encoding rules (according to step B.1). The vendor’s signatures and its corresponding decoded meaning are shown in [Table 4.2](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl2). According to the decoded signature shown in [Table 4.2,](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl2) the list of additional edges are between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), (V2 and V8), (V1 and V4), (V1 and V6), (V2 and V10), (V2 and V12), (V1 and V8), (V0 and V1), (V1 and V10), (V1 and V12), and (V1 and V14) (according to step B.2). Although according to the vendor’s signature, there are 14 additional edges to be added in the CIG, however, by default eight edges (i.e., edge between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), (V2 and V8), (V1 and V4), (V1 and V6), and (V0 and V1)) are already present in the graph. Hence, the constraints for these eight constraints are satisfied by default. Therefore, the objective is to satisfy the other six remaining constraints (i.e., edge between nodes (V2 and V10), (V2 and V12), (V1 and V8), (V1 and V10), (V1 and V12), and (V1 and V14)) in the IP core design. It can be observed that edge between node (V2 and V12) forces storage variable V2 and V12 to be executed through distinct register, therefore node color of V2 and V12 must be different which is green (G) now (see [Figure 4.12](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig12)). Hence to accommodate this constraint, the allocated register for storage variable V2 (Reg\_G) needs to swap with other storage variable of same control step. Scanning the storage variables from left to right, we can observe that swapping V2 with V0 is violating a constraint (due to edge between nodes V2 and V8), similarly, swapping V2 with V1 is violating a constraint (due to edge between nodes V1 and V12). However, swapping V2 with V3 does not violate any constraints; therefore, storage variable V2 is allocated to Reg\_LB and storage variable V3 is allocated to Reg\_G. Similarly, edge between nodes V1 and V14 forces storage variable V1 and V14 to be executed through distinct register which need swapping. Swapping V14 with V15 does not violate any constraints, therefore storage variable V14 is allocated to Reg\_G (previously allocated to Reg\_DB) and storage variable V15 is allocated to Reg\_DB (previously allocated to Reg\_G). (*Note: If no storage other variable is found to swap with the conflicting storage variable, a new register should be added in the CIG and assigned to that conflicting storage variable.*) After embedding all these additional edges in the CIG, the final modified graph (according to step B.3) is shown in [Figure 4.14](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig14). The register allocation table corresponding to the modified CIG (shown in [Figure 4.14](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig14)) is reported in [Table 4.3](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl3) (according to step B.3). The scheduled CDFG after modifying storage variable assignment and register allocation is shown in [Figure 4.15](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig15). The corresponding multiplexing schemes of ‘Reg\_G’, ‘Reg\_DB’, and ‘Reg\_LB’ before and after embedding watermark are shown in [Tables 4.4(a)](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl4a), [4.4](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl4b)(b) and [4.4](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl4c)(c), respectively. The multiplexers and demultiplexers of ‘Reg\_G’, ‘Reg\_DB’, and ‘Reg\_LB’ before embedding watermark are shown in [Figures 4.16](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig16a)(a), [4.17](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig17a)(a), and [4.18](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig18a)(a), respectively. The corresponding multiplexer and demultiplexer of ‘Reg\_G’, ‘Reg\_DB’, and ‘Reg\_LB’ after embedding watermark are shown in Figures [4.16](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig16a)(b), [4.17](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig17b)(b), and [4.18](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig18b)(b), respectively. The change in datapath after embedding watermark is marked as dotted lines to the mux inputs. For example, due to the swapping of storage variable V2 and V3 (due to the insertion of edge between nodes V1 and V12), input IN3 of Reg\_G moved Reg\_LB, similarly input IN4 of Reg\_LB moved to Reg\_G. The reflection of this alteration is also visible in the gate structure of the design. The partial gate structure of Mux of Reg\_G before embedding watermark is shown in [Figures 4.19(a)](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig19a) and [(c)](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig19c). The corresponding gate structure of the same part of Mux of Reg\_G after embedding watermark is shown in [Figures 4.19(b)](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig19b) and [(d)](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig19d).

#### 4.3.3 Design process of triple-phase watermarked IP core/hardware

In this section, we describe the design process of another watermarked DSP IP core/hardware. We describe a more robust triple-phase watermarking approach presented in Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) to design a DSP IP core. This approach does not protect non-HDL IP cores such as standard/pre-defined blocks or symbols that are present in the in-built library of a logic CAD tool. The triple-phase watermarking methodology protects the ownership of an IP core (especially for DSP/multimedia applications). In the process of embedding triple-phase watermark, it is presumed that same type of micro-IPs are available from at least two different third-party vendors to design a macro-IP core (which is a common practice in the industry).

Unlike single-phase watermarking approach (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016), triple-phase watermarking approach ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) for DSP core embeds watermarking constraints in multiple phases of HLS. More specifically, triple-phase watermarking approach embeds watermarking constraints in the scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation phase of HLS. In addition to implanting watermarking constraints in three different phases of HLS, the signature encoding scheme consists of seven different variables, where each variable carries a unique encoding rule. Thus, triple-phase watermarking approach enhances the robustness and minimizes the chance of malicious alteration or removal of the signature. Furthermore, for an adversary, it is also difficult to recognize the synthesis phase and in what way watermark constraints are implanted in the design.

In Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)), watermarking constraints are embedded during scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation phases by modifying three information: (a) ‘Non-critical operations (*μ*[*m*] > 0)’ timing table (*μ*[*m*] = the mobility of an operation), (b) ‘Functional unit allocation’ table, and (c) ‘Register allocation’ table (adopted from Sengupta *et al.*, 2016). As mentioned earlier, this watermarking approach has seven different variables, viz. ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’. Variable ‘γ’ modifies the timing table of ‘non-critical operations (*μ*[*m*] > 0)’ thus embedding watermarking constraints during scheduling (first phase). Variables ‘α’ and ‘β’ modifies the ‘functional unit allocation’ table thus embedding watermarking constraints during hardware allocation (second phase). Finally, variables ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, ‘!’ modify the ‘register allocation’ table thus embedding watermarking constraints during register allocation (third phase). The signature encoding process of each variable is described below ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)).

##### 4.3.3.1 Signature encoding scheme

A seven variables signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) where each variable embeds decoded watermarking constraint in any of the three phases (scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation) of synthesis process. More specifically, each decoded signature digit inserts a watermarking constraint by modifying any of the aforementioned tables. An IP owner can select his desired signature using any random combination of these seven variables, i.e., ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’. The encoded rule of each variable is as follows:

*   ‘γ’ = Move/shift a non-critical path’s operation with the highest mobility into immediate next control step (cs).
    
*   ‘α’ = *In odd control steps only*: Even operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 2 (U2) and odd operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 1 (U1).
    
*   ‘β’ = *In even control steps only*: Even operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 1 (U1) and odd operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 2 (U2).
    
*   ‘i’ = Add an additional edge between (prime, prime) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘I’ = Add an additional edge between (even, even) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘T’ = Add an additional edge between (odd, even) node pair of CIG.
    
*   ‘!’ = Add an additional edge between (0, any integer) node pair of CIG.
    

In Sengupta *et al.* ([2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)), 3rd phase watermarking variables, i.e., ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’ are independent of both 1st phase watermarking variable, i.e., ‘γ’ and 2nd phase watermarking variables, i.e., ‘α’ and ‘β’. Similarly, watermarking variable of 1st phase is independent of both watermarking variables of 2nd and 3rd phase. These advantages make the triple-phase watermarking approach exceptionally robust and tamper tolerant for an adversary. However, watermarking variable of 2nd phase is dependent on watermarking variables of 1st phase. Therefore, watermarking constraints of 2nd phase may be affected due to alteration of 1st phase watermark which is a limitation of this approach. Nevertheless, as mentioned earlier, it is tremendously tough for an adversary to detect in which step of synthesis, the 1st phase watermark is implanted, and how. Moreover, if 1st phase watermark is tampered somehow by an attacker, then still 3rd phase watermarking constraints (which is independent of 1st- and 2nd-phase watermark) are capable of resolving the ownership conflict and identifying the real IP core owner. Thus, triple-phase watermark provides a strong tamper tolerant watermarked IP core design.

##### 4.3.3.2 Watermark embedding process

In the previous sub-section, we have discussed encoding rule of seven variables of the triple-phase watermark. In this sub-section, we will discuss about how to embed a triple-phase watermark in a non-watermarked IP design. The triple-phase watermark embedding process is divided into four parts, i.e., pre-processing steps, 1st phase watermark embedding steps, 2nd phase watermark embedding steps, and 3rd phase watermark embedding steps. Detailed steps of this watermarking process are as follows ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)):

*   A. **Pre-processing steps**
    
    1.  Accept a non-watermarked DSP application as CDFG and schedule it based on user resource configuration.
        
    2.  Perform functional unit allocation and register allocation.
        
    3.  Construct the timing table for ‘non-critical operations (*μ*[*m*] > 0),’ ‘functional unit allocation’ table, and ‘register allocation’ table from the non-watermarked IP core design.
        
    4.  Sort the operations control stepwise based on their number in increasing order.
        
    5.  Accept an *n*\-digit vendor’s signature as a combination of ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’ variables.
        
*   B. **1st phase watermark embedding steps**
    
    1.  For each occurrence of ‘γ’, shift an operation of the non-critical path into its very next control step while checking from control step 1 onward (without re-occurrence), if both of the following conditions satisfied:
        
        *    (i) Respective operation does not have any child operation in very next control step.
            
        *   (ii) Shifting does not violate the hardware resource constraints.  
            (*Note: In case more than one operation is eligible to be shifted in the next control step, the operation with the highest mobility will be given the priority*).
            
    2.  Adjust the timing table of ‘non-critical operations (*μ*[*m*] > 0)’ after embedding all ‘γ’ variables.
        
*   C. **2nd phase watermark embedding steps**
    
    1.  Accept the 1st phase watermark embedded scheduled design as input to embed 2nd phase watermark.
        
    2.  For each occurrence of ‘α’ and/or ‘β’ variable in the vendor’s signature, re-allocation of functional unit needs to be performed according to the encoding rule of ‘α’ and ‘β’.
        
    3.  Modify the ‘functional unit allocation’ table after embedding all ‘α’ and ‘β’ variables.
        
*   D. **3rd phase watermark embedding steps**
    
    1.  Accept the dual phase (1st and 2nd phase) watermark embedded design as input to embed 3rd phase watermark.
        
    2.  Rest of the steps is similar to single-phase watermark embedding steps B.1–B.4 (refer Section 4.3.B).
        

##### 4.3.3.3 Signature detection process

The signature detection process is a crucial and compulsory step to resolve ownership conflict. The inputs required to detect triple-phase watermark are: (a) decoded vendor signature, (b) application, and (c) watermarked IP core in the form of controller and datapath HDL. The triple-phase watermark can be achieved in three steps and each step verifies the presence of watermarking constraints of each phase. In the signature detection and verification process of phase 1 watermark, the control steps of modified operations are extracted from the decoded signature which is then compared with the controller HDL of the watermarked IP. To detect and verify the phase 2 watermark, the allocated hardware of the watermarked operations are extracted from the decoded signature which is then identified with the help of original application and its corresponding inputs. Then, the watermarked hardware information fetched from the decoded watermark is compared with the datapath HDL of the watermarked IP. Similarly, to detect and verify the phase 3 watermark, the shared inputs of each multiplexer should be fetched from the datapath HDL of the watermarked IP. It is then compared with the 3rd phase watermarking constraints extracted from the decoded signature. If all the constraints of decode signature are available in the watermarked IP core then the vendor who provided the decoded signature is awarded as the original owner of that IP core. The complete signature detection process of triple phase watermark is shown in [Figure 4.26](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig26).

##### 4.3.3.4 Didactic example of triple-phase watermarking process

In this sub-section, we demonstrate an end-to-end triple-phase IP core watermark embedding process through a representative example. The DFG of discrete wavelet transformation (DWT) benchmark shown in [Figure 4.27](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig27) is taken as input and then scheduled using user given hardware configuration, i.e., three adders and three multipliers (according to step A.1). After that, the functional unit allocation of each operation and the register allocation of each storage variable (V0–V21) are performed (according to step A.2). In the triple-phase watermarking approach, two distinctive IP core vendors are employed to achieve better security. For example, in this case, out of three adders, two are acquired from vendor type 1 (A1) and one is acquired from vendor type 2 (A2), similarly, out of three multipliers, two are obtained from vendor type 1 (M1) and one is obtained from vendor type 2 (M2). The scheduled DFG after performing functional unit re-allocation and register re-allocation (before watermarking) is shown in [Figure 4.28](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig28). The IP core design before embedding watermarking constraints uses list scheduling algorithm and random functional unit allocation. Register allocation for the same design (before watermark) is performed based on CIG (shown in [Figure 4.29](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig29)). A CIG is constructed with 22 nodes, i.e., V0–V21 and five registers, i.e., register red (R), register green (G), register blue (B), register yellow (Y), and register purple (P). The timing table for ‘non-critical operations,’ ‘functional unit allocation’ table, and ‘register allocation’ table of the non-watermarked design are generated as shown in [Tables 4.6](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl6), [4.7,](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl7) and [4.8](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl8), respectively (according to step A.3). All the operations are sorted control step wise in ascending order (according to step A.4). As an example, a 12-digits vendor signature: ‘**ɣ ɣ ɑ β ɑ β β i I IT !’** is selected which is a combination of seven aforementioned signature variables (according to step A.5). All the pre-processing steps to embed single-phase watermark is complete now. The vendor’s signatures and its corresponding decoded meaning are shown in [Table 4.9](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl9). In the 1st phase of the triple-phase watermark, all the ‘γ’ digits should be embedded. According to the encoding rule of ‘γ’, the first ‘γ’ digit of vendor’s signature moves operation (opn.) two from control step (cs) 1 to cs 2. For next ‘γ’ digit, the next operation which satisfies all the rules of B.1 is opn.9, because operations 3, 4, and 5 do not satisfy the rule mentioned in B.1(i), and opn.7 does not satisfy the rule mentioned in B.1(ii). Because between operations 8 and 9, opn.9 has higher mobility value, hence it is moved from cs 3 to cs 4. The modified timing table for ‘non-critical operations’ and its corresponding scheduled DFG is shown in [Table 4.10](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl10) and [Figure 4.30](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig30) (according to step B.2). In the 2nd phase of the triple-phase watermark, all the ‘α’ and ‘β’ digits should be embedded on the top of 1st phase watermarked design (according to step C.1). According to the encoding rule of ‘α’, the third digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.1 from M2 (multiplier obtained from vendor type 2) to M1 (multiplier obtained from vendor type 1). Similarly, according to the encoding rule of ‘β’, the sixth digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.4 from M2 to M1. (*Note: no modification of hardware assignment is required for the fourth and fifth digit of the signature.*) Similarly, the seventh digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.5 from M1 to M2. The modified ‘functional unit allocation’ table and its corresponding scheduled DFG is shown in [Table 4.11](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl11) and [Figure 4.31](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig31) (according to step C.3). In the 3rd phase of the triple-phase watermark, hall the ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ digits should be embedded on the top of 1st and 2nd phase watermarked design (according to step D.1). According to the decoded signature shown in [Table 4.9](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl9), the list of additional edges includes edges between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), and (V0 and V1). Among these five edges except the edge between nodes (V2 and V6), all are already present in the constructed CIG. It can be observed that edge between node (V2 and V6) forces storage variable V2 and V6 to be executed through distinct register, therefore node color of V2 and V6 must be different which is blue (B) now (see [Figure 4.29](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig29) and [Table 4.8](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl8) marked in bold). Hence to accommodate this constraint, the allocated register for storage variable V6 (Reg\_B) needs to be swapped with another storage variable in same control step. Swapping V6 with V5 does not violate any constraints; therefore, storage variable V6 is now allocated to Reg\_R (previously allocated to Reg\_B) and storage variable V5 is now allocated to Reg\_B (previously allocated to Reg\_R). After embedding the additional edges in the CIG, the final modified graph is shown in [Figure 4.32](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig32). The modified register allocation table and its corresponding modified scheduled DFG containing watermark information is shown in [Table 4.12](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl12) and [Figure 4.33](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig33).

#### 4.3.4 Desired properties of IP core watermark

Every ideal IP core watermark should satisfy following properties:

*     (i) **Low-design overhead**: Embedding additional design constraints in the form of watermark may incur design overhead. However, an ideal IP core watermarking process should incur minimal design overhead as possible. The design overhead of both single- and triple-phase watermark discussed in this chapter in terms of design area and design latency is significantly low.
    
*    (ii) **Strong resiliency**: An ideal IP core watermark should be resilient against removal attack. Therefore, the watermarking constraints should be implanted as a core part of an IP core design. Both single- and triple-phase watermarks contain multi-variable encoding rules where the watermarking constraints are dispersed all over the design (especially in triple-phase watermarking process). Therefore, complete removal of watermarking constraints from the entire IP core design is enormously difficult for an attacker. Thus, substantial resiliency against removal attack is achieved in both watermarking processes.
    
*   (iii) **Strong tamper tolerance**: An ideal IP core watermark should have strong tamper tolerance ability, i.e., partial removal should not impact the proof of ownership of an IP core. The watermarking constraints of single- and triple-phase presented in this chapter are distributed using multiple encoding variables. Moreover, in triple-phase watermarking process, watermark constraints are embedded in three different phases of HLS. Additionally, as mentioned earlier, 1st and 3rd phase of triple-phase watermark is independent of other two phases. Thus, strong tamper tolerance ability is achieved in both watermarking process.
    
*   (iv) **Low-signature embedding and detection time**: A robust signature may incur complex signature decoding and high-embedding time; therefore, the total runtime to generate a watermarked IP core may increase massively. An ideal IP core watermark should be embedded with lower embedding time. Additionally, signature detection process for a genuine vendor (who has the thorough information of encoding rule and the signature) should be quick. Due to unobvious encoding rules and robust signature embedding process, the embedding time of both single- and triple-phase watermark phase presented in this chapter is low. Furthermore, signature detection time for a genuine entity is also straightforward and speedy.
    
*    (v) **Correct functionality**: In the process of embedding watermarking constraints, the correct functionality of an IP core must be preserved. Both single- and triple-phase watermarking processes phase presented in this chapter do not perform any alteration of IP core functionality while embedding watermarking constraints. Thus, functionality of an IP core does not get affected at all.
    

#### 4.3.5 Possible cases of dishonest claim of IP core/hardware ownership and its resolution

This section presents the possible threat scenarios of the false claim of IP core ownership and its resolution using watermarking process presented in this chapter. Let us assume ‘Alice’ is an IP vendor, designed a watermarked IP core with her signature and sold it to ‘Bob.’ In that case, Bob can claim his IP core ownership using any three possible scenarios as discussed below ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)):

*     (i) **Claiming any arbitrary design information as the signature**: After purchasing the watermarked IP core, Bob can reverse engineer the IP core and extract the complete information of the IP core design. Then, he may claim any random design information as his watermarking constraints, thus may claim his ownership of that IP core. Bob’s claim may valid for a single design, but will invalid for other watermarked design. Thus, Bob’s claim is not strong enough to prove his ownership. On the other hand, Alice’s watermarking constraints will be more meaningful and consistent for all watermarked design. In such scenario, the entity having more meaningful and consistent watermark will be awarded to the original owner of the IP core. The presented watermarking in this chapter is capable to resolve this threat.
    
*    (ii) **Inserting illegal signature**: Bob can embed his own signature on the top of the watermarked design purchased from Alice and then claim for his IP ownership. In such scenario, Alice can prove her ownership easily because the watermarked design coming from Alice contents only Alice’s watermark; however, the watermarked design coming from Bob contains both Alice’s and Bob’s watermark. The presented watermarking in this chapter is also capable to resolve this threat.
    
*   (iii) **Tampering/partial removing of original watermark**: Though it is recommended that watermarking constraints should be an integral part of the design, still sometime it may be possible to identify some design information as the watermarking constraints of the design. In such case, Bob may perform some modification/alteration in the design to remove those watermarks. In such scenario, if the watermarking constraints are independent of each other and distributed throughout the design removal of the complete watermark is extremely difficult. Therefore, ownership of Alice can be proved. Additionally, sometimes tampering of embedded watermarking constraints may force to perform all the pre-synthesis steps from the beginning, which is a costly and time-consuming process. The presented watermarking in this chapter is also capable to resolve this threat.
    

### 4.4 Analysis on case studies

In this section, we discuss the triple-phase watermarking process ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) on case studies/test cases and compare it with a multiple-variable single-phase watermarking process (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016) and a dual-variable single-phase watermarking process ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)). This section is divided into three sub-sections: (i) system setup, (ii) security analysis of triple-phase watermark, and (iii) design cost analysis of triple-phase watermark.

The baseline (original non-watermarked) design, dual-variable single-phase watermark design ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)), multi-variable single-phase watermark design (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016), and triple-phase watermark design ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22)) were all implemented in Java 8 and executed on Windows platform with 4 GB DDR3 primary memory with processor frequency of 3.20 GHz 15-nm NanGate based technology scales ([NanGate Open Cell Library, 2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib12)) is employed to assess both watermarked design area and design latency. While calculating the design cost, equal weightage is provided to both design area and design latency.

#### 4.4.1 Security analysis of triple-phase watermark for DSP IP cores

The possibility of generating the same solution before and after embedding watermark is calculated based on the probability of coincidence (*P*[*c*]) metric. Lower *P*[*c*] value indicates a higher strength of watermark. The metric partially adopted from Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) can be expressed below:

![image](OEBPS/images/c04_eqn10.gif)

where, ‘*w*’ is the watermark strength/size, *N*(*R*[*i*]) is the number of functional unit of type *i*, ‘*D*’ indicates the type of functional unit, and ‘*c*’ is the number of colors used in CIG before embedding watermark. [Table 4.13](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl13) reports the comparative study of the probability of coincidence between triple-phase watermarking (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) for signature size 80. It can be observed from [Table 4.13](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl13) that the triple-phase approach achieves 1.4 × 10^(27) times lower *P*[*c*] value in average compared with Sengupta *et al.* (2016) and Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) which indicates the higher robustness of watermark. Low *P*[*c*] value is desirable which is achievable by incrementing the watermark size. However, too bigger size of watermarking constraints may result in register overhead, thereby increasing the design cost. According to Sengupta *et al.* (2016), the desirable maximum range of signature size should be 80.

#### 4.4.2 Design cost analysis of triple-phase watermark for DSP IP cores

Design cost of the triple-phase watermark is calculated based on area and latency of the watermarked IP core design, where watermarked design cost is evaluated based on the following expression:

![image](OEBPS/images/c04_eqn12.gif)

where, *C*[*f*] (*X*[*i*]) is the watermarked design cost for user provided resource configuration *X*[*i*], *L*[total], and *A*[total] are total watermarked design latency and area, respectively. The total area and latency of design are calculated based on the models proposed in Sengupta *et al.* (2016). *L*[max] and *A*[max] indicate maximum design latency and area based on the available resources in the module library, *w*[1] and *w*[2] are weightage parameters for latency and area, respectively. [Figure 4.34](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig34) shows the comparison of design area between baseline and triple-phase (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)). [Figure 4.35](#Chapter4.html#c04_fig35) shows the comparison of design latency between baseline and triple phase (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)). Triple-phase watermark achieves lesser or equal design latency compared with Sengupta *et al.* (2016) and Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) and minimal latency overhead compared with baseline design. The comparison of design cost between baseline and triple phase (Sengupta *et al.*, 2016, [2018](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib22); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter4.html#c04_bib8)) is reported in [Table 4.15](#Chapter4.html#c04_tbl15). ### 4.5 Conclusion

This chapter discussed in details about hardware watermarking of DSP application based IP cores used in CE devices. Several selected state-of-the-art watermarking approaches at different abstraction levels were reviewed. Two watermarking approaches used for DSP cores have been presented with greater details. These approaches implant watermark signature digits before RTL synthesis (during high-level synthesis). Embedding watermarking before RTL synthesis enables watermarking constraints to propagate to the lower levels of design. For example, how gate level design of a DSP core reflects the watermarking constraints that is embedded at its higher design level is explained and demonstrated with examples in this chapter. This chapter also lucidly explains the design flow of designing a watermarked DSP core with some industry standard examples of FIR filter, IIR low-pass Butterworth filter, etc. Details on security metrics were also presented and analyzed. We also demonstrate why hardware watermarking is an extremely useful tool for combating false claim of ownership, IP piracy, forgery, and other attacks.
