## *Chapter 5*  
**Symmetrical protection of DSP IP core and integrated circuits using fingerprinting and watermarking**

This chapter discusses the use of watermarking and fingerprinting for symmetrical protection of DSP IP cores and integrated circuits. Symmetrical IP core protection is a mechanism in which both seller and buyers of an IP can have signature for double-proof of ownership and whereas significantly reducing false ownership claims. The chapter is structured as follows: Section 5.2 discusses the fundamentals of IP core protection with emphasis on symmetrical IP core protection techniques for DSP cores; Section 5.3 discusses the low-cost DSP core IP core protection; Section 5.4 explained that methodology with a motivational example. Section 5.5 discusses the results of that approach. The conclusion of this chapter is provided in Section 5.6.

### 5.1 Introduction

The designs of integrated circuits have evolved into greater sophistication than ever before with the revolution of implementation and application technology in consumer electronics industry. The usage of digital signal processing (DSP) intellectual property (IP) cores ([Castillo *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib1)) generated using architectural synthesis not only maintains a proper balance between time-to-market pressure and design productivity but additionally help in design cost reduction. High-level synthesis (HLS) ([Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib2), [2013](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib4)) is an automated design process that transforms an algorithmic/behavioral description of a digital circuit or IP into its corresponding register transfer level (RTL) digital hardware through numerous sub-processes like scheduling, hardware and register allocation, and binding ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib15)). In the process of manufacturing an IP core, two entities are involved, viz. seller and buyer. An IP seller also known as IP vendor is the creator of an IP, whereas an IP buyer also known as IP user is the purchaser of an IP. However, to maintain a viable application of IP cores in composite SoC-based designs, protection of both the entities against threats is extremely crucial. Let us now discuss on the protection aspect of IP buyer and IP seller. In an IP core, an IP buyer may claim buyer privilege as a buyer so that the same IP copy should not be usable/accessible to his competitors in the market. This is possible when customized specifications of an IP core are obtained by an IP seller from an IP buyer, thus creating an exclusive one-to-one mapping between both parties. Embedding a unique buyer’s signature (known as buyer fingerprint) into an IP core design facilitates detection of unlawfully redistributed/resold duplicates of an IP core by a deceitful seller ([Gang and Potkonjak, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib3)). Likewise, an IP seller must protect his design from piracy and false claim of ownership before selling it to an IP buyer. Embedding a unique seller’s signature (known as seller watermark) into an IP core design protects an IP core from ownership abuse ([Alkabani *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib5); [Sengupta and Kundu, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib6); Sengupta *et al.*, [2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib7), [2018](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib38); [Kougianos *et al.*, 2009](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib8); [Maltoni *et al.*, 2009](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib9); [Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10); [Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib11); Sengupta, [2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib36), [2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib35); [Sengupta and Roy, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib37)).

Therefore, symmetrical protection of DSP IP cores provides user right as well as nullifies IP ownership abuse. A thematic summary is highlighted in [Figure 5.1](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig1). Significant investments are required in terms of man-power, time and cost to design, and verify an IP core; however, it can be cloned, modified, or resold easily by a rough entity. Therefore, both seller and buyer of IP designs want to nullify the possibilities of false claiming and illegal reselling of an IP core. Symmetrical protection can be achieved by implanting dual entity signature scheme in a DSP IP core during any of the design abstraction level. Standard IP protection methods ([Yuan *et al.*, 2006](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib12)) such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, etc., are distributed, restricted in capacities, and insufficient in securing IP cores from buyer and seller viewpoint. Additionally, several signature embedding schemes in different multimedia applications, like image, text, video, and audio are also not appropriate to protect an IP core as it does not preserve the functionality and precision of a design in signature insertion. Thus, from the perspective of IP core protection, necessary action needs be taken to preserve the functionality and correctness of the design while embedding any signature.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-05-f01.jpg)

Figure 5.1 Thematic overview of symmetrical IP core protection

#### 5.1.1 Background on watermark and fingerprint

Watermark and fingerprint represents the signature of two distinct entities of a DSP reusable IP core to protect their corresponding ownership right. While fingerprint conveys the signature of an IP buyer, watermark is intended for an IP seller. An ideal signature for both cases must meet the below features:

*   It must be implanted as vital part of an IP design so that it must not be perceptible through traditional scanning.
    
*   It must be inimitable in nature so that the proof of ownership can be established easily.
    
*   For manifold signature implanting mechanism, each signature must be self-governing of each other.
    
*   It should be tamper tolerant so that partial removal of signature should not impact on the proof on ownership.
    
*   It should be resilient against attacks like reverse engineering.
    
*   Low embedding runtime.
    
*   Nominal latency and hardware overhead after implanting signatures.
    
*   Seamless signature detection process for an authentic owner with comprehensive cognizance of encoding rules ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18); [Cox *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib19)).
    
*   Must uphold logic correctness of an IP core post-implanting signatures.
    

#### 5.1.2 Threat model

The ultimate goals of IP core security are:

1.  ***Buyer’s standpoint:*** detect unlawfully redistributed/resold copies in the market by a deceitful IP seller ([Gang and Potkonjak, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib3)).
    
2.  ***Seller’s standpoint:*** security against ownership exploitation ([Yu and Zhu, 2011](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib13)).
    

#### 5.1.3 Benefits of protection at higher abstraction

Although DSP IP core protection can be provided in any of the design abstraction level, however, embedding buyer fingerprint and seller watermark architecture level (Mohanty *et al.*, [2002](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib15), [2014](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib16)) are beneficial as the signature constraints embedded in higher design abstraction level will automatically propagate in the lower design abstraction level; thus, it will protect the higher level as well as the lower level of the design. Additionally, symmetrical protection in higher level can be achieved in lesser signature embedding complexity while incurring lower design overhead. Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) presented a multi-variable fingerprinting and watermarking-based symmetrical IP core protection mechanism during multiple sub-steps of architectural synthesis/HLS process. Additionally, the approach incurs minimal design overhead while incorporating both signature constraints.

### 5.2 Fundamentals of IP core protection

This chapter discusses fundamentals of different reusable IP core protection mechanisms (shown in [Figure 5.2](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig2)) with emphasis on higher design abstraction level-based IP core protections that are available in the literature and how they are different when compared with symmetrical IP core protection. Reusable IP core protection mechanism can be classified into two parts: (a) non-symmetric approach and (b) symmetric approach.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-05-f02.jpg)

Figure 5.2 Classification and corresponding works on IP core protection

#### 5.2.1 Overview on non-symmetric IP core protection techniques

According to the literature, non-symmetric IP core protection techniques mainly provide protection from a seller’s perspective. It can be performed in three different techniques: (i) hardware obfuscation, (ii) computational forensic engineering (CFE), and (iii) watermark.

1.  ***Hardware obfuscation:*** Obfuscation is the process of transforming an original application or design into its functionally equivalent form to make the reverse engineering process significantly more challenging ([Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib28)). It can protect an IP core either by obscuring the IP design/code, known as structural obfuscation ([Hada, 2000](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib27); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib31)) or by generating a locked netlist ([Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib28)). A person who has the proper knowledge of the design of the correct key combination can only use it. In other words, structural obfuscation hides the functionality of an IP core whereas functional obfuscation hides the implementation of an IP core.
    
2.  ***Computational forensic engineering:*** Computational forensic engineering (CFE) is a signature-free driven process which can be performed in three steps, feature collection, feature extraction, and IP validation ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib30)). It tries to identify a list of features that can be used to identify an IP core uniquely ([Wong *et al.*, 2004](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib29)). In case of ownership conflict, these features can be used to recognize the real owner of the IP core.
    
3.  ***Watermark:*** IP protection of a single entity (for IP seller only) can be achieved by embedding a seller watermark in to the IP core design. Watermark can be inserted either at lower design abstraction level (Ziener and Teich, [2006](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib20), [2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib22); [Nie *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib21)) or at higher design abstraction level ([Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib14); [Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18); [Hong and Potkonjak, 1999](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib23); [Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib24); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib25)). Watermark at lower design level can be detected from the power supply pins of field programmable gate array (FPGA) ([Ziener and Teich, 2006](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib20)), or from the bit-stream of the IP core design ([Nie *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib21)), or by tracing the voltage ([Ziener and Teich, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib22)), etc. On the other hand, watermark at higher design level be identified from the datapath and/or the control path of the IP design.
    

#### 5.2.2 Overview on symmetric IP core protection techniques

The main goal of symmetrical IP core protection is to generating unique one to one mapped IP core between IP user and IP seller. From the seller side, it will not only protect the ownership of the IP seller but also he can identify the traitors among the list of IP buyers. If all the buyers get identical IP from the seller and one of them may unlawfully redistribute it identifying the actual dishonest buyer will become insurmountable ([Gang and Potkonjak, 2007](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib3)). There are only two approaches in the literature which have presented symmetrical IP core protection techniques. In the approach presented in Lach *et al.* ([2001](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib26)), a hidden encrypted mark is embedded into the physical layout of a digital circuit when it is placed and routed onto the FPGA. This mark uniquely identifies both the source of the circuit and original recipient of the circuit, which is also difficult to remove. Thus, the approach provides protection for both the entities (IP buyer and IP seller) but in lower design abstraction level, i.e. layout level, not in higher design abstraction level. On the other hand, the approach presented in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) provides symmetrical protection during HLS. This approach embeds hidden buyer’s and seller’s signature constraints as multi-variable fingerprint and watermark during register allocation and scheduling stages of architectural synthesis. Signature embedding process is not time consuming and less complex; additionally, overhead generated due to additional constraints is significantly low. Furthermore, detail explanation of this approach is discussed in the next section.

### 5.3 Symmetrical IP core protection for DSP core

The symmetrical protection approach presented in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) covertly inserts fingerprinting and watermarking constraints to protect the IP buyer as well as the IP seller during HLS. Based on the signature constraints provided by a buyer, an IP seller inserts buyer fingerprint with his own watermark; thus, safeguards the privileges of seller and buyer against popular IP threats like IP piracy, IP cloning, false claim of ownership, etc. (discussed in Section 5.1). Both buyer fingerprint and seller watermark taken as input from the respective entities are decoded to obtain the corresponding signature constraints. Firstly, the fingerprinting constraints are embedded in scheduling and register allocation phase within HLS (shown in [Figure 5.3](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig3)). Once the fingerprint implanted design is obtained; then, lastly the watermarking constraints are implanted in register allocation phase. Thus, a DSP IP core design has both fingerprinted and watermarked constraints, in addition to its normal design constraints (i.e. module library, resource configurations, etc.). The multiplexing process for each resource is generated to identify the resource interconnectivity, multiplexer size, and inputs/outputs of the watermarked and fingerprinted design. Using generated multiplexing scheme of each resource, the complete datapath and timing description of the control unit of the DSP IP core are developed. Thus, the final output of a symmetrically protected RTL design of an IP core is created as datapath and controller where each component is designed using hardware description language (HDL).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-05-f03.jpg)

Figure 5.3 Symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores

Thereafter, these HDL files are fed into computer-aided design (CAD) software for RTL synthesis. It produces optimal gate level description of the respective design. This is then subsequently verified and transformed to corresponding bitstreams for the validation on a programmable hardware. After being validated, it is then fed into CAD tools for physical designing. Lastly, the GDS design file generated is sent to the fab.

#### 5.3.1 Problem formulation

To determine an optimal symmetrically protected design solution for a particular data flow graph (DFG) within user specified area-delay constraints. It may be expressed as:

***Minimize:*** Embedding cost (*A*[total], *L*[total]) for an optimal design solution (*X*[*i*]), where (*X*[*i*]) = *N*(*R*[1]), *N*(*R*[2]),…, *N*(*R*[*D*]); and *N*(*R*[*D*]) is the number of resource type *R*[*D*].

***Subject to:*** *A*[total] ≤ *A*[cons] and *L*[total] ≤ *L*[cons] to symmetrically protect an IP core, where *A*[total] and *L*[total] are total area and latency of the symmetrically protected design and *A*[cons] and *L*[cons] are user provided area and latency constraints respectively.

#### 5.3.2 Symmetrically protected design—area evaluation model

Total design area (*A*[total]) consumed by a symmetrically protected reusable IP core is formulated by the following model ([Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c05_eqn1.gif)

Total design area is evaluated by adding total area of hardware resource units (like adder, subtractor, multiplier, etc.), interconnecting units (such as multiplexer and de-multiplexer), and storage units (such as register). The total design area is evaluated for module library of 15-nm NanGate-based technology ([NanGate, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib33)).

#### 5.3.3 Symmetrically protected design—delay evaluation model

Total design latency (*L*[total]) of symmetrically protected reusable IP core can be expressed by the metric below ([Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c05_eqn2.gif)

where total[cs] and delay[cs] indicate the total number of control step (CS) of the design and execution delay of each CS, respectively. The total design latency is evaluated with respect to module library of 15-nm NanGate-based technology ([NanGate, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib33)) with 1, GHz clock frequency.

#### 5.3.4 Symmetrically protected design—cost evaluation function

The design cost is assessed by following metric ([Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c05_eqn3.gif)

where, *C*[*f*](*X*[*i*]) is the design cost of the symmetrically protected reusable IP core with resource configuration *X*[*i*], *A*[max], and *L*[max] are the maximal area and latency in the design space, *w*1 and *w*2 are user provided area and latency weightage factor, to provide equal preference both is kept as 0.5.

#### 5.3.5 Encoding rules of buyer fingerprint and seller watermark for DSP IP cores

Signatures for both parties can be embedded into the design during HLS as encoded additional constraints. Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) encoded fingerprinting and watermarking constraints are implanted covertly in scheduling and register allocation phases of DSP core design methodology (using HLS as backbone). More specifically, buyer fingerprint constraints in scheduling step are performed by forcing particular operations in a particular CS while resolving scheduling conflict. It is a very intelligent process of embedding buyer fingerprint, as it will incur zero hardware and may incur nominal latency overhead. Additionally, during register allocation, the fingerprinting and watermarking constraints are inserted with the notion of colored interval graph (CIG), where each node of the graph indicates storage variables of the design and the connecting edges indicates execution-time overlapping between conforming storage variables.

More explicitly, if there is execution-time overlap between two storage variables, then there will be an edge between those corresponding nodes. Therefore, injecting extra edges as encoded signature constraints will force storage variables of a CIG to implement using distinctive registers. Corresponding illustration of the approach devised in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) is shown is [Figure 5.4](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig4).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-05-f04.jpg)

Figure 5.4 Design flow of symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores using fingerprint and watermark

Fingerprint encoding rules: The fingerprint encoding process devised in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) embeds additional constraints in both scheduling and register allocation phases of DSP core design to enhance the signature strength. The definition of fingerprint encoding rule for each variable devised in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) is as follows:

*   A = While resolving scheduling conflict force even operation in odd CS in scheduling phase.
    
*   B = While resolving scheduling conflict force odd operation in even CS in scheduling phase.
    
*   C = Add additional edge between node pair number (odd, odd) in the CIG.
    

The operations need to be sorted initially based on their operation number to apply the encoded fingerprinting constraints for ‘A’ and ‘B.’ Similarly, the storage variables need to be sorted before applying encoded fingerprinting constraints for ‘C’ (note: this encoded fingerprint embedding approach is demonstrated using a working application in the upcoming section). The robustness of buyer fingerprint is directly proportional with the signature strength. [Roy and Sengupta (2017)](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32) are capable to accept and embed any big size fingerprint. As seen, this fingerprint embedding process includes of three different variables and each variable carries a distinctive encoding rule which un-invites significant overhead to the design with respect to area and latency while preserving robustness.

It is recommended that while selecting buyer fingerprint, the signature should have higher number of ‘A’ and ‘B’ digits than ‘C’ digits. The reason is that, the encoding of ‘A’ and ‘B’ digit are formulated in a way that it incurs nil hardware area and trivial latency overhead. This is conceivable as both the digits are injected while resolving operation scheduling conflict, i.e. fingerprint encoding rule acts as conflict resolver. On the contrary, too many ‘C’ digits in the signature may yield hardware overhead. Nonetheless, it is a key digit as it augments additional security layer by implanting the fingerprint constraint in another phase of HLS.

Watermark encoding rules: The watermark encoding mechanism used in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) is adopted from ([Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib14)). In ([Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib14)), supplementary constraints for watermark are implanted in the register allocation by injecting the extra edges between the nodes of a CIG. Inserting extra edges mandates storage variables of a CIG to be implemented in distinctive registers. This methodology is flexible for injecting any number of extra edges in the register allocation step. The robustness of the watermark surges with the number of extra edges (i.e. signature magnitude) implanted. Although strength upsurges by increment in size of watermark signature, a bulky signature invites major design overhead. Consequently, it becomes obligatory to use a strong watermarking that delivers extensive protection with marginal design cost burden. As mentioned earlier, ([Roy and Sengupta 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) use a multi-variable watermark process from ([Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib14)). The watermark generation mechanism in Sengupta and Bhadauria ([2016](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib14)) consist of four different variables. The seller can generate unique watermark through an arbitrary blend of these four variables. Each variable depicts a unique encoding rule injects an extra edge between two specific nodes. More explicitly, choice of node pair from CIG to insert an extra edge is well explained in the encoding scheme. The explanation of the encoding scheme has been described below:

*   i = Add additional edge between node pair number (prime, prime) in the CIG.
    
*   I = Add additional edge between node pair number (even, even) in the CIG.
    
*   T = Add additional edge between node pair number (odd, even) in the CIG.
    
*   ! = Add additional edge between node pair number (0, any integer) in the CIG.
    

Although ‘C’ digit of fingerprint and ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ digits of watermark, implant signature constraints in register allocation phase through CIG, nevertheless as their encoding rules are distinctive; therefore, the ensuing constraints will be totally dissimilar.

#### 5.3.6 Multi-variable signature embedding process

The steps to achieve symmetrical IP protection by implanting fingerprint and watermark process are described in the rest of the section.

Process of implanting fingerprint

**Broad steps:**

1.  Choose buyer signature.
    
2.  Decode the signature to obtain equivalent fingerprinting constraints.
    
3.  Resolve operation conflict during scheduling to embed fingerprinting constraints.
    
4.  Construct the CIG based on assigning storage variables into register.
    
5.  Perform re-allocation of register if necessary while inserting additional edges in CIG based on fingerprinting constraints.
    

**Detailed steps:**

1.  Receive a preferred signature as random mixture of: ‘A,’ ‘B,’ and ‘C’ digits from buyer.
    
2.  Construct a sorted list of operations of the DFG in increasing order based on their operation number.
    
3.  Decode fingerprinting constraint corresponding to digits ‘A’ and ‘B’ that will help to resolve operation conflict during scheduling phase.
    
4.  Initiate DFG scheduling based on the given resource configuration.
    
5.  In case of operation conflict during scheduling, apply decoded fingerprint constraints (in step 3) to resolve the conflict. *Note*: *When there are no fingerprinting constraints available, conflict is broken based on sorted ordering*.
    
6.  Allocate storage variables in the partially fingerprinting constraints embedded scheduling and construct a CIG to identify the least number of registers compulsory for assignment.
    
7.  Sort the allocated storage variables in increasing order based on their number.
    
8.  Construct a timing table for register allocation based on the generated CIG.
    
9.  Generate a list of extra edge pairs conforming to ‘C’ digit(s) by traversing the sorted storage variables in step 7.
    
10.  Inject the extra edges in the CIG based on decoded fingerprint constraints and perform re-allocation of register if necessary.
     

After executing the aforesaid steps, a buyer fingerprint implanted IP design is produced. This buyer fingerprint implanted IP design acts as an input for implanting the seller watermark next.

Process of implanting watermark

**Broad steps:**

1.  Choose seller signature.
    
2.  Decode the signature to obtain equivalent watermarking constraints.
    
3.  Construct the CIG from the fingerprint constraints embedded scheduling.
    
4.  Perform re-allocation of register if necessary while inserting extra edges in CIG based on watermarking constraints.
    

**Detailed steps:**

1.  Accept fingerprint constraints implanted IP design as an input.
    
2.  Sort the allocated storage variables in increasing order based on their number.
    
3.  Admit a chosen signature as random blend of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ from seller where each character carries a unique value of additional edges to be inserted.
    
4.  Create a list of additional edge pairs corresponding to its encoded values by scanning the sorted nodes.
    
5.  Inject the extra edges in the CIG of fingerprint implanted design as watermark constraints.
    
6.  Alter the timing table design of register allocation based on generated watermark.
    

Post-execution of the aforesaid steps, an IP design with seller watermark is also produced. Therefore, the IP design contains signature of the dual entities.

#### 5.3.7 Signature detection process

This process is obligatory for any encoded signature embedding scheme. As evident, in this phase, the implanted signature constraints are detected from an IP core. It is a crucial process to resolve ownership conflict. Signature detection presented in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) is a two-step process:

*   *Design inspection*: Design inspection step collects the pertinent evidence in terms of specification, structural feature, etc., from a signature implanted IP core design. The objective is to rebuild the controller and the datapath.
    
*   *Signature verification*: Signature verification step performs validation of the signatures in the received IP core. The existences of signature constraints are corroborated in the controller and datapath design to determine the seller’s and buyer’s right.
    

#### 5.3.8 Desirable properties of signature

The signatures embedded into the symmetrically protected IP core design contain the properties below:

*   *Lower embedding cost*: An ideal signature should incur marginal design overhead with respect to hardware area and latency. In Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)), both fingerprint and watermark imposes low design overhead.
    
*   *Resiliency against attacks*: An ideal signature must be so strong and robust that it cannot be removed or tampered easily by an attacker. In Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)), both fingerprint and watermark are equipped with strong protection. In the absence of comprehensive information of both encoding rules, it is extremely challenging to eliminate or meddle the fingerprint and watermark. Additionally, it is also difficult to identify in which HLS step the signatures are embedded. Besides, the signatures’ constraints are distributed all over the IP design which renders it more resistant against attacks.
    
*   *Fault tolerance ability*: An ideal signature must be distributed enough throughout the design so that partial removal of the signature constraints does not prevent the proof of ownership. As in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)), the signature scheme dispenses the constraints all over the design; therefore, ownership remains intact even after fractional elimination of the signature constraints.
    
*   *Adaptability to modern CAD tool*: An ideal signature must be easily adaptable into any modern CAD tool. In the approach ([Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)), both the signature inserting procedure is well-suited to any CAD software. It can be incorporated effortlessly.
    
*   *Lower time*: An ideal signature creation process must not be very composite to generate a signature. In Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)), the signature creation time for both fingerprint and watermark are significantly low. Additionally, for an authentic entity (who has the comprehensive cognizance of encoding rules), the signature detection methodology is straightforward.
    

### 5.4 Case study of symmetrical IP core protection

This section is divided into two subsections: the first subsection demonstrates the fingerprint formation and embedding process while next portion demonstrates the watermark formation and embedding scheme of Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)). As stated earlier, fingerprint constraints of ‘A’ and ‘B’ have been implanted during scheduling phase by allocating particular operations to particular CS, during schedule conflict resolution mechanism. On the other hand, variable ‘C’ injects extra edges in register allocation phase by forcing specific storage variables to implement in distinctive registers. On the contrary, watermarking constraints (as a mix of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’) are implanted in the register allocation step by forcing specific storage variables to implement in diverse registers.

#### 5.4.1 Demonstration of fingerprinting constraints embedding process

DFG of MESA benchmark is taken for demonstration purpose. Additionally, two adders and three multipliers are provided as resource configuration. The scheduled DFG of MESA benchmark using aforesaid resource configuration is shown in [Figure 5.5](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig5). No signature constraint is embedded in that design. Corresponding tabular representation of the same scheduling is shown in [Table 5.1](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl1). Now let us assume that a 7-digit buyer signature is provided as: **‘AAABACC’**. The signature provided by the buyer is then deciphered. The signature and its respective deciphered constraints are depicted in [Table 5.2](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl2). Deciphered constraints are attained using the fingerprint encoding rules described in Section 5.3.E. Now, the DFG of MESA benchmark needs is subjected to scheduling based on the resource configuration with fingerprinting constraints. In cs 1, four multiplication operations, viz., opn 1, opn 2, opn 3, and opn 4, are ready to be scheduled but only three multiplier units are present. This creates schedule operation conflict situation. This conflict can be resolved by inserting decoded fingerprint constraints in the scheduling phase. For instance, first digit ‘A’ forces even multiplication operation, i.e. opn 2 into odd CS, i.e. cs 1 while resolving scheduling conflict. Likewise, the next digit ‘A’ forces multiplication opn 4 in odd cs 1, while resolving the scheduling conflict. In case of the third digit ‘A’, no even operation is available to schedule; therefore, next multiplication is scheduled in cs 1 by merely picking the first operation from the sorted list. Hence, opn 1 is chosen and scheduled in cs 1. Similarly, for fourth digit ‘B’ odd operation, i.e. opn 5 is scheduled in even cs 2, while resolving scheduling conflict. Further even operation, i.e. opn 6 is scheduled in odd cs 3 for fingerprint encoding of digit ‘A’. This fingerprint constraint implanting mechanism in scheduling will operate up until all operation conflicts resolutions are done. The final schedule after embedding buyer fingerprint is shown in [Table 5.3](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl3). It can be observed from [Table 5.1](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl1) (no constraints embedded) and [Table 5.3](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl3) (with fingerprint constraints) that both the scheduled design has same number of CS and same resource configuration. Consequently, the buyer fingerprint is implanted in the design with completely nil area and nil latency overhead, without changing the functionality.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-05-f05.jpg)

Figure 5.5 Scheduled DFG of MESA benchmark using two adders and three multipliers without embedding any constraints

![image](OEBPS/images/tab5.1.jpg)

**Table 5.2** Fingerprint and watermark and its corresponding decoded constraints

**Table 5.3** Tabular representation of scheduled MESA benchmark using two adders and three multipliers post implanting fingerprint constraints

Subsequently, the storage variables (S1–S17) are allocated in the fingerprint embedded scheduling and its equivalent CIG is generated (shown in [Figure 5.6](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig6)). In the CIG of [Figures 5.6](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig6) and [5.7](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig7), red node is indicated by R, yellow node by Y, blue node by B, and green node by G. Similar convention is applicable for [Tables 5.4](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl4) and [5.5](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl5). The timing table of register allocation of the same CIG is shown in [Table 5.4](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl4). Corresponding to two ‘C’ digits, two additional edges need to be inserted in the generated CIG as fingerprint constraints. Although two extra edges have to be inserted, but fortuitously an edge between S1, S3 is previously present in the CIG. Therefore, only one new edge between S1, S5 needs to be added. This indicates storage variable S1 and S5 must be executed through distinct register. According to [Table 5.4](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl4), both S1 and S5 are executed through same register (Green), which indicates that modification in register allocation process is required. The revised timing table of register allocation is evident in [Table 5.5](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl5), where S1 is executed through register green and S5 is executed through register red.

#### 5.4.2 Demonstration of watermarking constraints embedding process

After implanting buyer fingerprinting constraints in the design, the fingerprint embedded design is now fed into the block for watermark insertion. For demo purpose, a 7-digit seller signature is chosen as: **‘i i i I I T !’**. The signature and its equivalent deciphered constraints as extra edge between nodes in CIG are shown in [Table 5.2](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl2). It can be observed using the CIG shown in [Figure 5.6](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig6), only two extra edges ((S2, S7) and (S1, S4)) as constraints requires implanting in the CIG, because rest of the five edges are previously existing. Because of an extra edge injected between S1 and S4, both are forced to execute in distinctive registers. S2 and S7 are by default implemented using distinctive registers as apparent in [Table 5.5](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl5). The final revised CIG is shown in [Figure 5.7](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig7), and [Table 5.6](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl6) depicts its corresponding timing table for register allocation. In [Figure 5.7](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig7), dotted edge between S1 and S5 indicates fingerprint constraints and dotted edge between S2 and S7 indicates watermark constraints. It is evident that nil area and latency overhead are obtained after implanting watermark. Therefore, in case of MESA application, implanting both fingerprint and watermark attains completely nil area and latency design.

### 5.5 Analysis of case studies for DSP cores

Symmetrical IP core protection mechanism in Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) generates a low overhead strongly secured DSP IP core design. To validate the robustness and low overhead, following metrics are used by Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)):

*   Implanting cost for both signatures in a design indicating design quality.
    
*   Area overhead with respect to resources and extra register needed while implanting fingerprint and watermark.
    
*   Time consumed to generate signature.
    
*   Strength of signature in terms of probability of coincidence.
    
*   Influence of large size fingerprint and watermark on design area, design delay, and implanting cost.
    
*   Scalability to deal with bigger size applications.
    

Therefore, the analysis/case study section is divided as follows: (i) result of symmetrical IP core protection approach ([Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) in context of design latency, design area, embedding cost, and strength of signature, and (ii) comparative study between Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) and unsymmetrical IP core protection approach ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)). (Note: as no approach for symmetrical IP core protection exists for DSP core.)

#### 5.5.1 Analysis of embedding cost, security metric on DSP Cores symmetrical protection

The analysis of design latency, design area, and implanting cost of DSP cores for both fingerprint strength (*F*) and watermark strength (*W*) equal to 30 is shown in [Table 5.7](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl7). For instance, for JPEG, the resultant latency, area, and embedding cost are 14.24 ps, 724.30 μm², and 0.7349, respectively. (Note: module library includes resources corresponding to 15-nm technology scale extracted from NanGate ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib33)).) The cost of each solution is calculated based on Eq. (3).

The strength of watermark signature is indicated through probability of coincidence (*P*[*c*]) metric. It calculates the possibility of redeveloping the same design solution with the watermark signature; thus, designates the evidence of authorship. The *P*[*c*] which is derived from Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) can be defined as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c05_eqn4.gif)

where *c* is the number of color required and *W* is the size of watermarking constraints. It can be observed from [Table 5.8](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl8) that with the increment in signature size, *P*[*c*] decreases. A lower *P*[*c*] value indicates stronger proof of ownership. Therefore, to achieve a sturdier proof of ownership, a bigger size signature should be selected.

**Table 5.8** Measuring strength of watermark using probability of coincidence (P[c]) ([Roy et al., 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10))

![image](OEBPS/images/tab5.8.jpg)

The effect of increasing fingerprint strength on the design latency, hardware area, and implanting cost is shown in [Table 5.9](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl9). Three different fingerprint sizes is selected, viz. 10, 20, and 30 to observe the comparative outcome on various design metrics. It can be observed from [Table 5.9](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl9) that for most of the benchmarks, the increment of design area is zero with the increment of fingerprint size. The reason is that out of three different fingerprint encoding variables only ‘*C*’ variable embeds fingerprinting constraints during register allocation phase, which may incur area overhead. Therefore, with the increase in fingerprint size, the possibility of incurring design area overhead is very minimal. On the other hand, minimal increment in design latency can be observed with the increment of fingerprint size from [Table 5.9](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl9). The reason is that adding fingerprinting constraints during scheduling phase while resolving operation conflict. However, for both design area and design latency, the increment is minimal. Therefore, nominal increment in cost with increment in fingerprint size can be observed for some benchmarks.

**Table 5.9** Change of latency, area and cost with the change of fingerprint constraints ([Roy et al., 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10))

![image](OEBPS/images/tab5.9.jpg)

The effect of increasing watermark strength (after implanting fingerprint) on the design latency, hardware area, and implanting cost is shown in [Table 5.10](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl10). As mentioned earlier, watermark is embedded after embedding fingerprint; therefore, diverse watermark sizes chosen are shown by both *W* and *F*. In [Table 5.10](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl10), the seller watermark strength is altered (by retaining the buyer fingerprint strength to maximal strength, i.e. *F* = 30) to observe its comparative consequence on aforementioned design objectives. Three different watermark sizes are selected, viz. *W* = 10 and *F* = 30, *W* = 20 and *F* = 30, and *W* = 30 and *F* = 30. It can be observed from [Table 5.10](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl10) that for all the benchmarks the increment of design latency is zero with the augmentation of watermark size. The reason is watermarking constraints are not implanted during scheduling (which thus does not incur latency overhead). Therefore, increment in latency is zero with the increment in watermark size. On the other hand, minimal increment in design area can be observed by increasing the watermark size (in [Table 5.10](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl10)). The reason is that augmenting more watermarking constraints during register allocation phase may result into register overhead. Therefore, marginal upsurge in cost by increasing watermark size can be witnessed for some benchmarks.

#### 5.5.2 Comparative study between symmetrical and non-symmetrical technique

The DSP IP designs produced through Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) are compared with baseline IP core design, where baseline design indicates an unprotected design (i.e. a design without fingerprint and watermark) in terms of design latency, design area, and implanting cost. As shown in [Table 5.11](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl11), symmetrical IP protection can be achieved at minimal latency overhead (avg. 1.87%), at minimal area overhead (avg. 0.24%), and at very minimal design cost overhead (less than 1%) in comparison to original baseline.

As stated previously, except Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)), there is no symmetrical IP core protection approach for DSP cores. Therefore, symmetrical protection approach ([Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) is compared with Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) (inserts seller watermark only) in context of design latency, design area, and implanting cost. It can be observed from [Table 5.12](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl12), symmetrical IP protection can be achieved at nil area overhead (0%), trivial latency overhead (avg. 1.87%), and at very low design cost overhead (lesser than 1%) relative to Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)).

**Table 5.12** Comparative study between a non-symmetrical design ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) and symmetrically protected IP core design with respect to latency, area, and cost ([Roy et al., 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10))

It can be observed from the table that the register overhead of Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) is zero compared with Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)), where only seller watermark is present. Furthermore, the register overhead of the symmetrical protection approach ([Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) is almost negligible compared with baseline design (less than 0.07%). Additionally, [Table 5.13](#Chapter5.html#c05_tbl13) also shows comparison of Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)) with Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) in terms of signature generation time. For Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)), signature generation time contains creation time of buyer fingerprint and seller watermark; on the contrary, for Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) signature, generation time contains creation time of seller watermark only. It can be observed from the table that Roy *et al.* ([2008](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib10)), while embedding both multi-variable fingerprint and watermark marginally increments the runtime overhead relative to Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib18)) (which only inserts two-variable based signature). This pattern can be seen for all size application; thus, confirming the scalability of Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)).

Design cost overhead for different sizes tested DSP cores is shown in [Figure 5.8](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig8). It can be observed from the graph shown in [Figure 5.8](#Chapter5.html#c05_fig8) that increment in benchmark size (i.e. amount of parallel operations) causes design cost overhead percentage to fall. Cost overhead of Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) is maximum for ARF benchmark (which includes least possible number of parallel operations), while it is minimal for JPEG benchmark (which includes maximum number of parallel operations). The reason of the following: Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) embed fingerprint constraints, while resolving operation scheduling conflict which happens frequently for larger size benchmarks (having huge amount of parallel operations) operating within a given/explored resource constraint. Thus, Roy and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter5.html#c05_bib32)) attain almost insignificant overhead for large size benchmarks, thus satisfying the scalability property.

### 5.6 Conclusion

This chapter presents a symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores. This approach incurs very low overhead in the context of design latency, design area, and embedding cost compared with baseline design. Furthermore, the fingerprint and watermark encoding mechanisms discussed in this chapter are very strong in terms of security. In addition to producing marginal overhead and providing strong robustness, this approach has fault tolerance ability, lower signature embedding time, and adaptability to any CAD tool. The robustness of the symmetrical protection discussed in chapter can be improved by embedding signature constraints in other steps of HLS like resource binding, hardware allocation, etc. This would allow executing a relative investigative study between distinctive HLS phases to explore the well-matched step for signature implanting. Additionally, robustness can also be improved by adding more variables in the signature encoding process.

1.  Why symmetrical IP core protection necessary?
    
2.  Why embedding symmetrical protection scheme is necessary?
    
3.  Which HLS step enables insertion of fingerprint?
    
4.  Write the difference between watermark and fingerprint?
    
5.  In symmetrical protection of DSP core which entity protection is performed earlier?
    
6.  What are the steps to obtain CIG?
    
7.  Where are the storage variables inserted and how?
    
8.  How is resource const. scheduling performed using list scheduling?
    
9.  What does additional edge in CIG represents?
    
10.  What is the impact of FP size on the number of additional edges?
     
11.  Implement a 6th-order FIR filter that incorporate eight digit fingerprint and watermark.
     
12.  How can a design reduce design overhead during symmetrical protect of IP core without compromising security?
     
13.  Explain the threat models of buyer entity and seller entity?
     
14.  Explain some of the existing IP protection schemes?
     
15.  Why symmetrical IP core protection is performed at architecture level?
     
16.  Explain some of the desirable properties of a fingerprint?
     
17.  What is the role of a colored interval graph in fingerprinting? How is it different from its role in watermarking?
     
18.  Explain the detailed steps of fingerprinting of DSP cores?
     
19.  What is fault tolerance in case of symmetrical IP core protection?
     
20.  How do you ascertain the design cost overhead of a symmetrically protected IP core? What is the trend? Which DSP cores have higher cost overhead and why?

Sengupta A., Roy D., and Mohanty S. P., ‘Triple-phase watermarking for reusable IP core protection during architecture synthesis,’ *IEEE Transactions on CAD of Integrated Circuits and Systems*, 2018, **vol. 37** (4), pp. 742–755.

Sengupta A., Bhadauria S., and Mohanty S. P., ‘Embedding low cost optimal watermark during high level synthesis for reusable IP core protection’, in Proceedings of 48th IEEE International Symposium on Circuits & Systems (ISCAS), Montreal, May 2016, pp. 974–977.
