## *Chapter 6*  
**Computational forensic engineering for resolving ownership conflict of DSP IP core**

Some of previous chapters focused on watermarking and fingerprinting for ownership protection. This chapter focuses on another technique called forensic engineering (FE) for ownership protection. FE extracts the features of IP cores and matches to statistically suggest the original ownership. It also discusses various steps involved in FE of a hard IP core and presents specific details with case study examples.

### 6.1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of electronic/SoC industry along with the fierce competition should be considered to remain competent. To beat the competition, companies seek to reduce time-to-market and design cost. These goals can be easily met through utilization of reusable IP core(s) ([Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib22); [Kachave and Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib9)). This is because reusable IP core(s) minimize design time by reducing the manpower required to reproduce an IP. Therefore, reusable IP core has become a mandatory component of generic SoC/IC design flow. Moreover, a design process at higher level of design abstraction such as HLS is always crucial for complex SoCs such as DSP/multimedia cores (Sengupta and Sedaghat, [2010](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib29), [2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib30)). This is because a higher level of design abstraction reduces design complexity and identifies optimal (low-cost) design architecture based on several orthogonal design objectives. Therefore, reusable IP core(s), such as DSP/multimedia core generated through HLS, is an essential component for consumer electronics devices. However, an IP core is vulnerable to various threats such as IP piracy, Trojan insertion, IP overbuilding, and false claim of ownership ([Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib23); [Yasin *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib37); [Sengupta and Kundu, 2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib27)). An estimate based on the report presented in the [International Chamber of Commerce (2011)](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib8) shows that electronics industry lose roughly minimum 1.5 trillion USD annually due to piracy and counterfeiting ([Zhang, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib39)). Therefore, it becomes mandatory to devise methodologies that can safeguard an IP core from these aforementioned threats. There are several IP protection mechanisms to overcome these threats, as shown in [Figure 6.1](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig1).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f01.jpg)

Figure 6.1 CFE vs. watermarking for IP core protection

Another technique that targets protection of IP core(s) is hardware obfuscation. Obfuscation targets protection against IP piracy and Trojan insertion ([Yasin *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib37)). It aims to obfuscate a design through either structural ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib34); [Li and Zhou, 2013](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib15)) or functional obfuscation ([Lao and Parhi, 2014](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib14)). The primary aim is to increase the efforts of an attacker to identify correct functionality of an IP ([Yasin *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib37)), thus making it hard for an attacker to secretly insert Trojan that can go undetectable during testing phase of an IC design. Further, this also makes it difficult to resell or utilize an IP core because its correct functionality is unknown to an adversary. Obfuscation does not aim to provide protection against ownership conflict (since it does not insert a unique ID or signature). However, functional obfuscation can be used to protect against reverse engineering of an IP core. Functional obfuscation implements a locking technique that can be used to safeguard an IP core against reverse engineering of its netlist. However, an adversary can reverse engineer an IP core, identify the correct key through various attacks, and misuse the IP core.

Yet another technique named “IP metering” aims to provide protection against IP piracy and IP overbuilding. This methodology seeks to distinguish one IP from another made through same fabrication process ([Koushanfar and Qu, 2001](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib11)). Therefore, when the IP core passes through untrustworthy design phases ([Yasin *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib37)) of a generic IC design flow, those which are pirated or not reported by the foundry (overbuild) can be detected. Since each IC contains a unique ID, they can detect piracy or overbuilding whenever required.

Another mechanism that primarily aims to provide protection against false claim of ownership is watermarking (Sengupta *et al.*, [2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib22), [2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib32); [Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib24)). Watermarking embeds a signature in an IP during design phases and detects it to resolve false claim of ownership (see Chapter 3). However, it is vulnerable to reverse engineering-based attacks such as signature tampering. Further, signature insertion may incur hardware overhead ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib32); [Sengupta and Roy, 2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib28)). To overcome some of the limitations of hardware watermarking, another alternative method suggested is computational forensics engineering-based IP core protection that can resolve ownership conflicts with 0% design overhead and no chances of signature tampering.

#### 6.1.1 Overview of forensic engineering

FE has always been an impactful technique for resolving conflicts during criminal cases. Although it has been used intensively in fields such as image tampering and failure analysis, there has been little to no effort made in the literature to utilize such an impactful technique for intellectual property core protection. A good description of computational forensics can be found in Franke and Srihari ([2008](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib4)). A generic computational forensic engineering problem can be formulated as follows: given a solution S to a problem *P*, having a finite set of algorithms/tools A\_n (*n* = 1, …, *I*), applicable to problem P that can produce solution *S*, CFE targets automated identification with a very high degree of confidence that the algorithm/tool A\_i has been applied, to produce solution *S*. The approaches that utilize FE for IP protection are Kachave and Sengupta ([2016](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib9)), [Sengupta and Kachave (2018),](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26) and Wong *et al.* ([2004](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib36)). However, method presented by Wong *et al.* ([2004](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib36)) requires multiple instances of an IP core (obtained through distinct implementation of an algorithm) for providing IP protection, which is not always feasible in real-world scenarios. Further, the technique (“feature-set”) presented in that approach is limited/only applicable to graph coloring and Boolean satisfiability. Additionally, the approach presented in Wong *et al.* ([2004](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib36)) is not applicable to DSP IP core.

A generic CFE approach comprises four steps, namely feature and statistical data collection, feature extraction, entity clustering, and validation (as shown in [Figure 6.2](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig2)). The purpose of these steps is explained as follows:

*   Feature and statistical data collection: In this step, the goal is to observe the solution(s) to problem *P* obtained by algorithm A\_*i* (*i* = 1, …, *n*) and deciding various features that could help in distinguishing one IP core solution from another. These unique features are typically processed through some statistical techniques. Therefore, this step is termed as feature and statistical data collection.
    
*   *Feature extraction*: Once the features are decided, one IP core solution from another solution can be distinguished, the next aim is to extract all these features from each IP core solution through some feature extraction rules.
    
*   *Entity clustering*: In this step, our aim is to divide “s” number of solutions into “k” number of clusters such that each cluster contains solutions that are closely matched. Through this step, the aim is to reduce complexity of problem. Thus, instead of considering “s” solutions separately, it is grouped based on the similarities, and then “k” groups are considered instead of “s” solutions. Further, a generic assumption is that solutions produced through different implementations of same algorithm A\_*i* will have closely matched features. Thus, a cluster should contain solutions generated from different implementations of same algorithm.
    
*   *Validation*: In this step, the features of IP core solution “S” obtained through algorithm A\_*i* is matched with the features of the IP core under test (see problem statement).
    

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f02.jpg)

Figure 6.2 Generic CFE

### 6.2 Computational FE technology

A generic CFE-based methodology comprises four steps as discussed earlier. However, customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) adopts only three steps (as shown in [Figure 6.3](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig3)) and customizes them for resolving IP core ownership conflict. The entity-clustering step is not adopted, because in a typical IP core ownership conflict scenario, the number of entities claiming ownership of an IP is not huge. Therefore, entity-clustering step is not mandatory in customized CFE approach. [Figure 6.4](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig4) ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) shows the flow of customized CFE approach. The customized CFE approach takes input in the form of DSP IP cores generated through HLS tool of vendors competing for ownership of an IP core (termed as IP[*Vn*], where “n” is the number of vendors claiming ownership of IP core) as well as IP core whose ownership is to be awarded/IP core under test (termed as IP[ID]). Note that only executable version of competing vendor’s tool is required. Thus, competing vendors are not concerned about their source code or trade secrets being revealed through the executable version of the HLS tool. Further, if a competing vendor refuses to provide executable version of his/her HLS tool, he/she is discarded from the ownership-awarding process. This is because the rightful owner of an IP core will never hesitate to provide executable version of his/her HLS tool (since ownership of his/her IP is at stake). The initial step of customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) comprises four substeps as shown in [Figure 6.4](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig4). In the initial substep, studies of HLS tools as well as the sample DSP IP cores generated through corresponding HLS tools of each competing vendor are made. Based on this study, various features are decided that can distinguish one IP core solution from the other. The decided features are clubbed as “feature set.” These features can further be classified as generic features and unique features. Generic features are those steps that are either integral part of HLS process (such as scheduling, allocation, and binding) or features ubiquitously present in every DSP IP core generated through HLS tool. The identified generic IP core features for CFE are *scheduling algorithm, resource type*, and *bus width support*. A naïve question may be how generic features can distinguish one IP core from another, if the feature is present in all other competing IP cores. The reason is, for example, in case of scheduling algorithm feature there are several algorithms to implement scheduling which will not be same for every HLS tool. Thus, though property (scheduling) is integral to a HLS methodology, feature (scheduling algorithm) can be different for each HLS tool. Similar reasoning exists for other generic features such as *resource type* and *bus width support.* The property is integral for all HLS tools; however, the feature may be different.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f03.jpg)

Figure 6.3 Customized CFE

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f04.jpg)

Figure 6.4 Customized CFE approach

Unique features are the ones that are not present in each DSP IP core generated through HLS. However, these features are present in IP core of at least one of the competing HLS tools. Thus, unique features will be able to distinguish at least one IP core from all remaining IPs. Once the feature-set is identified, feature extraction rules are devised for extracting these features from each IP core available in the form of HDL. *Note: these feature extraction rules are automated in the form of a computer program*. Further, in the next step of customized CFE approach, automated feature extraction of IP core corresponding to each competing HLS tool as well as IP[ID] core is executed. Finally, ownership of IP[ID] is awarded to vendor whose “feature-set” matches exactly with the “feature-set” of IP[ID]. This final step is termed as IP core validation. The customized CFE approach can be understood more effectively through following case study.

### 6.3 IP core feature extraction algorithms

In a scenario where there is a DSP IP core ownership conflict among tools vendors of Harish Ram *et al.* ([2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib6)), Inoue *et al.* ([2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7)), Sengupta and Sedaghat ([2015](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib31)), Koushanfar *et al.* ([2005](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib12)), Rajendran *et al.* ([2013](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib21)), Mishra and Sengupta ([2014](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib18)), and Sengupta and Bhadauria ([2015](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib24)), the IP core extraction rules can be explained through the aid of a demonstration. Further, it is assumed that executable versions of HLS tools corresponding to each competing vendor are also available.

IP cores are generated and properties are decided that can distinguish at least one IP from another. Based on these properties, features are devised and a “feature-set” is created. The created “feature-set” ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) may comprise generic features and unique features as shown below:

![image](OEBPS/images/disp54.gif)

Once feature-set is determined, feature extraction rules are devised for each feature of the feature-set. Section 6.3.1 discusses feature extraction rules in detail.

#### 6.3.1 Feature extraction rules

*Scheduling algorithm*: Scheduling is an integral step in DSP IP core design ([Paulin and Knight, 1989](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib20); [McFarland, 1988](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib16)). The three most commonly used scheduling algorithms are As Soon As Possible (ASAP), As Late As Possible (ALAP), and List algorithm. There are few other useful scheduling algorithms, but this case study is limited to these three most commonly used scheduling algorithms. The flow graph to identify which scheduling algorithm is utilized to create a DSP IP core is shown in [Figure 6.5](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig5). The feature extraction methodology initially checks for the presence of ASAP scheduling in controller HDL of IP core. If both the rules to identify ASAP scheduling are satisfied, then the scheduling algorithm utilized to create an IP is detected as ASAP. However, if any one of the rules is not satisfied, then the possibility of employing ALAP scheduling in creating an IP core is checked. If both the conditions of ALAP scheduling are satisfied, the scheduling algorithm in IP core is detected as ALAP. Otherwise, the scheduling algorithm detected is LIST.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f05.jpg)

Figure 6.5 Feature extraction methodology for scheduling algorithm

*Resource type*: To identify the presence of resource type feature, the top-level entity datapath HDL of IP core is checked and name of the components are identified. Further, a set of names resembling that of a functional unit (FU) are created as indicators as “type of resources” used to generate a DSP IP core. As shown in [Figure 6.6](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig6), the name of the component is “Mul\_4×4” which indicates a 4×4 multiplier. Similarly, all other component’s names are checked.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f06.jpg)

Figure 6.6 Partial HDL code of an IP core

*Bus width support*: The feature extraction process, devised to identify bus width in an IP core, reads the top-level entity datapath HDL of the respective IP core as input. Subsequently, a list of component names is prepared. Next, the input/output size for each component is extracted as the bus width in that IP core. [Figure 6.7](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig7) shows partial HDL code of a representative IP core. The variable size of the register component named as “Reg\_r1” is size of r1 = size of reg\_r1 = 16 bits. Similarly, sizes of other components are determined and variable size is determined as bus width supported by that IP core design.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f07.jpg)

Figure 6.7 Partial HDL code of an IP core

*Chaining*: As explained in [Sengupta and Kachave (2018)](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26) and Kachave and Sengupta ([2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib10)), the flow diagram of algorithm devised to detect the presence of chaining feature is shown in [Figure 6.8](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig8). The feature extraction algorithm accepts controller HDL of an IP core as input and produces output as whether chaining feature is detected or not. Detection of chaining is ascertained as follows: if during execution time of *i*th FU, multiple (“m”) instances of *j*th FU are executed then chaining feature is present in an IP core design. The algorithm is executed for *i* = 1–*n*, where “*n*” is the total number of FUs present in a particular IP core. The second “if” statement (in [Figure 6.8](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig8)) ensures that algorithm runs for all *j*th FU, other than the *i*th FU. Subsequently, the third “if” statement allows only those instances of *j*th FU to be compared with *i*th FU that started (represented as *CS*[*S*]*(FU*[***i***]*) ≤ CS*[*S*]*(FU*[***j***]*)*) and ended (represented as *CS*[*E*]*(FU*[***i***]*) ≥ CS*[*E*]*(FU*[***j***]*)*) between a single instance of *i*th FU, where *CS*[*S*]*(FU*[***i***]) and *CS*[*S*]*(FU*[***j***]*)* represent starting control step of *i*th and *j*th FU, respectively. Similarly, *CS*[*E*]*(FU*[***i***]) and *CS*[*E*]*(FU*[***j***]) symbolize ending control step of *i*th and *j*th FU, respectively. Finally, the last “if” statement checks whether during execution time (*CS*[*E*]*(FU*[*i*]*) – CS*[*S*]*(FU*[*i*]*)*) of FU of *i*th type, multiple instances of FU of *j*th type are executed or not. Thus, if the last *if* condition is satisfied, then chaining feature is detected in a DSP IP core. [Figure 6.9](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig9) shows the partial HDL code of controller of an IP core. As shown in controller’s HDL, the multiplier FU is enabled in control step 1 represented by statement MUL\_En\_1<= “1”. Adder FU is enabled in the first CS and disabled in the second CS. Further, second instance of Adder FU is activated in third CS and deactivated in fourth CS. Last, multiplier FU execution continues until it is disabled in CS = 40. Thus, during execution of single multiplier FU, multiple instances of adder FU are executed. This indicates that chaining feature is present in this IP core design.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f08.jpg)

Figure 6.8 Algorithm to extract chaining feature

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f09.jpg)

Figure 6.9 Partial controller HDL code of an IP

1.  *Multicycling*: To detect multicycling feature in an IP core, the feature extraction rule reads the controller HDL code of the respective IP core. It checks to detect if the execution time of any FU consumes more than one CS. If the condition is true then it is inferred that multicycling feature is present in that IP core design. The condition to detect the presence of multicycling in the controller HDL code of an IP core is given as: *CS*[*E*]*(FU*[*i*]*)* > *CS*[*S*]*(FU*[*i*]*)*, where *CS*[*S*]*(FU*[*i*]*)* and *CS*[*E*]*(FU*[*i*]*)* represent starting and ending control steps of *i*th FU, respectively.
    
2.  *Data pipelining*: Another optimization technique termed as “Data Pipelining” targets the latency reduction of overall schedule delay of an IP core. This is achieved through performing some operations of the consecutive data sets in parallel as shown in [Figure 6.10](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig10). The devised feature extraction algorithm accepts controller HDL of an IP core as input. Subsequently, if the following condition stated in (6.1) is satisfied, the time overlap between operations of consecutive datasets is detected in an IP core controller design.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f10.jpg)
    
    Figure 6.10 Schedule diagram representing data pipelining between two data sets of a representative IP core
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/c06_eqn61.gif)
    
    where *CS*[*S*]*(N)*[1] represents the starting control step of data set 1, *CS*[*E*]*(N)*[1] and *CS*[*E*]*(N)*[2] represent the ending control step of data set 1 and 2, respectively. As shown in [Figure 6.11(a)](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig11a) and [6.11(b)](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig11b), the starting control step is identified as the control step at which the first FU (such as Multiplier FU in this example) is activated. Further, ending control step of data set 1 is the CS at which the output register (Reg Y) of a data set is enabled for the first time. Similarly, the ending control step of data set 2 is the CS at which the output register (Reg Y) is enabled for the second time. As shown in [Figure 6.11(a)](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig11a) and [6.11(b)](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig11b), register Y is activated for first time at CS 42 and is again activated at CS 82 for the second time. Thus, the condition stated in (6.1) is satisfied. Therefore, data pipelining is detected in an IP core, as demonstrated through this representative example.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f11a.jpg)
    
    Figure 6.11(a) Partial controller HDL code of an IP
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f11b.jpg)
    
    Figure 6.11(b) Partial controller HDL code of an IP
    
3.  *Design objective*: A generic HLS tool used to design an IP core typically has at least one design objective. The design objectives are typically optimization based on power-delay trade-off or area-delay tradeoff, etc. Based on the design objectives supported, one tool used for IP core creation can be distinguished from another. The feature extraction algorithm for extracting design objective feature takes user interface (graphical or nongraphical) of executable version of HLS tool as input. Subsequently, the extraction algorithm reads the interface and determines the design objectives available for selection in a tool’s user interface. Subsequently, the interface’s design objectives are matched and validated with the design objective details mentioned in the datasheet of the IP core under test.
    
4.  *Reliability*: Reliability can take multiple forms such as reliability (detectability/security) against transient fault, reliability (detectability/security) against permanent faults ([Inoue *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7); [Nomura *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib19)). A typical approach that aims to design a reliable system utilizes modular redundancy ([Inoue *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7); [Yu and McCluskey, 2001](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib38); [D’Angelo *et al.*, 1999](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib2)). Redundancy may be dual modular redundancy (DMR), triple modular redundancy, or multimodular redundancy. However, so far in the literature, such as Inoue *et al.* ([2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7)), DSP IP core vendors have only implemented reliability against transient fault using DMR. Therefore, feature extraction rule is discussed only for this feature. The rule aims to detect the presence of DMR logic in DSP IP core design.
    
    Reliability feature extraction process accepts datapath HDL of an IP core as input and aims to detect the presence of a DMR system. As shown in [Figure 6.12](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig12), in a typical DMR system, the outputs of each module of a DMR system are compared using a comparator component to determine whether the fault is detected or not. This comparator component accepts one input from output register of the first module (original) and another from the second module (duplicate). If a port mapping similar to following port map statement in HDL: *port map (output register signal 1, output register signal 2, comparator output signal)* is detected, the reliability feature is present in the respective IP core.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f12.jpg)
    
    Figure 6.12 Schedule diagram of a DMR system
    
5.  *Loop support feature*: The loop support feature aims to detect the type of application that can be fed as an input to an HLS tool used in the IP core design. In other words, this feature extracts whether input format of a tool can support loop-based application in the form of control data flow graph (CDFG) or non-loop-based application in the form of DFG ([Gupta, 2003](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib5); [Kurra and Panda, 2007](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib13); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib34)). The devised rule to identify loop support feature requires input application in C-code. This C-code is fed into executable version of HLS tool. If HLS tool runs correctly without any error and produce comprehensible RTL code, then it supports the respective input format.
    
    Note: this case study only considers executable versions of HLS tools that do not require manual intervention.
    
6.  *Trojan security feature*: In hardware domain, Trojan can be understood as a malicious modification of a hardware design that aims to achieve malicious intention of an attacker ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib21); [Bhunia *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib1); [Zhang and Tehranipoor, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib40)). An attacker may intend to leak information, generate incorrect output, trigger denial of service attacks, etc. There can be several techniques to provide security against Trojan based on their intent. However, so far in the literature for DSP IP cores, protection against Trojan, which intends to harm correct functionality of an IP by generating incorrect output, has been considered. Thus, during the feature extraction rule, only this special Trojan for DSP cores is accounted for. Typically, Trojan security for DSP cores requires modules from at least two different IP vendors. Further, Trojan detection (security) is typically performed using modules from at least two distinct vendors and using them in DMR system as shown in [Figure 6.13](#Chapter6.html#c06_fig13). Therefore, the feature extraction algorithm accepts datapath HDL of an IP core as well as module library of HLS tool as inputs. The presence of DMR is detected (as discussed in reliability feature extraction process) by identifying the presence of a comparator component having port map similar to following port mapping statement: *port map (output register signal 1, output register signal 2, comparator output signal).* Additionally, if the module library comprises design objectives (such as area, power, delay) corresponding to at least two different IP vendors, the presence of Trojan security feature is present in the IP core design.
    
    Note: The main difference between reliability and Trojan security properties is that reliability does not require modules from two distinct IP vendors. On the other hand, Trojan security requires module from two distinct vendors.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-06-f13.jpg)
    
    Figure 6.13 Schedule diagram of a DMR-based Trojan security system
    

#### 6.3.2 IP core validation

Once all the features are extracted, the feature-set of each DSP IP core generated corresponding to competing vendors as well as IP whose ownership is to be determined (i.e., IP[ID]) are created. Subsequently, the feature-set of competing IP vendor is matched with the feature-set of IP[ID] as per (6.2). If match percent (*µ*) of 100% is obtained, then the ownership of IP[ID] is awarded to that particular IP vendor.

![image](OEBPS/images/c06_eqn62.gif)

In a typical scenario, the feature-set used in CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26); [Inoue *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7)) is enough for resolving the IP core ownership conflict. However, we would like to discuss various exceptional scenarios and procedure to follow to resolve the ownership conflict in those scenarios.

*    I. **None of the competing IP vendors has a 100% match**: In such a scenario, the ownership of IP[ID] will not be awarded to any of the vendors competing for claiming the ownership of IP[ID].
    
*   II. **More than one competing IP vendors have a 100% match**: In such a scenario (called “deadlock in IP resolution”), the feature-set should be expanded by identifying additional properties that may distinguish between two or more competing IP vendors. This is performed by further investigating each and every IP core to identify should there be additional properties that could be considered to break this deadlock. Based on this further investigation, new features are added in the feature set. In other words, the feature-set is expanded to incorporate these new features. Further, feature extraction rules need to be devised corresponding to these newly added features. Next, feature extraction is performed now for these newly features from the IP cores who are in deadlock. Subsequently, feature matching is performed with the updated feature-set. Finally, if there is no exceptional scenario, the ownership is awarded to the IP vendor whose feature-set matches 100% with that of IP[ID].
    

#### 6.3.3 Important characteristics of customized CFE

*   Customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) is applicable to a scenario where each competing IP vendor has a unique HLS tool for claiming ownership of IP[ID]. However, in scenarios when two or more IP vendors are claiming ownership based on same HLS tool obtained through third party, then the devised “feature-set” of customized CFE is not suffice for resolving ownership conflict.
    
*   As already discussed in Section 6.2, customized CFE approach requires only executable version of HLS tool. Further, it does not require source code of these HLS tools. Thus, there is no concern for IP vendors about source code or breach of confidential information. Additionally, if some competing IP vendor refuses to provide executable version of HLS tool, the vendor is discarded from ownership-awarding process. This is because, typically, the rightful owner of an IP would not hesitate in providing executable version of his/her HLS tool, as ownership of the IP core is at stake.
    
*   Customized CFE is applicable for IP vendors of DSP IP cores. However, IP vendors for FPGA would not fall within the scope of [Sengupta and Kachave (2018)](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26).
    

### 6.4 Analysis on case studies

This section reports the analysis on case studies for the automated customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) and ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib12)). The customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) was tested on express DSP benchmark suite from Express Benchmark Suite ([http://www.ece.ucsb.edu/EXPRESS/benchmark/](http://www.ece.ucsb.edu/EXPRESS/benchmark/)). The benchmarks primarily comprise DSP applications. The customized CFE approach was executed for data-intensive IP cores (such as ARF, BPF, and DCT), control-intensive IP core (such as FFT and FIR), as well as multimedia data-intensive IP core (such as JPEG IDCT).

#### 6.4.1 Results of the customized CFE approach

For intensive testing of the generic applicability of [Sengupta and Kachave (2018)](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26), diverse IP vendors with their different HLS tools (from academia as well as industry) were selected. Moreover, latest HLS tools of vendors (published in last 10 years) having versatile design objectives (such as area-execution time, power-execution time), different DSE methodologies (such as PSO, GA, and BFOA), and properties (such as Trojan security, fault tolerance, and watermarking) were also included during the analysis. The IP vendors with their HLS tools considered are listed below:

1.  IP Vendor 1: Hybrid PSO-GA-based HLS tool ([Harish Ram *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib6))
    
2.  IP Vendor 2: Fault tolerant-based HLS tool ([Inoue *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib7))
    
3.  IP Vendor 3: Fault secure-based HLS tool ([Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2015](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib31))
    
4.  IP Vendor 4: Watermarking-based HLS tool ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib12))
    
5.  IP Vendor 5: Trojan security-based HLS tool ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib21))
    
6.  IP Vendor 6: PSO-based HLS tool ([Mishra and Sengupta, 2014](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib18))
    
7.  IP Vendor 7: BFOA-based HLS tool ([Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2015](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib24))
    

Tables [6.1](#Chapter6.html#c06_tbl1) to [6.6](#Chapter6.html#c06_tbl6) show the results of analysis obtained for various DSP and multimedia cores. As evident from these tables, customized CFE approach ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) was able to resolve the ownership conflict for each of these cores. Further, even if several IP core features overlap between competing IP vendors, yet customized CFE was still able to resolve the ownership conflict. This shows that customized CFE approach is strongly capable of resolving ownership conflict with the current feature set. It is interesting to note that one feature is enough to distinguish between competing IP vendors. For example, out of the ten features in the feature-set, even if nine features of both IP cores (corresponding to the two competing IP vendors) overlap with IP under test, but only one feature remains distinct to each other, it may be enough identifying the actual IP owner. This is because the competing IP vendor with nine overlapping features will have 90% match with IP[ID] while the actual IP vendor will have 100% match with IP[ID]. For example, as shown in [Table 6.1](#Chapter6.html#c06_tbl1), even though IP[V1], IP[V5], and IP[V7] have eight features common in them, the ownership conflict among these tools with respect to IP[ID] was resolved based on the remaining two features and ownership was awarded to IP core vendor 5. The results obtained for FIR benchmark show an exceptional case as discussed in section III.B, where none of the competing vendor’s “feature-set” matches 100% with the “feature-set” of IP[ID]. In such a case, ownership is not awarded to any of the competing vendors.

As evident from the results, CFE ([Sengupta and Kachave, 2018](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26)) incurs 0% design overhead as compared to hardware watermarking ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib12)). This is because hardware watermarking requires embedding vendor signature into the IP core design, which may incur storage overhead. On the other hand, CFE is performed after IP core has been generated. Therefore, customized CFE does not incur design overheads. Further, due to the same reason, CFE does not impact design performance of an IP core; however, signature insertion during hardware watermarking may impact the performance of an IP core.

### 6.5 Conclusion

This chapter discussed an alternative ownership protection methodology called CFE from [Sengupta and Kachave (2018)](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib26), applicable for resolving ownership conflict of DSP IP cores. Further, the chapter described several features of the “feature-set” that are used as means of resolving ownership conflict with 0% degradation in hardware performance, and incur 0% storage overhead compared to the popular hardware watermarking-based ownership protection for DSP cores ([Koushanfar *et al.*, 2005](#Chapter6.html#c06_bib12)).

The future directions could target devising novel “expanded feature-set” that can resolve ownership conflict of DSP IP core in case of “deadlocks.” Further, feature extraction rules for “scheduling algorithm” feature can be modified to include other scheduling algorithms such as force directed scheduling.

## *Chapter 7*  
**Structural obfuscation of DSP cores used in CE devices**

Previous chapters, watermarking, fingerprinting, and forensic engineering have been discussed for resolving various ownership-related problems. This chapter discusses structural obfuscation approaches to thwart IP piracy and reverse engineering (RE). This approach, when effective, can save billions of dollars of revenue losses in CE and semiconductor industry. Especially, a multi-high-level transformation-based structural obfuscation process has been presented for DSP IP cores as hardware-hardening technique. The chapter is structured as follows: Section 7.2 highlights the fundamentals of obfuscation with stress on structural obfuscation; Section 7.3 discusses different compiler transformation-driven structural obfuscation methodology. Section 7.4 discusses low-cost structurally obfuscated design exploring technique. Section 7.5 demonstrates a multistage structural obfuscation technique through a motivational example. Section 7.6 presents the results of a case study.

### 7.1 Introduction

Today’s CE devices, ranging from modern smart phone, smart TV, home appliance, set-top box, tablet, digicam to recent smart speaker, are designed using SoC platforms ([Thavalengal and Corcoran, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib40); [Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib18); [Kim *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib12)). These SoCs comprise various system modules such as memory (SRAM, Flash), A-to-D converter, custom processor, or co-processor, DSP kernels, A/V codecs, and wireless modems. Among these modules, DSP kernels in the form of IP cores are primarily responsible for data/power-intensive computation at high speed, minimal silicon area, and low power in an SoC ([Li *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib16)). Thus, DSP IP cores are the heart of every SoC-based CE devices. For example, ConnX D2 DSP IP core used in telecom infrastructure of voice-over internet protocol (VoIP) and wireless mobile device ([ConnX, 2009](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib42)). In a cellular telephone system, it is used in speech encoding/decoding process. Low-end DSP IP cores are included in digital camera, portable phones, consumer audio, headsets, while mid-end DSP cores are included in cellular phone, fax/voice receiver. Finally, high-end DSP IP cores are included in various CE systems including wireless base station and cable modems. Further, reusability of DSP IP core maximizes design productivity to cope with the increasing design complexity in electronic systems ([Castillo *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib6)), thus maintaining a balance in global supply chains for SoC-based CE devices (Sengupta and Sedaghat, [2011](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib33), [2013](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib34)).

These reusable DSP IP cores warrant a substantial investment in research, workforce, money, and time by an IP vendor/designer. Therefore, these mandate protection from emerging IP threats such as cloning and/or infringement, and RE ([Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib24); [Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib28); [Wong *et al.*, 2004](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib47); [Koushanfar, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib13); [Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib1); [Sengupta and Kundu, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib29); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2018](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib35)). According to literature sources, the total fiscal revenue loss due to piracy and counterfeiting in 2013 for G20 nations was $96–130 billion which will increase to $199–270 billion in 2022. It is projected that 10% of the internationally sold electronics products are forged ([Guajardo *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib11); [Lao and Parhi, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)). An attacker can “silently” reuse a DSP IP core without legal permission from the IP owner to save design time, cost, and effort ([Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib26)). He/she can easily identify the functionality of a DSP IP core from its architecture through RE. RE of an IP core is a process of identifying its design, structure, and functionality ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib22)). Using RE, one can identify the device technology ([Intel Transistors, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib39)), extract the gate-level netlist ([Torrance and James, 2009](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib43)), and infer the IP functionality ([ExtremeTech, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib10)). Though according to the Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984 (SCPA), RE is a legal process for teaching, analysis, and evaluation purpose; however, an attacker can use RE process for IP piracy/attacks which is illegal. An attacker can also insert malicious Trojan logic into an IP core, if he/she can identify the functionality of a DSP IP core through RE. Therefore, it is very crucial to design a DSP IP core in a way that it provides substantial resiliency against RE ([Yang *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib48); [Parhi, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib20); [Lao and Parhi, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14); [Walz and Schrder, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib45); [Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib27)). A thematic attack scenario of protected DSP IP core for different CE devices is shown in [Figure 7.1](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig1) ([Mohanty, 2003](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib17); [Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib26)). One way to achieve resilience against RE is to obscure the functionality of a DSP IP core by transforming its architecture. This transformation should change the standard structure of a DSP IP core into an unobvious architecture while preserving correct functionality. Therefore, the functionality will not be easily identifiable from its structure, thereby increasing the RE complexity for an adversary. This process is known as structural obfuscation. More broadly, obfuscation is a process of obscuring or disguising the actual functionality of the design (product) in order to protect its intellectual property content. Though hardware obfuscation is motivated from software obfuscation, the former is more complex than the latter, despite both of them fundamentally having the same objective. Software obfuscation aims to conceal the implementation code of an algorithm using techniques such as dead code elimination, code unrolling, while hardware obfuscation aims to obscure the circuit (hardware) functionality/structure. This process is classified, as it is achievable through several complex techniques, depending on which form (design abstraction layer. Refer [Figure 7.2](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig2)) the hardware circuit is described at, e.g., RTL codes, netlist, layout, fabricated chip. Sometimes, the software obfuscation methods after customization can be applied for hardware obfuscation. However, a completely exclusive method may be needed for hardware obfuscation depending on the hardware design abstraction level. In summary, a hardware obfuscator (process or algorithm) is responsible for transforming a design representation “D” into its obfuscated form “O(D)” that has the same functionality as “D,” yet is unintelligible to an adversary targeting to recover “D” from “O(D).” More details on the threat model of obfuscation are explained in the following sections of this chapter.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f01.jpg)

Figure 7.1 A thematic representation of secured DSP IP core for CE devices that is resilient from adversary

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f02.jpg)

Figure 7.2 Abstraction levels of integrated circuit design

#### 7.1.1 Threat model

Hardware structural obfuscation transforms the original hardware design architecture of an IP core into a nonobvious structural architecture. Thus enhancing the RE complexity as it is more tough for an attacker to discover the actual functionality of an IP core from its transformed structure. Consequently, it provides defense against threats resulting due to **RE** such as **IP piracy, IP infringement (counterfeit),** and **Trojan insertion**.

#### 7.1.2 Benefits of providing security at higher design abstraction level

The designing process of a DSP application in the form of an IP core is very complex. Therefore, the DSP IP core design flow is divided into multiple design abstraction levels such as system level, algorithmic level, register transfer level, logic level, and layout level (as shown in [Figure 7.2](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig2)). Every layer has its exclusive design automation or CAD method which enables the design of DSP IP cores with lesser design time. Architectural synthesis (also known as HLS) is one such automatic CAD process, which is responsible for generating equivalent register-transfer-level hardware description languages such as VHDL, Verilog of DSP applications. Examples of a few well-known commercial and academic HLS tools for DSP core/multimedia are shown in [Figure 7.3](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig3) ([Sengupta, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib26); [Mohanty, 2003](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib17)). As shown in [Figure 7.3](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig3), each HLS tool is represented as tool name, followed by the owner name (highlighted in bold) and the launching year of the tool. However, none of these tools incorporate security through obfuscation.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f03.jpg)

Figure 7.3 Classification and examples of HLS tools based on license

The resilience of a DSP IP core against RE can be provided in any abstraction level of the design flow. However, providing resilience against RE attack through structural obfuscation during architectural synthesis is beneficial as the structural change performed in higher design abstraction level obfuscates the datapath and control unit structures of the application. Thus, it also obfuscates the gate structure (netlist) of the application. Additionally, architectural synthesis for digital IPs is way matured to achieve hardware area minimization, power optimization, performance enhancement, and fault-tolerant IP design solution with lesser design complexity. Therefore, structural obfuscation during architectural synthesis is capable of generating a strongly obscured design which is functionally equivalent but appears remarkably different than the original structure. The only way to use this type of obfuscated design is as a “black-box” module ([Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib7)).

### 7.2 Obfuscation for IP core protection—a broad view

This section discusses the fundamentals of different obfuscation-based IP core protection mechanisms with emphasis on high-level transformation-based structural obfuscation mechanisms that are available in the literature.

Obfuscation-based IP protection can be achieved in three different ways: (1) by transforming the HDL code, known as “source code-based obfuscation,” (2) by using key-based logic locking, known as “logic obfuscation,” and (3) by hiding the functionalities of a design, known as “structural obfuscation.”

#### 7.2.1 Code obfuscation techniques

To thwart an attacker from intercepting the HDL code, it either alters ([Brzozowski and Yarmolik, 2007](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib4)) the source code into a compound version or encrypts ([Barria *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib2)) it. In Brzozowski and Yarmolik ([2007](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib4)), HDL code obfuscation is achieved using diverse alteration approaches which are challenging to reverse engineer. In Barria *et al.* ([2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib2)), the source code is encrypted using “Dead Code Addition” approach on a Crypter.

#### 7.2.2 Logic obfuscation techniques

Logic obfuscation (also known as logic encryption) locks the implementation of a design by implanting supplementary components into it. These components are controlled by key gates. Applying incorrect key will produce functionally different output than the correct output of the design. Logic obfuscation is of two types: (1) sequential and (2) combinational ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2013](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib22)). In sequential logic obfuscation, the additional components could exist in a key-controlled obfuscation mode. For example, in Chakraborty and Bhunia ([2009](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib7)), dummy states are added with the original states of the FSM of a design to obfuscate it. These dummy states are controlled by an external key. Applying incorrect key leads to obfuscation mode or invalid state whereas applying correct key leads to normal mode. In Desai *et al.* ([2013](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib8)), the design is locked based on internally generated key sequence (known as Code-Word). This technique hides the design using this Code-Word in the transition function. On applying the incorrect key, the FSM will deviate from the correct transition path.

In combinational logic obfuscation, the additional components could be XOR/XNOR gates ([Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib25); [Rajendran *et al.*, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib21); [Rajendran *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib23)), AND/OR gates ([Dupuis *et al.*, 2014](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib9)), Lookup Table (LUT) ([Baumgarten *et al.*, 2010](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib3)), muxes ([Wang *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib46); [Zhang, 2016](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib49)), or combination of these elements ([Lee and Touba, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib15)). EPIC ([Roy *et al.*, 2008](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib25)) is one of the primary work where the framework of logic obfuscation is proposed. In this approach, XOR/XNOR gates are inserted as key-gates in the random location of the design. Random insertion of key-gates into a design does not always guarantee that wrong output is produced for all input patterns on application of incorrect key. Additionally, in this approach, the key can be sensitized by input pattern. Rajendran *et al.* ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib23)) inserted XOR/XNOR key-gates in the design in such a way that the Hamming distance (HD) between the incorrect output and correct output became maximum. In Lee and Touba ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib15)), XOR/XNOR key-gates are combined with mux key-gates to achieve a higher HD between correct and incorrect output. Key-controlled LUT-based logic obfuscation is proposed in Baumgarten *et al.* ([2010](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib3)). In this approach, the complete IP is divided into multiple fixed and configurable parts. The configurable part is then realized as a key-controlled LUT. As the logic type of the reconfigurable part can be changed after fabrication, an adversarial foundry cannot misuse the IP. Several attack strategies are available against these logic obfuscation techniques, such as key-sensitization ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib23)), Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and hill-climbing search-based attack ([Subramanyan *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib38)). These logic obfuscation techniques have proven to be powerful for combinational/sequential circuits. However, in the context of DSP cores, these techniques incur more design overhead due to extra key-gates been implanted into the design, as well as lack of framework to select low-cost design architecture. Moreover, if the key is leaked somehow, the IP designer cannot prevent any attack until the IP is redesigned for a new key. More details on this technique are provided in Chapter 8.

#### 7.2.3 Structural obfuscation techniques

On the other hand, structural obfuscation tries to hide the correct functionalities of a design through transformations, arbitrary assignment of logic components, inserting dummy wires, or irregular routing ([Vijayakumar *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib44)). In other words, structural obfuscation changes the architecture of an IP core from its standard structure to an unobvious structure while preserving its functionality. Therefore, even if an adversary physically tampers or REs the IP core to obtain its design, it will be harder for him/her to discover its functionality by inspecting its structure. Structural obfuscation does not insert any additional component as key-gate into the design. Therefore, there is no such design overhead for structural obfuscation. In structural obfuscation technique, a design is secured until its functionality is hidden from an adversary. However, if the application is traced by the attacker, structural obfuscation cannot protect an IP core.

High-level transformations such as pipelining, interleaving, unfolding, folding, tree height transformation (THT), redundant operation elimination, and look-ahead transformations can be applied during architectural synthesis of a DSP IP core to achieve a trade-off between multiple design objectives such as area, power, and delay. However, these transformations can also be used as structural obfuscation techniques ([Sengupta and Roy, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib32); [Parhi, 2012](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib20)). These high-level transformations modify the structure of a DSP IP core significantly while keeping the actual functionality unchanged. These alterations result in multiple ambiguous architectures of the same DSP IP core. Authors in Lao and Parhi ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)) have performed structural obfuscation for DSP circuits through a single high-level transformation technique, i.e., folding (Note: Though authors in Lao and Parhi ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)) have performed both structural and functional obfuscation, we are only focusing on the structural obfuscation portion in this chapter). The folding transformation generates various meaningful modes which increase the complexity for an attacker to distinguish the correct functionalities within different modes. Additionally, different folding factors cause different equivalent circuits which lead to ambiguity for an attacker. According to Lao and Parhi ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)), it can be observed that due to folding transformation, circuits with different functionality may have the same structure, and circuits with same functionality may have dissimilar structure. Since folding factor has a crucial impact on the design cost, selecting an appropriate folding factor may lead to an optimized DSP circuit design. However, no optimal folding factor evaluation is presented in the aforesaid approach. Thus, it may lead to higher design overhead. Additionally, single high-level transformation-based ([Lao and Parhi, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)) structural obfuscation for DSP applications is less secured compared to a multistage high-level transformation-based structural obfuscation ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)).

Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)) performed a multiple compiler-driven high-level transformations-based structural obfuscation for DSP core/kernels during architectural synthesis. Unlike Lao and Parhi ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)), this approach is capable of obfuscating loop-based DSP applications also. Further, due to multiple high-level transformations, the obfuscated DSP IP core impacts gate-level structure significantly different than its original structure, thus enhancing the RE complexity. Additionally, this approach performs optimization to select a low-cost architecture that meets the design objectives such as latency, area, and all-inclusive design cost. Therefore, a compiler-driven, low-cost, multistage transformation-based structural obfuscation with stronger robustness is presented in Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)). A detailed explanation of this approach is discussed in Section 7.3.

### 7.3 Compiler transformation-driven structural obfuscation

As mentioned earlier, due to the insertion of additional logic elements, the design as well as lack of framework to select low cost design architecture, overhead of logic obfuscation is significantly larger than the structural obfuscation in the context of DSP IP cores. Additionally, logic obfuscation techniques are vulnerable to multiple attack strategies such as key-sensitization ([Rajendran *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib23)), Boolean SAT, and hill-climbing search-based attack ([Subramanyan *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib38)). Further, the structural obfuscation presented in Lao and Parhi ([2015](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib14)) is less secured against the RE attacks due to its single-stage transformation-based obfuscation technique. The multistage structural obfuscation approach presented in Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)) hides the functionality of a DSP application by transforming its design into an unobvious structure through several successive compiler-driven transformation techniques. Though compiler-driven transformation is a known concept for design optimization, to the best of authors’ knowledge, these transformation techniques have been never used before to perform structural obfuscation. These transformations increase the complexity for an adversary to discover its functionality. Five high-level transformation approaches, i.e., redundant operation elimination (ROE), logic transformation (LT), THT, loop unrolling (LU), and loop-invariant code motion (LICM) are used to obfuscate both loop and non-loop-based DSP IP cores ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)). However, loop-based transformations (i.e., LU and LICM) are not applicable to non-loop-based DSP applications. The structurally obfuscated design is further explored using PSO-based design exploration (DSE) to obtain the low-cost design architecture ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)). Lastly, a low-cost, structurally obscured DSP IP is created. The illustration of low-cost multistage-driven structural obfuscation process is shown in [Figure 7.4](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig4). Detailed explanation of each high-level transformation process used in Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)) is explained in Section 7.3.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f04.jpg)

Figure 7.4 Overview of low-cost multistage-driven structural obfuscation process

#### 7.3.1 Formulation and evaluation models

##### 7.3.1.1 Formulation

To determine a low-cost, structurally obfuscated design for a given DSP core expressed as C-code/DFG or loop-based CDFG within user-specified area-delay constraints.

***Minimize:*** Minimize structurally obfuscated design cost (*A*[total]^(obf), *L*[total]^(obf)) for an optimal design solution (*X*[*i*]), where (*X*[*i*]) = *N*(*R*[1]), *N*(*R*[2]), … , *N*(*R*[D]), at the behavioral level; and *N*(*R*[D]) is the number of resource-type *R*[D].

***Subject to:** A*[total]^(obf) ≤ *A*[cons] and *L*[total]^(obf) ≤ *L*[cons] and RE-resilient IP core through structural obfuscation, where *A*[total]^(obf) and *L*[total]^(obf) are the total area and latency of the structurally obfuscated design and *A*[cons] and *L*[cons] are the user-provided area and latency constraints, respectively.

##### 7.3.1.2 Evaluation models

*   a. Design area evaluation model
    
    Total design area (*A*[total]^(obf)) consumed by a structurally obfuscated reusable DSP IP core is expressed by the following model ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)):
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/c07_eqn1.gif)
    
    Total design area is evaluated by adding total area of hardware resource units (such as adder, subtractor, multiplier), interconnecting units (such as multiplexer and de-multiplexer), and storage units (such as register). The total design area is assessed with respect to module library of 15 nm NanGate-based technology ([Open Cell Library, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib50)).
    
*   b. Design delay evaluation model
    
    Total design latency (*L*[total]^(obf)) of structurally obfuscated reusable IP core is expressed by the following model ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)):
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/c07_eqn2.gif)
    
    In the above expression, *L*[body]^(obf) is the single iteration execution delay of the loop body of obfuscated CDFG; *I* is the total loop iteration (loop count); *L*[first]^(obf) is the delay to execute the first iteration of obfuscated CDFG. The total design latency is evaluated with respect to the module library of 15 nm NanGate-based technology ([Open Cell Library, 2017](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib50)) at 1 GHz clock frequency.
    
*   c. Design cost evaluation function
    
    The solution design cost is estimated using the following function ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)):
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/c07_eqn3.gif)
    
    where *C*[*f*](*X*[*i*]) is the design cost of the structurally obfuscated DSP IP core with resource configuration *X*[*i*], *A*[max]^(obf) and *L*[max]^(obf) are the maximum possible area and latency in the design space, respectively, *w*[1] and *w*[2] are user-specified area and latency weightage factor, respectively; to provide equal preference, both are preset as 0.5.
    

#### 7.3.2 Multistage high-level transformation techniques

As mentioned earlier, the multistage structural obfuscation methodology ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)) is achieved using ROE-, LT-, THT-, LU-, and LICM-based techniques. In this approach, a DSP core is taken as input as C-Code/CDFG or DFG. Each of these transformation techniques is then applied to the input application in order to transform it. Each transformation technique is explained and demonstrated through an example. For example, a nonsecured CDFG (present in [Figure 7.5](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig5)) is accepted as input for demonstration purpose. (Note: Application in [Figure 7.5](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig5) is chosen, as it enables all the five multistage transformations to be demonstrated over a single example. However, any application could have been used.) The application is then scheduled based on user-defined resource configuration (example: three adders and four multipliers). The respective nonobfuscated scheduled CDFG and its corresponding circuit representation are depicted in [Figures 7.6](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig6) and [7.7,](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig7) respectively. The circuit presented in [Figure 7.7](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig7) employs 6 numbers of 4:1 switches, 4 numbers of 2:1 switches, 10 numbers of input registers, 1 number of output register, and 8 numbers of delay elements. This nonobfuscated CDFG is used as an example to explain each transformation technique in the following subsections.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f05.jpg)

Figure 7.5 Original non-obfuscated CDFG

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f06.jpg)

Figure 7.6 Scheduled CDFG of DSP IP design with three adders and four multipliers

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f07.jpg)

Figure 7.7 DSP circuit of a non-obfuscated design

1.  Redundant operation elimination, process: This compiler-driven transformation technique removes the redundant or duplicate operations from a set of operations in a DSP application and then performs necessary adjustment if required. In the context of DFG/CDFG, each operation is represented by a node. Therefore, in the input DFG/CDFG of a DSP core, a node can be recognized as a redundant node, if another node with the same pair of parents and operation type (i.e., adder, multiplier, comparator, etc.) is also available in that DSP application. According to Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)), if a pair of such nodes is found, then the nodes with higher node number are removed from the application. However, to keep the correct functionality of the application, necessary adjustment is required in the graph. Lastly, ROE-based structurally obfuscated DSP circuit is generated as intermediate output which is fed to the next obfuscation stage.
    
    For instance, in the nonobfuscated design depicted in [Figure 7.5](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig5), the redundant operations are nodes 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, which are removed using ROE method as depicted in [Figure 7.8](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig8). In order to preserve the functionality of the circuit, the inputs of nodes 14 and 16 are adjusted accordingly, as shown in [Figure 7.8](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig8).
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f08.jpg)
    
    Figure 7.8 ROE-based obfuscated design
    
2.  Logic transformation process: This compiler-driven transformation technique modifies the functionality of an application by generating a different logically equivalent function. In the context of DFG/CDFG, logic transformation alters the nodes of the input graph such that the structure of the graph appears significantly different compared to the original while satisfying the correct functionality of the application. Finally, LT-based structurally obfuscated DSP circuit is produced as output. This transformation is powerful to reflect change at the gate level after HLS.
    
    For example, [Figure 7.9](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig9) represents the logic transformation-driven obfuscated form of the input graph ([Figure 7.8](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig8)); newly added/modified nodes are shown through node numbers 20 & 7 and the modified dependencies are marked with dotted line. Post HLS, the design is functionally equivalent but structurally obfuscated.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f09.jpg)
    
    Figure 7.9 Logic transformation-based obfuscated design
    
3.  THT process: This transformation technique changes the critical path dependency of the input application accepted as DFG/CDFG, thus modifying the height of the graph. More specifically, THT divides the critical path computation into multiple sub-computations and then executes each sub-computation in parallel. Thus, THTs generate structurally dissimilar yet functionally equivalent graphs. Finally, THT-based structurally obfuscated DSP circuit is produced as output post-HLS design process.
    
    For example, in [Figure 7.10](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig10), THT-based structurally obfuscated form of the input graph (shown in [Figure 7.9](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig9)) is shown. It reduces the height of the obfuscated graph from 10 to 8 compared to its input design. The computation of nodes 17 and 18 in obfuscated design is executed earlier compared to the original design. The dependencies of the obfuscated graphs are adjusted to maintain the correct functionality. The modified dependencies are marked with deep lines.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f10.jpg)
    
    Figure 7.10 THT-based obfuscated design
    
4.  LU process: This loop transformation approach unfolds or unrolls a loop-based application considering the unrolling factor. LU can be performed by executing the same calculation present inside a loop multiple times. Lastly, LU-driven structurally obfuscated DSP circuit is generated as output, post HLS.
    
    For instance, [Figure 7.11](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig11) unrolls the input CDFG based on the unrolling factor 2. In Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)), a low-cost unrolling factor can be explored through PSO-driven DSE process ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)). LU minimizes the execution time as well as, concurrently, structurally obfuscates the IP design.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f11.jpg)
    
    Figure 7.11 Obfuscated design-based on LU (unrolled twice)
    
5.  Loop-invariant code motion process: This loop transformation process identifies those loop-independent operations which are presented inside the loop and moves them out the loop. In the context of CDFG, the nodes which are independent of loop are shifted out from the loop body. More specifically, LICM transformation moves out those nodes whose iterative execution inside the loop or single execution outside the loop does not make any difference in the final output of the application. Therefore LICM produces structurally different, yet functionally same designs. Lastly, LICM-based structurally obfuscated DSP circuit is produced as output after processing through HLS.
    
    For instance, [Figure 7.12](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig12) depicts the LICM-based structurally obfuscated version of the input CDFG. The dotted box indicates the loop-independent nodes. As per [Figure 7.12](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig12), for unrolling factor 2, loop-independent operations are performed once, whereas loop-dependent operations are performed twice.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f12.jpg)
    
    Figure 7.12 LICM-based obfuscated design (unrolled twice)
    

### 7.4 Low-cost structural obfuscation for DSP IP core

Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib36)) explored a low-cost DSP design solution through PSO-based exploration ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)). It accepts the structurally obfuscated design of the DSP core as C-code/loop-based CDFG, module library, and user-provided delay-area restrictions with terminating criteria and control parameters of PSO (such as social factor, cognitive factor, inertia weight) as inputs and produces structurally obfuscated, low-cost DSP circuit as output. The description of the PSO-DSE process is explained in the following subsections.

#### 7.4.1 Overview on PSO

PSO is an optimization process driven through population-based searching that iteratively explores an optimal solution from a pool of available solutions, known as search space. Each possible resource configuration is encoded as a particle and the fitness of each particle is assessed through an objective function to find an optimal solution. Each particle’s velocity guides that particle toward an optimal solution. The velocity of each particle is calculated using the current global best “gbest” and its own best location “lbest.” After discovering a better global or local best, velocity and position of a particle are updated, thus moving toward the optimal solution.

In the context of the low-cost DSP design solution, each particle represents a resource configuration and an unrolling factor value as a design solution. The first three particles are initialized with the minimum (min), maximum (max), and mid-resources configuration along with its unrolling factor value. If the initial population size is more than three particles, then the rest of the particles are initialized randomly within the range of min and max resource configuration value. The fitness of each particle is calculated using the cost function shown in [(7.3)](#Chapter7.html#c07_eqn3). PSO-DSE is also explained in detail in Chapter 3.

#### 7.4.2 Movement of particle

As mentioned in Section 7.4.1, the movement of a particle is guided through its velocity. In other words, velocity of a particle is used to generate a new particle position with better fitness value. In the PSO-DSE process, each dimension (*d*) of a particle velocity (![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-1.gif)) is updated based on the following expression ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c07_eqn4.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-2.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-3.gif)are current and new velocities of *i*th particle in *d*th dimension, respectively; ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-4.gif)indicates the resource value or unrolling factor of *i*th particle in *d*th dimension; ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-5.gif)is the local best position of *i*th particle in *d*th dimension; and ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-6.gif)is global best of *d*th dimension; *ω* is the inertia weight, *b*[1] and *b*[2] are social and cognitive factors, respectively; *r*[1] and *r*[2] are random numbers between 0 and 1. The new particle position is generated based on the following equation ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c07_eqn5.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c7-Eqn-in-7.gif)is new resource value or unrolling factor of *i*th particle in the *d*th dimension. The movement of particle for PSO-DSE process is shown in [Figure 7.13](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig13).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f13.jpg)

Figure 7.13 Particle movement in PSO-DSE process (Note: X[di] indicates dth dimension of ith particle including datapath resource configuration, unrolling factor, or mixture of both)

#### 7.4.3 Terminating condition of PSO

This DSE process searches for a low-cost design solution for DSP circuit iteratively. However, this iterative searching process terminates based on the following two conditions. The first condition is: if the number of iteration reaches the maximum number of predefined iteration count (*I*[max]), and second is: if no improvement in global best is found for a predefined (*δ*) number of iteration. According to Sengupta *et al.* ([2017b](#Chapter7.html#c07_bib37)), the values of *I*[max] and *δ* can be set as 100 and 10, respectively.

### 7.5 A case study for multistage structural obfuscation

For the ease of demonstration of the multistage structural obfuscation process, we are taking the same nonobfuscated CDFG depicted in [Figure 7.5](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig5) as an input. In the graph, lighter nodes denote adder and darker nodes denote multiplier. The integer value on the side of each node designates the respective node number. As shown in [Figure 7.5](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig5), three arrays, i.e., A, B, and C with two constant values, i.e., *u* and *v* are taken as primary inputs to the design. The arrays are loop-dependent variables and the constant values are loop-independent variables. Before applying any transformation technique, the total number of nodes in the graph is 19 and the height of the graph is 9. Let us assume this loop-based CDFG has loop size as 8. After applying multiple successive transformations on the input DSP graph, the final structurally obfuscated design is shown in [Figure 7.14](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig14). Due to ROE, node numbers 9, 11, 12, 13, and 15 are removed from the original design; due to LT, node numbers 6, 7, 14, 16, and 39 are altered; due to THT, the height of the graph is decreased from 9 to 8; based on unrolling factor 2, the CDFG is unrolled two times; and finally due to LICM, the loop-invariant nodes are kept outside the loop. Therefore, the total number of nodes present in the original design is incremented from 19 to 21 in the final obfuscated DSP design (in the form of CDFG).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-07-f14.jpg)

Figure 7.14 Final multistage-driven obfuscated design

As mentioned earlier, this structurally obfuscated design is next fed as input with the module library and PSO control parameters to explore a low-cost design solution of DSP circuit through PSO. [Figure 7.15](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig15) represents the final low-cost, structurally obscured scheduled IP design using three adders and one multiplier (obtained through PSO-DSE). The DSP circuit representation of the same is depicted in [Figure 7.16](#Chapter7.html#c07_fig16). It uses eight 8:1 switches, 18 input registers, 2 output registers, and 13 delay elements. The changes (due to structural obfuscation) in the DSP circuit for this application at register-transfer/module level and gate level are reported in [Table 7.1](#Chapter7.html#c07_tbl1). (Note: Similarly, functionally equivalent obfuscated DSP IP core can be obtained for well-known applications such as FIR, IIR, HWT, JPEG CODEC, DCT, and IDCT. A case study of obfuscated JPEG CODEC is described in Chapter 9).
