Yasin M., Mazumdar B., Sinanoglu O., and Rajendran J., ’Removal attacks on logic locking and camouflaging techniques,’ *IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computing*, 2017, doi: 10.1109/TETC.2017.2740364.

Zhang J., ‘A practical logic obfuscation technique for hardware security,’ *IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration Systems*, 2016, **vol. 24** (3), pp. 1193–1197.

## *Chapter 9*  
**Obfuscation of JPEG CODEC IP core for CE devices**

Joint Picture Export Group (JPEG) is the most commonly used image compression standard in the world. One cannot comprehend a CE system that does not process a JPEG. Without JPEG there is no smartphone photography, no social media. So, authors feel strongly that this important multimedia core “JPEG” needs to give well-deserving credit in terms of securing it when security/protection of “DSP core” has been a major focus of all the discussions in this book so far. The chapter is organized as follows: Section 9.2 provides an overview of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression process. Section 9.3 explains the design process of generating structurally obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core; Section 9.4 provides a detailed insight on the implementation process of obfuscated JPEG codec IP core in a CAD synthesis tool. Section 9.5 provides implementation and analysis of JPEG CODEC IP core as well as compressed images through the devised JPEG CODEC IP core.

### 9.1 Introduction

Most of the modern CE device comprises a dedicated lens or camera to capture and/or display digital images such as smartphone, tablets, scanner, laptop, smartwatch ([Thavalengal and Corcoran, 2016](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib34); [Kim *et al.*, 2015](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib13); [Corcoran and Andrae, 2014](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib5); [Tang *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib33)). Due to the enhancement of camera lenses, recording components, and displaying components, current digital imaging systems are capable of capturing and displaying high-resolution images ([Corcoran *et al.*, 2001](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib6); [Andorko *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib3)). As high-resolution images contain too much detailed information, they are large in size. Storing or transmitting these large size images is a critical issue for storage space and transmission bandwidth, respectively. Reducing the size of an image while storing and/or transferring is one of the popular and commercially successful techniques to address this crisis. JPEG standard formed in 1992 proposed DCT-based image compression. Image compressions are of two types: (1) lossy and (2) lossless. In lossy image compression, less important information of an image is discarded permanently ([Mohanty *et al.*, 2003](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib18); [Mohanty, 1999](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib17)). Camera ([Corcoran *et al.*, 2001](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib6); [Andorko *et al.*, 2011](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib3)) in a smartphone, tablets, laptop, smartwatch, etc. uses lossy image compression ([Hnesh and Demirel, 2016](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib11)). In lossless image compression, no loss of information occurs. Camera in medical imaging ([Bilgin and Marcellin, 1998](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib4)), satellite imaging, forensic imaging, etc. uses lossless image compression ([Li *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib16); [Scarmana and McDougall, 2015](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib24)).

DCT-based JPEG image compression is lossy by nature ([Obukhov and Kharlamov, 2008](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib21)). DCT segregates an image into multiple subparts or blocks based on the visual quality of the image and then converts each block to the frequency domain from spatial domain. It discards small high-frequency components; therefore, DCT-based JPEG image compression method is lossy.

Image compression and decompression (CODEC) is a major data-intensive/power-intensive computational process in the SoC of almost all smart CE devices. Therefore, in these CE products, JPEG-based CODEC is a vital function implemented through a dedicated IP core to perform the data-intensive/power-intensive computational process for image compression and decompression ([Roy and Sengupta, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib23)). The use of JPEG CODEC in the form of an IP core not only balances the trade-off between hardware area and processing speed but also enhances the design productivity. For these aforementioned advantages, JPEG CODEC IP core may face several threats such as IP piracy ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018a](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib31)), IP infringement ([Sengupta and Roy, 2017a](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib26); [Roy and Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib22); [Wong *et al.*, 2004](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib36); [Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib2)), malicious Trojan insertion ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017a](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib29)), RE ([Sengupta and Roy, 2017b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib27); [Lao and Parhi, 2015](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib15); [Vijayakumar *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib35); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib30)), which therefore demands its protection ([Sengupta, 2017](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib25)). The motivation for designing a protected JPEG CODEC IP core is explained in the rest of the section.

**Motivation:** Standard JPEG CODEC design process is not capable (also does not aim) to obscure the functionality from an adversary by transforming the architecture. This does not deter RE process for an adversary. Successful RE attack enables an adversary (in the foundry) to identify the functionality of the design to counterfeit the netlist of the design and make several copies of it without the knowledge of the IP vendor/owner. Further, if an adversary is able to identify the functionality of the design from its functional structure, he/she can make a malicious modification (i.e., insert Trojan) into the design and create malfunctioning. Both these threats can be avoided if RE process is made harder for an adversary. This is possible by structurally obfuscating the JPEG CODEC design such that the functionality of it becomes unobvious to an adversary, i.e., architecture designed to be hidden to an adversary. This strongly hinders the RE process, thus thwarting the threats. Therefore, a JPEG CODEC is considered secure, if its architecture is not obvious, i.e., its functionality is not easily discoverable by inspecting its structure ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2018b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib32)). A thematic attack scenario of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core is shown in [Figure 9.1](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig1).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f01.jpg)

Figure 9.1. A pictorial representation of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core use in different camera-based CE devices

JPEG CODEC is selected as a case study in this chapter because it is a very vital core widely used in several CE applications. Keeping in view the recent surge of IP counterfeits and hardware Trojan, it is essential to secure JPEG CODEC IP cores against RE threats as failing to do so may lead to serious functional failures (due to Trojan) and/or significant loss to CE industry (due to IP counterfeit). There has not been much discussion to addresses this concern; therefore, this chapter provides a detailed discussion on this crucial aspect.

### 9.2 Overview of JPEG compression and decompression

Typically, JPEG is a lossy image compression technique based on DCT. DCT is a Fourier-like transformation technique proposed by Ahmed *et al.* ([1974](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib1)). However, unlike Fourier transformation which represents a signal as a mixture of sine and cosine expansion, DCT represents a signal in only cosine expansion. Based on the image’s visual quality, DCT segregates it into multiple parts or spectral sub-bands. It converts an input image from the spatial domain to the frequency domain. The DCT is known for its high “energy compaction” property, meaning that the transformed signal can be easily analyzed using few low-frequency components. In simpler terms, DCT discards small high-frequency components, i.e., sharp transitions in intensity for grayscale images. Therefore, DCT-based image compression method is lossy, where less important information of an image is discarded. The process of discarding less important information is known as quantization. Image compression ratio with image quality can be controlled through quantization factor. The output bitstream is generated from the quantized coefficients through different encoding mechanisms and is then stored into a storage device. Reconstruction of the compressed image starts with decoding the bitstream data. De-quantization and inverse DCT (IDCT) is applied back to back on the decoded data to generate the decompressed image. The complete end-to-end flow of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression is shown in [Figure 9.2](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig2) ([Mohanty *et al.*, 2003](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib18); [Mohanty, 1999](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib17)). Each step of JPEG image compression and decompression process is discussed in the rest of the section.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f02.jpg)

Figure 9.2. End-to-end flow of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression process

#### 9.2.1 DCT-based JPEG image compression process

##### 9.2.1.1 Processing of the input image

In an 8-bit grayscale image, the pixel intensity ranges from \[0–255\], where 0 indicates pure black and 255 indicates pure white. Therefore, each grayscale image is represented using 256 shades of gray. To reduce the dynamic range (required in DCT processing), the midpoint of this range, i.e., 128 is subtracted from each pixel value of the image. Therefore, the modified data range, i.e., \[−128, 127\] is centered on zero. The generic 2D-DCT coefficient matrix (*T*) for a sample of *N*×*N* can be expressed as follows ([DCT matrix, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib10)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn1.gif)

where “N” is the size of the DCT matrix, “i” and “j” is the *i*th row, *j*th column component of the 2D-DCT matrix. In standard JPEG process, “N” is equal to 8 and *i* and *j* vary from 0 to 7. The 2D-DCT coefficient matrix for an 8 × 8 block is shown in [Figure 9.3](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig3) (also explained in Chapter 3). According to [Figure 9.3](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig3), all elements of the first row (*i* = 0) are equal to 1/√8 according to ([9.1)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn1). As “T” is an orthogonal matrix, the inverse of “T” (i.e., *T*^(−1)) is equal to the transpose of “T” (i.e., *T*^(trans)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f03.jpg)

Figure 9.3. 2D-DCT coefficient matrix

##### 9.2.1.2 Perform DCT on input image

To perform DCT on the input image, the image should be subdivided into multiple nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks. Each block can be processed independently, therefore block-wise parallelism is possible for transformation, which is the key feature of 8 × 8 DCT. A generic 8 × 8 block “M” of input image matrix is shown in [Figure 9.4](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig4), where *m*[*ij*] express pixel intensity of *i*th row, *j*th column component of the “M” block. The DCT on the “M” block can be performed through following matrix multiplications:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn2.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f04.jpg)

Figure 9.4. Generic 8×8 block of input image

In the above expression, *D* is calculated as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn3.gif)

The “D” matrix (*d*[11], *d*[12], …, *d*[88]) transforms the rows of the “M” block. Further, “X” matrix (*X*[11], *X*[12], …, *X*[88]) transforms the columns of the “D” matrix. Thus, transforms both rows and columns of the “M” block. Therefore, “X” is the DCT block of “M” block.

##### 9.2.1.3 Perform quantization

The transformed block “X” is now ready to compress through quantization. As human eye is not good in distinguishing the high-frequency brightness deviation in an image, a large amount of information reduction is possible from the high-frequency components of an image. This is achieved by dividing each element of transformed block “X” by the corresponding element of the quantization matrix (*Q*) and then rounding to the nearest integer. As a result, most of the high-frequency components are rounded to zero, which indicates discarding less important high-frequency components. Additionally, many of the remaining components become small positive or negative numbers, which take fewer bits to represent. The quantization matrix is designed in such a way that it provides more resolution to higher perceivable frequency components over lower perceivable frequency components. The designing process of standard quantization matrix (**Q**[**50**]) involves subjective experiment of human visual system. In the range of 1 to 100, standard quantization matrix provides quality level as 50. It thus provides a balance between image compression ratio and image quality. The standard quantization matrix is shown in [Figure 9.5](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig5). However, image quality and compression ratio can vary by changing the quantization matrix. To obtain a quantization matrix with quality level greater than **Q**[**50**], each element of **Q**[**50**] should be multiplied with (100−quality level)/50 and then rounding to the nearest integer. Similarly, to obtain a quantization matrix with quality level lower than **Q**[**50**], each element of **Q**[**50**] should be multiplied with 50/quality level and then rounding to the nearest integer.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f05.jpg)

Figure 9.5. Standard quantization matrix (**Q**[**50**])

##### 9.2.1.4 Data encoding

The 2D quantized 8 × 8 block (X′) is now ready to be compressed through encoding. The block is converted to a 1D array through “zigzag” scanning. Thereafter, employing *run-length encoding (RLE),* enables grouping similar frequencies together. The encoded data is then converted into binary to generate a bitstream. Finally, the bitstream data of the compressed image is stored into a storage device.

#### 9.2.2 DCT-based JPEG image decompression process

##### 9.2.2.1 Data decoding

Image reconstruction process starts with data decoding. The stored data is first fetched from the storage device and decoded through RLE. The quantized 2D 8 × 8 block (X′) is reconstructed through “inverse zigzag” scanning from the 1D array.

##### 9.2.2.2 Perform inverse quantization

The reconstructed X′ is now ready to be decompressed through inverse quantization. Decompression is achieved by multiplying each element of reconstructed block by the corresponding element of quantization matrix, to obtain block (X″).

##### 9.2.2.3 Perform IDCT on decompressed image

Similar to applying DCT on the input block in the JPEG compression process, IDCT is applied on the decompressed block (X″). The IDCT on the X″ block can be performed through following matrix multiplications:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn4.gif)

In the above expression, *E* is calculated as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn5.gif)

The “E” matrix (*e*[11], *e*[12], …, *e*[88]) transforms the rows of the X″ block. Further, “O” matrix (*o*[11], *o*[12], …, *o*[88]) transforms the columns of the “E” matrix. Thus the above transformations, transform both the rows and columns of the X″ block. Therefore, “O” is the IDCT block of X″ block. After applying IDCT on the decompressed block, each element is rounded to the nearest integer.

##### 9.2.2.4 Reconstruct the decompressed image

To reconstruct the decompressed image from the inversely transformed decompressed block, 128 is added to each of the element of the decompressed block to keep the range of output image pixel between \[0, 255\] instead of \[−128, 127\].

### 9.3 Design process of structurally obfuscated JPEG IP core

#### 9.3.1 Threat model, problem formulation, and optimization framework

##### 9.3.1.1 Threat model

To protect a JPEG CODEC IP core from RE and Trojan insertion through structural obfuscation. In order to maximize protection ability, impede the correct functionality of the application by generating a functionally equivalent but structurally nonobvious architecture of JPEG CODEC IP Core. (Note: Motivation of using structural obfuscation to guard against RE was thoroughly explained in Chapter 7).

##### 9.3.1.2 Problem formulation

In order to protect a JPEG CODEC IP core from RE threat, design a structurally obfuscated, low-cost hardware. The hardware design cost is evaluated by calculating the total hardware area and total design latency. The hardware design cost adopted from Sengupta *et al.* ([2018b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib32)) is formulated as:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn6.gif)

where *Cf*(*X*[*i*]) is the hardware design cost for design solution *Xi*; *L*[total]^(JPEG) and *A*[total]^(JPEG) represent the total design latency and total hardware area of the obfuscated JPEG IP core, respectively; *L*[max]^(JPEG) and *A*[max]^(JPEG) indicate the maximum possible design latency and hardware area, respectively, using the specified module library; weightage factor of two design parameters (latency-area) is controlled via *w*[1] and *w*[2].

##### 9.3.1.3 Optimization framework

To obtain a low-cost hardware for JPEG IP core, PSO-driven DSE framework is used. This particle-based heuristic approach iteratively searches for a new global optima based on local minima and current global optima. Detailed explanation of the PSO-DSE process and formulation models is provided in Chapter 3 and in Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib29)). Benefits of the PSO-DSE process are as follows:

*     (i) Capable of obtaining global optima while bypassing local minima
    
*    (ii) Capable of incorporating stochasticity during exploration process
    
*   (iii) Capable of preserving a proper balance between exploitation and exploration throughout the iterations
    

#### 9.3.2 Constructing non-obfuscated DFG for JPEG compression

The generic steps to design a structurally obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core are shown in [Figure 9.6](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig6). In this section, we discuss how to construct a standard (non-obfuscated) DFG from the matrix expression of JPEG compression. Equations ([9.2)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn2) and ([9.3)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn3) represent the function of applying 2D-DCT on the input image block M. (Note: Detailed explanation of generating DCT matrix and its corresponding graph is given in Chapter 3.) This function is expanded and modeled as a mathematical expression to design an equivalent DFG. Further, this DFG is fed to an HLS engine to obtain a JPEG compression IP core. Based on ([9.2)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn2), the corresponding mathematical expression for the first pixel (*X*[11]) of the transformed block is modeled as:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn7.gif)

whereas based on ([9.3)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn3), *d*[11], *d*[12], …, *d*[18] are modeled as:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn8.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn9.gif)

Similarly,

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn10.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f06.jpg)

Figure 9.6. Steps to design a low-cost obfuscated JPEG IP core

Similarly, mathematical expression for the rest of the pixels of the transformed block can also be modeled, where the pixel values (*m*[11]–*m*[88]) and DCT coefficient will change depending on the pixel coordinate of the transformed block. However, the overall pattern of operations of the expression will be same. Based on this pattern, a DFG is generated where different pixel values and DCT coefficients are fed as the input. As in ([9.7),](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn7) we have modeled the mathematical expression for the first pixel (*X*[11]) of the transformed block, and the corresponding DFG is shown in [Figure 9.7](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig7). In the process of computing *X*[11] through the complete DFG, termed as macro IP, each *d*[*ij*] (represented through ([9.8](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn8)–[9.10](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn10))) is computed through a sub-DFG termed as micro-IP. For example, micro-IP8, represented through blue node executes *d*[18]. The zoom in representation of micro-IP8 is also shown in [Figure 9.7](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig7). Totally 16 nodes (node no. 113–128) are part of micro-IP, where darker nodes indicate multiplication operation and lighter nodes indicate addition operation. Similarly, micro-IP1-7 executes *d*[11]–*d*[17]. The macro IP contains total 136 nodes; among these, the output of node number 135 produces the transformed pixel intensity of *X*[11]. As mentioned earlier, quantization is applied on the each pixel of the transformed block, where each element of the transformed block is divided with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix. In this DFG, the output of node number 135 is multiplied with the inverse value of corresponding number (i.e., instead of division, multiplication is performed with the inverse of the number) of the quantization matrix (**Q**). This *q* value is fed as another input of the DFG based on the quality level of the compressed image. For higher quality level, the *q* value will be less and vice versa while calculating the same pixel. Subsequently, the output of node number 136 produces the compressed pixel intensities (*X*[11]′) as the final output. This standard structure of JPEG DFG is common for most of the applications; therefore, identifying functionality from its structure is easy for an attacker. This invites threats such as RE, insertion of Trojan logic, counterfeits as fraudulent means of designing/maligning JPEG IP Core. This can be shielded to a certain extent by hiding functionality of the design. In the next subsections, we first discuss how to design a structurally obfuscated DFG for JPEG compression, followed up with its obfuscated hardware design.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f07.jpg)

Figure 9.7. Non-obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression for calculating first compressed image pixel (X′ 11)

#### 9.3.3 Generating structurally obfuscated JPEG compression IP core

Structural obfuscation hinders the RE process by transforming the standard architecture of JPEG hardware to an unobvious design. Therefore, identifying the original functionality of the structurally obfuscated design is harder for an attacker. THT-based structural obfuscation is applied to the standard structure of JPEG DFG ([Sengupta *et al.*, 2017b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib30)). It is a compiler-driven optimization technique which parallelizes the dependent critical path operations by dividing it into temporary sub-computations. However, this technique has not been used to generate a structurally obfuscated DFG for JPEG. The standard structure of JPEG DFG shown in [Figure 9.7](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig7) is structurally obfuscated through THT. The transformed structure of JPEG DFG is shown in [Figure 9.8](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig8). The zoom-in representation of obfuscated micro-IP8 is also shown in the figure. Due to this transformation, each micro-IP, as well as macro-IP, is modified. For example, in micro-IP8, 12 nodes among 16 nodes are affected. They are node no. 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120, 122, 123, 124, 125, 126, and 127. Therefore, in the eight micro-IPs, 96 nodes are affected. Additionally in the macro IP, six nodes are affected which include 130, 131, 132, 133, 134, and 135. A node is considered affected if its parents or child is changed or the operation type of that node is changed compared to the original one. These changes produce a different structure of datapath, interconnectivity logic, multiplexers/demultiplexers, and controller logic, once processed through high-level synthesis.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f08.jpg)

Figure 9.8. Obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression for calculating first compressed image pixel (X′11)

The design process of obfuscated, low-cost JPEG compression IP core is shown in [Figure 9.9](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig9). As shown in this figure, the primary input is the non-obfuscated (standard) DFG of JPEG compression (designed in the previous section). Then it is structurally obfuscated through THT (explained initially in this section). A low-cost hardware configuration for obfuscated JPEG DFG is explored through PSO-DSE which is used to design a JPEG compression IP core in HLS framework ([Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib28); [Coussy *et al.*, 2009](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib7)). In order to perform this process, PSO-DSE accepts additional inputs such as resource constraints, module library, and control parameters. For a detailed explanation of the PSO-DSE process, see Chapter 3 and Sengupta *et al.* ([2017a](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib29)). Finally, a dedicated IP core for JPEG compression is developed which is structurally obfuscated and low cost by nature. This IP core accepts leveled-off pixel intensity, 2D-DCT coefficient, and quantization matrix as inputs and produces transformed compressed pixel intensity as output.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f09.jpg)

Figure 9.9. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG compression

#### 9.3.4 Generating structurally obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core

In this section, we discuss how to construct an obfuscated DFG from the matrix expression of JPEG decompression. The compressed block X′ is decompressed through inverse quantization. In this process, each element of X′ is multiplied with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix of the same quality level, to obtain decompressed block X″. Then 2D-IDCT is performed on the decompressed block X″. Equations ([9.4)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn4) and ([9.5)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn5) represent the function of applying 2D-IDCT on the decompressed block X″. Similar to JPEG compression process, this function is expanded and modeled as a mathematical expression to design an equivalent DFG. Further, this DFG is fed to a HLS engine to obtain a JPEG decompression IP core. Based on ([9.4)](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn4), the corresponding mathematical expression for the first pixel (*o*[11]) of the inversely transformed block is modeled as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn11.gif)

In the above expression, *e*[11], *e*[12], …, *e*[18] can be expressed as :

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn12.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn13.gif)

Similarly,

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn14.gif)

Similarly, the mathematical expression for rest of the pixels of the inversely transformed block can be modeled, where the pixel values of X″[11]–X″[88] and IDCT coefficients will change depending on the pixel coordinate of the inversely transformed block. Since the overall pattern of operations of the expression is same as DCT-based JPEG compression process, we can conclude that the DFG of JPEG DCT and IDCT are almost same except for few things. For example, in case of compression we assumed that each element of the compressed block is multiplied with the corresponding element (*q*) of the quantization matrix, to perform quantization (through node number 136). However, quantization through node number 136 is not required in DFG of JPEG IDCT. Instead, the last node (node 136) can be used to perform de-levelization by adding 128 to the pixel intensity of the decompressed block. Thus, the total number of nodes in the DFG for both JPEG compression and decompression remains the same. Therefore, THT-based structurally obfuscated DFG can be similarly generated for the JPEG decompression also.

The design process of obfuscated, low-cost JPEG decompression IP core is almost similar to JPEG compression IP core. The obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is shown in [Figure 9.10](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig10). As shown, the decompression IP core accepts processed (i.e., after multiplying each element of compressed block with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix) compressed pixel intensity and 2D-DCT coefficient as inputs and produces inversely transformed decompressed pixel intensity as output.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f10.jpg)

Figure 9.10. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG decompression

### 9.4 Implementation of JPEG CODEC IP core

#### 9.4.1 Designing obfuscated JPEG compression IP core

The complete design flow of JPEG compression process using devised low-cost, obfuscated JPEG compression IP core is shown in [Figure 9.11](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig11). In this complete design flow, partial steps are performed through hardware and the remaining steps are performed through software. More specifically, 2D-DCT transformation and quantization steps are performed through devised JPEG compression IP core and leveling of input image pixel intensity and data encoding is performed through software. Each 8 × 8 block leveled-off pixel intensity, stored in a hardware queue, is provided as input to the devised JPEG compression IP core, along with quantization matrix and 2D-DCT coefficient matrix. In this section, we emphasize the implementation of hardware portion of JPEG compression IP core design process. The JPEG compression IP core is designed using HLS framework ([Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib28); [Coussy *et al.*, 2009](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib7)), where the obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression (shown in [Figure 9.8](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig8)) is first scheduled based on a resource configuration. As mentioned earlier, the resource configuration which generates a low-cost design is explored through PSO-DSE process. Here, the DFG is scheduled based on the list-scheduling algorithm with three adders (Adder\_A1, Adder\_A2, and Adder\_A3) and three multipliers (Multiplier\_M1, Multiplier\_M2, and Multiplier\_M3). This indicates, based on the dependency, each CS of the scheduled DFG can have maximum three additions and three multiplication operations out of 136 operations available in the DFG. In each CS, every scheduled operation is assigned to its corresponding hardware and operations assigned to a same hardware are bound (shared) together. [Table 9.1](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl1) represents all the 136 operations, their CS, and corresponding assigned hardware. Total 30 CS are required to schedule all the operations. Both adders and multipliers are designed in IEEE 754 half precision floating-point format. Therefore, all the operators have bit-width 16 bits. The implemented JPEG compression IP core consists of two units: data path unit and controller unit. The data path unit represents the required number of resources and their interconnections while the controller unit synchronizes those resources by changing their signals (e.g., enables, selectors, strobes). In other words, controller unit is responsible for controlling the data flow through the data path by activating and deactivating different components of data path in different clock cycle, thus synchronizing each component to generate an error-free output. The generic block diagram representation of data path unit of low-cost obfuscated JPEG IP is shown in [Figure 9.12](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig12). As shown in this figure, the data-path consist of three adders and multipliers, ten multiplexer of type 32:1, two multiplexer of type 16:1, five demultiplexer of type 1:32, one demultiplexer of type 1:16, forty registers of 16-bits and 18 latches. The primary inputs are represented through A1,…A8,…Q1,…Q8 and the dependent inputs are represented through *i*[1], *i*[2], …, *i*[135], while *i*[136] represents the output. The implemented schematic representation of the data path unit and the complete IP core are shown in Figures [9.13](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig13) and [9.14](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig14), respectively, and the complete controller unit signal description is available in the “Appendix.” Both data path and controller is implemented using Quartus CAD tool in Intel Cyclone II ([Cyclone II FPGA, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib8)) FPGA.

#### 9.4.2 Designing obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core

The complete design flow of JPEG decompression process using devised low-cost obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is shown in [Figure 9.15](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig15). Similar to the JPEG compression design flow, few steps are performed through software and rest is performed through hardware. More specifically, data decoding and inverse quantization are performed through software and 2D-IDCT transformation and leveling of output image pixel intensity are performed through devised JPEG decompression IP. Finally, each 8 × 8 block with leveled-off decompressed pixel intensity is stored in an output hardware queue.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f15.jpg)

Figure 9.15. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG decompression

Similar to JPEG compression, during DFG scheduling, same resource configuration is used. The same number of components, i.e., three adders and multipliers of 16-bits, ten multiplexers of type 32:1, two multiplexers of type 16:1, five demultiplexers of type 1:32, one demultiplexer of type 1:16, Forty registers of 16-bits and 18 latches are used in the data path unit. Similar to the JPEG compression IP core, both data-path and controller of JPEG decompression IP core are also implemented using Quartus CAD tool in Intel Cyclone II ([Cyclone II FPGA, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib8)) FPGA.

#### 9.4.3 End-to-end JPEG CODEC through designed hardware/IP core

In this section, we discuss the end-to-end JPEG CODEC process through the devised JPEG IP core. This discussion has three segments. In the first segment, we discuss about each step of image compression starting from an input image to generating a quantized image through an illustrative example. In the second segment, we present about data encoding and decoding process through RLE algorithm using an illustrative example. In the last segment, we discuss about each step of image decompression starting from a de-quantized image to generate the post-compression reconstructed image pixel through another illustrative example.

A grayscale image of 512 × 512 taken from “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” ([Standard dataset, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib9)) is selected as an input image. The input image is shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(a). To perform DCT on the input image, multiple leveled-off, nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks of the image pixel are formed from the input image. Out of multiple nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks, a randomly selected block for the input image is shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(b). This block (containing 64-pixel values) is provided as one of the primary inputs to the devised obfuscated JPEG compression IP core (shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(c)). The designing process of obfuscated JPEG compression IP core is discussed in Section 9.4.1. The designed IP core performs DCT and quantization on the input block and produces transformed and quantized image as output. In this example, we have performed compression based on quality level 90, i.e., using quantization matrix **Q**[**90**]. This process is repeated until all the 8 × 8 blocks of the input image is transformed and quantized. The generated transformed and quantized image is shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(d).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f16.jpg)

Figure 9.16. Motivational example of JPEG compression through compression IP core

Data encoding, which is a form of lossless data compression, is performed on each quantized block, before storing the pixel data into a storage device. It involves arranging the data of the quantized block in “zigzag” fashion then employing RLE algorithm on it. [Figure 9.17](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig17)(a) shows the quantized block corresponding to input image block (shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(b)). Zigzag scanning (the format of zigzag scanning is shown in [Figure 9.17](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig17)(b)) is performed on the quantized block and the output is shown in [Figure 9.17](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig17)(c). The quantized data sequenced in zigzag fashion is encoded through RLE algorithm. RLE replaces **each nonzero AC coefficient** value with a pair (RUNLENGTH, AMPLITUDE), where “RUNLENGTH” is the **number of zeroes** that came before that nonzero AC coefficient and “AMPLITUDE” is the value of that particular nonzero coefficient. The encoded version of the quantized data using RLE is shown in [Figure 9.17](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig17)(d), where (0, 0) always indicates the end of the block. The remaining elements (from the 64 available slots) of the 1D array in RLE encoded data are not stored, as they are all zeroes. (Note: The first value of the matrix, i.e., 16 is the DC coefficient; it is not encoded through RLE.) Each of these encoded values is converted to its equivalent binary form to generate the corresponding bitstream of the block and then stored in a storage device. To regenerate the quantized block from the bitstream data, decoding needs to be performed. To achieve the decoding of data, all the aforementioned steps have to be performed in reverse order. Thus while obtaining (decoding) 1D array from RLE encoded data, the vacant slots from the 64 elements (of 8 × 8 block) are filled up with zeroes. The inverse zig-zagging is performed to obtain 2D array of 8 × 8 block of quantized block.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f17.jpg)

Figure 9.17. Demonstrative example of data encoding through RLE algorithm

To reconstruct the image from its transformed and quantized form, each block is de-quantized using the same quantization matrix used for compression. As in this example, we have performed compression using quantization matrix **Q**[**90**,] the de-quantization (inverse quantization) is performed based on quantization matrix **Q**[**90**] only. The generated de-quantized image is shown in [Figure 9.18](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig18)(a). The 8 × 8 de-quantized block (containing 64-pixel values) is provided as one of the primary input to the devised obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core (shown in [Figure 9.18](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig18)(b)). The designing process of obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is discussed in Section 9.4.2. The designed IP core performs IDCT and leveling-off of the de-quantized block and produces 8 × 8 decompressed image pixel intensity values as output. The corresponding decompressed image pixel intensity of the same 8 × 8 block (shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(b)) is shown in [Figure 9.18](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig18)(c). Again, this process is repeated until all the 8 × 8 de-quantized blocks are inversely transformed and leveled off. Finally, the post-compression reconstructed image is generated by combining all the 8 × 8 inversely transformed and leveled-off blocks. The reconstructed image of the corresponding input image (shown in [Figure 9.16](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig16)(a)) is shown in [Figure 9.18](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig18)(d).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-09-f18.jpg)

Figure 9.18. Informative example of JPEG decompression through devised JPEG decompression IP core

### 9.5 Analysis on case studies

To verify the devised IP cores for JPEG compression and decompression, images (bit depth equal to 4 bits) provided as input are taken from two different image datasets. They are “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” ([Standard dataset, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib9)) and “NASA images” ([NASA images, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib20)). Both the devised IP cores are designed, implemented, and simulated in Intel Quartus ([Intel Quartus, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib12)) v7.2 software with respect to Cyclone II family ([Cyclone II FPGA, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib8)), device no. EP2C35F672C6 at 50-MHz clock frequency. However, it can be emulated in any FPGA device. [Table 9.2](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl2) reports the device utilization summary of devised JPEG compression IP core for the aforementioned target device. The devised JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated and low-cost in nature is compared with another JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated but not optimized in nature indicating the design configuration of the obfuscated IP core is not explored through any optimization framework/engine. Therefore, deficiency of any low-cost DSE framework results in higher design cost overhead. [Table 9.3](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl3) reports the comparative analysis between these two aforementioned IP cores in terms of design area, latency, and cost. A 15 nm technology scale based on NanGate library ([Open Cell Library, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib19)) is used to evaluate the design area and the design latency of both IP cores, where area is in μm² and latency is calculated in picoseconds. Based on the weighted normalized design area and design latency of the obfuscated JPEG IP core, design cost is calculated using ([9.6](#Chapter9.html#c09_eqn6)).

**Table 9.2** Device utilization summary of devised JPEG CODEC IP cores w.r.t. Intel Cyclone II FPGA

![image](OEBPS/images/tab9.2.jpg)

**Table 9.3** Comparison of low-cost obfuscated IP core with nonoptimized obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core in terms of area, latency, and cost

![image](OEBPS/images/tab9.3.jpg)

Therefore, design cost of the obfuscated JPEG IP core is unitless. According to the results shown in [Table 9.3](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl3), the devised JPEG CODEC IP core design achieves more than 5% lower design cost than the non-optimized obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design. The reason for achieving lower design cost is due to the involvement of PSO-DSE engine, which explores the low-cost design configuration. Therefore, it is referred as “low-cost” JPEG CODEC IP core.

The devised JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated and low-cost in nature is also compared with another JPEG CODEC IP core which is not structurally obfuscated indicating that no structural transformation technique is performed in the DFG of JPEG CODEC to hide its structural identity. Therefore, deficiency of any structural transformation technique results in nonsecured design which is vulnerable to RE attack. [Table 9.4](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl4) reports the comparative analysis between these two aforementioned IP cores in terms of design area, latency, cost, and SoO. The SoO of JPEG CODEC IP core is measured through a metric, which is partially adopted from Sengupta *et al.* ([2018b](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib32)), expressed as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c09_eqn15.gif)

where *a*[JPEG] indicates that the number of nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC is altered due to structural transformation; *a*[JPEG]^(Total) indicates the total available nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC before applying THT technique. The robustness of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core is measured through SoO metric, a higher SoO value indicates stronger robustness in the range of \[0, 1\]. In other words, SoO metric indicates how much the structure of an obfuscated IP core differs from its original structure. The more a design differs from its original structure the harder it will be for an attacker to identify the application through RE. Therefore, insertion of any malicious logic in the IP design or performing IP piracy is extremely difficult without knowing the actual functionality of the application. According to the results shown in [Table 9.4](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl4), the devised obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design achieves more than 76% SoO than a non-obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design. The structural obfuscation is obtained using THT which is responsible for obfuscating the original design of JPEG CODEC by transforming the height of the data flow graph representing the JPEG CODEC, thus modifying the nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC. Modification of a node in a DFG indicates whether, (1) the source/parents of a node is changed; (2) the child of a node is changed; or (3) operation type of a node is changed, compared to the original. The effect of modification of nodes is also reflected in the gate structure/netlist of the design. According to the results shown in [Table 9.4](#Chapter9.html#c09_tbl4), more than 10,000 gates are affected due to the modification of nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC. This is achieved due to the transformation in gate-level architecture of functional resources, multiplexers, demultiplexers, and registers. This enormous transformation in gate-level architecture of the complete JPEG CODEC IP core makes it an unobvious structure. Therefore, identifying the correct functionality of this unobvious structure is extremely complex and tedious for an attacker. [Figure 9.19](#Chapter9.html#c09_fig19)(a)–(c) shows the comparison between devised, non-obfuscated, and nonoptimized JPEG CODEC IP core in terms of area, latency, and cost, respectively.

To compress standard input images using devised JPEG CODEC IP core, totally six images are chosen from “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” ([Standard dataset, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib9)) and “NASA images” ([NASA images, 2018](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib20)) datasets. The compression is performed for two different quality levels, i.e., quality level 90 (**Q**[**90**]) and 70 (**Q**[**70**]). Additionally, the mean square error (MSE) and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the corresponding compressed images obtained through devised JPEG CODEC IP core design are also calculated. As PSNR is commonly used to calculate the quality of the reconstructed image of lossy compression, we have used PSNR to evaluate image degradation of compressed images obtained through devised JPEG CODEC IP core. PSNR is defined for two images A and B of size *M* × *N* as ([Kougianos *et al.*, 2016](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib14); [Obukhov and Kharlamov, 2008](#Chapter9.html#c09_bib21)):

### 9.6 Conclusion

This chapter discussed a case study of structural obfuscation using JPEG CODEC IP core which is available in almost every CE devices. The design mechanism and implementation process of low-cost obfuscated on-chip IP core design for 2D-DCT-based JPEG image compression and decompression are explained here. This structural obfuscation hides an application and its implementation from an adversary by transforming its standard architecture to a non-obvious one. In this process, THT is used to structurally obfuscate the design and low-cost hardware configuration is explored through PSO-DSE engine. The devised IP core is synthesized and simulated through Intel Quartus Cyclone II FPGA. The designed IP core can be used as a dedicated IP core in any camera-based CE devices to perform image CODEC. Further, the robustness of the structurally obfuscated design is measured through SoO metric, which indicates that more than 76% SoO is achieved compared to a standard non-obfuscated JPEG CODEC design. Additionally, as structural obfuscation does not incur any design overhead, therefore, it is an extremely useful method of protection for Trojan insertion, IP piracy/counterfeit. The SoO of the devised JPEG CODEC IP core discussed in this chapter can be enhanced by performing multiple transformation techniques on the DFG of the JPEG CODEC IP core as a part of future work. Additionally, combination of functional obfuscation technique with structural obfuscation can also enhance the robustness for DSP applications. This would enable to hide an application and its implementation from an adversary.

## *Chapter 10*  
**Advanced encryption standard (AES) and its hardware watermarking for ownership protection**

In this era of consumer electronics, cyber security is one of the key challenges. Any security, privacy, or protection methods that are deployed rely on cryptography. Advance encryption standard (AES) is one of the heavily used cryptography algorithms for its advantages. This chapter is dedicated to the process of AES and its hardware design in the form of IP core. Several hardware security techniques rely on AES IP core as an important block. Additionally, since this is such an important core, its self-protection against forgery/piracy is also crucial. Thus, this chapter will also discuss about AES IP core protection using watermarking.

### 10.1 Introduction

Cryptography is very widely used in everyday life, ranging from established applications such as wireless local area network, procuring items with a credit or debit card, installing a software update, smart cards, banking application, voice of internet protocol (VOIP) to emergent domains, such as electronic health system, internet of things security, smart city security, and hardware security ([Paar and Pelzl, 2009](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5); [Bhunia and Tehranipoor, 2018](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib1); [Sengupta, 2013](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib6), [2015](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib7), [2017](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib8); [Sengupta *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib13); [Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib9); [Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib12); [Mishra *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib3); Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2013; [Sengupta and Roy, 2017a](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib10), [2017b](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib11)). Cryptography comprises cryptographic algorithms that are symmetrical by nature. There is tremendous usage of symmetric ciphers, especially for the encryption of data and integrity check of messages. Furthermore, cryptographic protocol deals with the application of cryptographic algorithms. An example of cryptographic protocol is transport layer security (TLS) scheme, widely employed in browser advanced encryption standard (AES) is a very popular symmetric cipher used today. The AES, also known by its original name Rijndael, is a specification for the encryption of electronic data recognized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). In the context of AES (Rijndael family), three members were designated by NIST, each with a block size of 128 bits, but dissimilar key lengths: 128, 192, and 256 bits. It is a mandatory standard in several industry/commercial systems and US government applications such as Wi-Fi encryption standard IEEE 802.11i, TLS, and VOIP ([Paar and Pelzl, 2009](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5)).

In this chapter, we focus on the following aspects: (a) AES algorithm—description of each step and its flow diagram, (b) corresponding hardware mapping of AES block cipher—overview of how each step can be mapped to a specific hardware sub-block, (c) key scheduler—description of each step, (d) corresponding hardware mapping of key scheduler used in AES, (e) watermarking encoding of AES hardware—protecting an AES hardware against threats such as false claim of ownership and piracy, (f) design of watermarked AES hardware—description of the watermark embedding process, and (g) impact of several different watermark signature types on AES hardware and its implementation on FPGA—to highlight the overhead due to watermark.

### 10.2 AES algorithm

#### 10.2.1 Overview of AES

AES algorithm has three different variations of key sizes, i.e., 128 bits or 192 bits or 256 bits. The input data size is 128 bits and the output encrypted data is also 128 bits. The input data is called the plain text and the output encrypted data is called cypher text. [Figure 10.1](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig1) shows the AES input/output parameters. The core structure of AES comprises the following components: (i) byte substitution layer, (ii) diffusion layer, (iii) key addition layer, and (iv) key schedule ([Kosaraju *et al.*, 2006](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib2); [Mohanty *et al.*, 2007](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib4)). Three key lengths are supported in AES. The number of internal rounds of the cipher depends on the key length. For example, in case of 128 bit key length, the number of internal rounds (*n*[*r*]) is 10, while for 192 bit key length, the number of internal rounds is 12, and finally for 256 bit key length, the value of *n*[*r*] is 14, respectively.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f01.jpg)

Figure 10.1 AES block cipher

#### 10.2.2 AES algorithm—description and custom hardware design

The first major phase of AES algorithm is ‘byte substitution layer (S-box)’ which is responsible for non-linear transformation using lookup tables for each element of the state. The main significance of this step is to add ‘*confusion*’ to the data elements. In other words, the transformation achieved in individual state bits is rapidly propagated into the datapath. The second major phase is called ‘*Diffusion*’ which consists of two sub-layers, viz. ‘*ShiftRows*’ that permutes the data at the byte level and ‘*MixColumn*’ is a matrix based operation that is responsible for mixing of blocks of four bytes of data. The significance of ‘*Diffusion*’ is to introduce diffusion property to the data element. The third major phase is ‘*key addition*’ layer which is responsible for XOR-ing the 128 bit key (or its derived key) to the state of each element obtained after performing ‘*MixColumn*’ operation. Finally, the ‘*key schedule’* calculates round keys or subkeys (*k*[0], *k*[1],…,*k*[*nr*]) from the original AES key. [Figure 10.2](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig2) shows the major steps of the AES algorithm in terms of design flow highlighting each block responsible for performing specific operation. As an example, we use key length of 128 bits for demonstration ([Paar and Pelzl, 2009](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f02.jpg)

Figure 10.2 Round ‘i’ (1–10) of AES algorithm for 128 bit key and 128 bit I/O

##### 10.2.2.1 Byte substitution (S-box) layer

S-box is the non-linear component of AES which is accountable for bit manipulation. It consists of 16 S-boxes all of which are identical to each other. All 256 possible input elements have a unique mapping to one output element. S-box is shown in [Figure 10.3](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig3) and is adopted from [Paar and Pelzl (2009)](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5). For example, if input byte to the S-box is (B2)[hex], then based on the mapping available in S-box, the output byte is (37)[hex]. In other words, S((B2)[hex]) → (37)[hex] → S(10110010) → 00110111. This clearly shows how bit manipulation is achieved using byte substitution layer of AES. As shown in [Figure 10.2](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig2), bytes X[0], X[1], X[2],…,X[15] are substituted with Y[0], Y[1], Y[3],…,Y[15] using S-box. Every four bytes of data X[0], X[1], X[2], X[3] gets transformed into Y[0], Y[1], Y[2], Y[3]. Similarly, for next four bytes X[4], X[5], X[6], X[7] gets transformed into Y[4], Y[5], Y[6], Y[7]. Further similarly, next four bytes X[8], X[9], X[10], X[11] gets transformed into Y[8], Y[9], Y[10], Y[11]. Finally, last four bytes X[12], X[13], X[14], X[15] gets transformed into Y[12], Y[13], Y[14], Y[15].

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f03.jpg)

Figure 10.3 S-box ([Paar and Pelzl, 2009](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5))

##### 10.2.2.2 Row-shifting diffusion layer

The significance of the *ShiftRows* transformation is to upsurge the diffusion process of AES. This transformation works as follows:

1.  First row is retained unaffected.
    
2.  Second row is cyclically moved three bytes to the right.
    
3.  Third row is cyclically moved two bytes to the right.
    
4.  Fourth row is cyclically moved one byte to the right.
    

The output of *byte substitution* layer is fed as an input to the *ShiftRows* diffusion layer as shown below. Let us assume the output of *byte substitution* layer is Y[0], Y[1], Y[2], Y[3],…,Y[15]. It is arranged in matrix form as shown below in [Table 10.1](#Chapter10.html#c10_ufig1). The transformation applied on each row is indicated through notes on the top of the arrow. The outputs for every four input byte are indicated in each column. For example, corresponding to the input four bytes Y[0], Y[1], Y[2], Y[3], the transformed output four bytes are Y[0], Y[5], Y[10], Y[15] as shown in [Table 10.2](#Chapter10.html#c10_ufig1). Similarly, the outputs are obtained for the remaining four bytes in each column.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-u01.jpg)

 

##### 10.2.2.3 MixColumn diffusion layer

This step is a major diffusion process in AES since each every input byte impacts four output bytes. It is responsible for mixing each column of the state matrix. The input to the *MixColumn* diffusion layer is the output of *ShiftRows* diffusion layer. In order to perform *MixColumn* diffusion each 4-byte column is assumed as a vector and multiplied by a fixed 4 × 4 matrix. The matrix comprises of some constant values. The main important thing to note is that the matrix addition and multiplication is performed in Galois Field (GF) arithmetic (not integer arithmetic). The first four output bytes of *ShiftRows* diffusion acting as input to *MixColumn* diffusion are Y[0], Y[5], Y[10], Y[15] which is assumed as a vector and multiplied by a fixed 4 × 4 matrix as shown below. Similarly, the next four bytes of *ShiftRows* diffusion acting as input to *MixColumn* diffusion are Y[4], Y[9], Y[14], Y[3]. Furthermore, the next four bytes of *ShiftRows* diffusion acting as input to *MixColumn* diffusion are Y[8], Y[13], Y[2], Y[7]. Finally, the last four bytes of *ShiftRows* diffusion acting as input to *MixColumn* diffusion are Y[12], Y[1], Y[6], Y[11]. The respective outputs are Z[0], Z[1], Z[2], Z[3]; Z[4], Z[5], Z[6], Z[7]; Z[8], Z[9], Z[10], Z[11]; Z[12], Z[13], Z[14], Z[15].

![image](OEBPS/images/c10-Eqn-disp-6.gif)

After performing matrix multiplication, the following equations are obtained on which GF arithmetic is performed.

![image](OEBPS/images/c10_eqn1.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c10_eqn2.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c10_eqn3.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c10_eqn4.gif)

Similarly, the rest of the equations can be derived from matrix multiplications, followed by GF arithmetic computation. Note: in GF arithmetic, the additions are simple bitwise XORs of the respective bytes. Multiplication by 01 is multiplication by the identity and does not include any specific operation. Multiplication by 02 can be realized as a multiplication by *x*, which is a left shift by one bit, and a modular reduction with *P*(*x*) = (*x*⁸ + *x*⁴ + *x*³ + *x* + 1) for 8 bit data or (*x*⁴ + *x* + 1) for 4 bit data. Note: In AES, 4-bit product is not possible after multiplication, thus *P*(*x*) = (*x*⁸ + *x*⁴ + *x*³ + *x* + 1) → (100011011) is used. Similarly, multiplication by 03, which represents the polynomial (*x* + 1), can be realized by a left shift by one bit and addition of the original value, subsequently by performing modular reduction with *P*(*x*).

For instance, let us consider eqn. (10.1) above as: Z[0] = (0[2] · Y[0]) + (0[3] · Y[5]) + (0[1] · Y[10]) + (0[1] · Y[15]).

Furthermore, let us consider the state of input to *MixColumn* diffusion as: (Y[0], Y[5], Y[10], Y[15]) = (25, 25, 25, 25).

Now converting (25)[hex] in hexadecimal format to binary is: 00100101. This is also equivalent to polynomial: *x*⁵ + *x*² + 1. Now inserting the binary of (25)[hex] = 00100101 in eqn. (10.1) we get:

![image](OEBPS/images/c10-Eqn-disp-7.gif)

*(Note: Multiplying by 01 is same value; multiplying by 02 is left shift by 1 bit; multiplying by 03 is left shift by 1 bit and addition of the original value followed by a modular reduction with P(x) if required. The addition is achieved by XOR the bytes.)*

![image](OEBPS/images/c10-Eqn-disp-8.gif)

The above value is equivalent to *x*⁵ + *x*² + 1. Since the order of power is less than 8, thus modular reduction is not required. Similarly, the rest of the values (Z[1], Z[2],…,Z[15]) can be computed.

##### 10.2.2.4 Key addition layer

The inputs to the *key addition* layer are the output of *MixColumn* diffusion layer (current 16-byte state matrix) and a *subkey* which also comprises of 16 bytes. Bitwise XOR is performed on the two inputs to yield the output O[0]–O[15] for the next round (see [Figure 10.2](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig2)). This output is used as an input for byte substitution layer in next round. The example below illustrates the process in Tables 10.3 and 10.4. As seen below, keys (K[0]–K[3]) are bitwise XOR-ed with state matrix element (Z[0]–Z[3]) to obtain outputs (O[0]–O[3]) which is fed as an input for the next round. Similarly for the remaining elements of the state matrix, the output is computed (see [Figure 10.2](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig2)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-u02.jpg)

 

##### 10.2.2.5 Key scheduler for 128-bit AES

The main role of key scheduler in AES is to accept the original 128 bit key and derive the subkeys for the next rounds of AES. The number of subkeys needed is obtained by adding one to the number of rounds. Hence, for key length of 128 bits, the number of rounds is *n*[*r*] = 10, and there are 11 subkeys, each of 128 bits. The AES with a 192-bit key requires 13 subkeys of length 128 bits, and AES with a 256-bit key has 15 subkeys. The AES subkeys are calculated recursively, i.e., in order to derive subkey *k*[*i*], subkey *k*[*i*−1] must be known. We will discuss the process of key scheduler in more details a little later. But now since all major phases of AES algorithm has been discussed, thus let us have a look at the hardware mapping process of AES in [Figure 10.4](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig4). This is the generic hardware mapping process that is used to develop a custom hardware-based AES block. We will look into the hardware block of diffusion layer 2 (*MixColumn*) from the context of optimization now and digital watermarking later. The *MixColumn* hardware block can be designed as shown in [Figure 10.5](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig5). However, in order to achieve delay and resource optimization, the hardware structure in [Figure 10.5](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig5) can be re-designed/re-configured as shown in [Figure 10.6](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig6).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f04.jpg)

Figure 10.4 Hardware mapping of 128 bit AES algorithm

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f05.jpg)

Figure 10.5 MixColumn (diffusion layer 2) hardware before optimization

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f06.jpg)

Figure 10.6 MixColumn (diffusion layer 2) hardware after optimization

The AES key schedule is word-oriented, where 1 word = 32 bits. Subkeys are stored in a key expansion array M that comprises of words. [Figure 10.7](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig7) shows the *key scheduler* process for round ‘*i*’. Similarly, how the keys for round 1 have been generated, and the keys for next rounds using key scheduler are obtained. The g-function in the key scheduler process is responsible for non-linearity in the key scheduling. It accepts a four-byte input and produces a four-byte output. The sub-steps inside g-function are following: left rotation (e.g., V[0], V[1], V[2], V[3] changes to V[1], V[2], V[3], V[0]), byte substitution using S-box, and adding round coefficient (RC). The RC is an element of the GF (2⁸), i.e., an 8-bit value. It is only added to the leftmost byte in the function g. The RC value varies round to round and is added as per the following rule based on eqn. (10.5) in [Paar and Pelzl (2009)](#Chapter10.html#c10_bib5):

![image](OEBPS/images/c10_eqn5.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f07.jpg)

Figure 10.7 AES key schedule for 128-bit key size for round ‘i’

But we know GF(2⁸) = *x*⁸ + *x*⁴ + *x*³ + *x* + 1 = 100011011.

Thus, for example when we compute RC\[9\] = *x*⁸ using eqn. (10.5):

![image](OEBPS/images/c10-Eqn-disp-9.gif)

Furthermore, RC\[10\] = *x*⁹ = 2 × *x*⁸ which is equivalent to left shifting the value RC\[9\], i.e., (000011011)[2] → (00110110)[2].

The respective hardware mapping of key scheduler process is shown in [Figure 10.8,](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig8) which indicates the hardware structures necessary for rotation, S-box implementation, RC, as well as the others units.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f08.jpg)

Figure 10.8 Hardware mapping of AES key schedule

### 10.3 AES digital watermarking

We have learnt about the motivation of embedding watermark in an IP core or hardware. Similarly, in order to provide protection (provide deterrent) against false claim of ownership, piracy, forgery, digital watermark needs to be implanted in AES hardware design. In the chapter, we show how to implant watermark in a certain portion of AES hardware structure. The selected portion of AES structure where watermarking is embedded in ‘*MixColumn diffusion layer 2* hardware block’ (shown in Figures [10.4](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig4) and [10.5](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig5), respectively).

This portion of AES hardware is selected for watermarking because of following desirable properties:

1.  Option of embedding watermark without much design overhead.
    
2.  Ease of implementation.
    
3.  Seamless signature detection.
    
4.  No chance of hardware functionality being affected.
    
5.  Maximal opportunity of adding several signature digits corresponding to a watermark.
    

#### 10.3.1 AES watermark encoding

In this chapter, we present a new encoding scheme for embedding signature digits ‘*α*’ and ‘*β*’ into the AES diffusion layer to design structure. The formal definition of digits ‘*α*’ and ‘*β*’ are as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/disp96.gif)

For example, [Figure 10.9a](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig9) represents the portion of *MixColumn* structure responsible for computing Z0 (refer [Figure 10.5](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig5)). Embedding of ‘*α*’ indicates double sharing of two consecutive XOR blocks (indicated in [Figure 10.9a](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig9)), while embedding of ‘*β*’ indicates triple sharing of three consecutive XOR blocks (also indicated in [Figure 10.9a](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig9)). [Figure 10.9b](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig9) shows the resultant structure after embedding a ‘*α*’ digit in the original AES MixColumn structure. The resultant structure now contains two extra 2:1 multiplexers and one 1:2 demultiplexer (and storage registers) with a minimization of one XOR block. On the other hand, if a ‘*β*’ digit is implanted in the original AES MixColumn structure, then the resultant structure is shown in [Figure 10.9c](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig9). The resultant structure now contains two extra 4:1 multiplexers and one 1:4 demultiplexer (and storage registers) with a minimization of two XOR block. Thus, evident different area-delay tradeoff is possible due to choice of different watermark signature digits. Moreover, the design overhead would also vary depending on the choice of the signature digits. We further present the portion of original *MixColumn* structure (with no watermark) responsible for computing Z[1], Z[2], and Z[3], along with its corresponding watermarked design in Figures [10.10](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig10), [10.11](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig11), and [10.12](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig12), respectively.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f09.jpg)

Figure 10.9 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z[0] MixColumn structure of AES

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f10.jpg)

Figure 10.10 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z[1] MixColumn structure of AES

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f11.jpg)

Figure 10.11 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z[2] MixColumn structure of AES

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-10-f12.jpg)

Figure 10.12 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z[3] MixColumn structure of AE

#### 10.3.2 Process of embedding watermark in AES

1.  Sort the output variables of *MixColumn* hardware structure in ascending order, i.e., Z[0], Z[1], Z[2],…,Z[15] and store in list L\[*k*\].
    
2.  Create a desired 16 digit watermark signature using random combinations of *α* and *β* digits.
    
3.  For each occurrence of *α* or *β* digits, apply design changes (reconfiguration) to the *MixColumn* hardware structure corresponding to sorted output variables. Example, first *α* or *β* digit in a signature will affect the hardware structure corresponding to first sorted variable Z[0] (as it first in the sorted list L\[*k*\]), followed by next *α* or *β* digit affects the hardware structure corresponding to next sorted variable Z[1] and so on.
    
4.  Insert registers after each multiplexer and demultiplexer in the modified *MixColumn* hardware structure.
    

#### 10.3.3 Signature detection

Signature detection is performed through the following two phases:

1.  Inspection of the datapath of AES *MixColumn* structure to collect relevant hardware information.
    
2.  Signature verification is performed to authenticate the existence of vendor’s signature in the AES IP core design. Firstly, the encoded signature is decoded through the cognizance of the encoding rules. Subsequently, the presence of extra constraints as watermark is verified in the *MixColumn* hardware structure.
    

### 10.4 Case study of a watermarked AES hardware

The AES design was implemented in VHDL in Altera Quartus v.13 and run on AMD A8-4500M with 4 GB DDR3. The target hardware platform selected was Cyclone II—Device EP2C70F896C6.

For the sake of analysis, two different watermark signature sizes were chosen, viz. 8-digit and 16-digit for embedding into the AES hardware design. Three types of experiments were conducted: (a) variation of different 8-digit signature combinations and its impact on synthesis results of AES hardware, (b) variation of different 16-digit signature combinations and its impact on synthesis results of AES hardware, and (c) overhead obtained due to 8-digit signature and 16-digit signature compared to non-watermarked AES. Following parameters were observed and analyzed: total logic elements, total combinational functions, dedicated logic registers, total registers, and total pins. Results of implementation of AES for 8-digit and 16-digit watermark signature as well as non-watermark AES hardware is reported in Tables [10.5](#Chapter10.html#c10_tbl5) and [10.6](#Chapter10.html#c10_tbl6), respectively. A portion of watermarked AES hardware corresponding to signature ααββααββ is shown in [Figure 10.13](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig13). [Figure 10.14](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig14) shows the comparison of non-watermarked AES128 design with three different combinations of 8-digit watermarked design in terms of logic elements. Figures [10.14](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig14) and [10.15](#Chapter10.html#c10_fig15) shows comparison of non-watermarked AES128 hardware with different combinations of 8-digit and 16-digit watermarked AES.

### 10.5 Conclusion

This chapter presented the following novel and interesting aspects: (a) AES algorithm—description of each step and its flow diagram, (b) corresponding hardware mapping of AES block cipher—overview of how each step can be mapped to a specific hardware sub-block, (c) key scheduler—description of each step, (d) corresponding hardware mapping of key scheduler used in AES, (e) watermarking encoding of AES hardware—protecting an AES hardware against threats such as false claim of ownership and piracy, (f) design of watermarked AES hardware—description of the watermark embedding process, and (g) impact of several different watermark signature types on AES hardware and its implementation on FPGA—to highlight the overhead due to watermark. There is no chapter that deals with the design flow of AES algorithm, its hardware design perspective as well as its digital watermarking process for different signature digits. Finally, it provides a lucid comparative study of watermarked AES hardware with a non-watermarked AES hardware. The content of this chapter is useful in understanding the details of AES described in conjunction with functional obfuscation of digital signal processing cores presented in Chapter 08.
