P., ‘TL-HLS: Methodology for low cost hardware Trojan security aware scheduling with optimal loop unrolling factor during high level synthesis,’ *IEEE Transactions on Computer Aided Design of Integrated Circuits & Systems (TCAD)*, 2017, **vol. 36** (4), pp. 655–668.

## *Chapter 11*  
**Hardware approaches for media and information protection and authentication**

Technology scaling has allowed us to design high-performance devices with a low-power consumption. The advent of IoT has increased the versatility of data collection and there are many different ways of collecting and transferring data over the Internet. The data that is being collected is also in different forms, that is, text, images, videos, and audios. When they are shared, for a legit use, attackers can break the security and use them for illegible purposes or claim ownership to sell them commercially. This has been the trend lately where many counterfeit products are appearing in the market. This section discusses the digital watermarking, different schemes of digital watermarking, and how a media object can be secured using a watermark. They are also not completely resistant to attacks and measures need to be taken to secure the content that is being watermarked. The chapter also presents different issues with the watermark implementations, attacks and countermeasures to those attacks on watermarking. Section 11.1 presents a broad overview of the IP protection. Section 11.2 discusses the generic overview and components of any watermark system. Section 11.3 summarizes various types of watermarks. Section 11.4 discusses various applications of watermarking. Section 11.5 presents desired characteristics of watermarks. Sections 11.6 discusses the technical challenges of the watermarking. Section 11.7 discusses hardware-based watermarking systems available in the current literature. Section 11.8 discusses about watermarking in smart vehicles. Section 11.9 discusses about medical signal authentication. Section 11.10 highlights side-channel information leakage and its countermeasures. Section 11.11 outlines various forms of attacks on watermarks and watermarking systems. Section 11.12 presents the difficulties involved in making use of them in practice.

### 11.1 IP Protection—a broad overview

With the advent of new technology, new devices are being introduced into the world and high-performance applications are being designed. With better systems coming out every day, there is also a problem that they are used for various malicious applications like counterfeiting, which is a major problem in hardware and in media also. Many people nowadays are producing content and sharing it with the world ([Krishnamurthy, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib47); [Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib67)). But the content that they own is being illegally used by many commercially, without paying royalties to the owner and in some cases, the content is being misused also. This raises many problems pertaining to the IPR and their protection. [Figure 11.1](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig1) shows a broad overview on the area of counterfeiting. An image can be produced by the owner and watermarked but an attacker can attack, tamper, or remove the watermark from the image and can claim ownership. This creates many issues on the copyrights and ownership rights.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f01.jpg)

Figure 11.1 Broad overview of IP protection ([Mohanty, 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib66); [Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71))

#### 11.1.1 Digital rights management

[Figure 11.2](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig2) shows different media and threat levels which are vulnerable to attacks. A cinema will have a high privacy, whereas a broadcast content will have low security. This has become a major issue lately where the content of the owner is being reproduced without paying royalties to him/her.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f02.jpg)

Figure 11.2 Multimedia video overview ([Mohanty, 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib66); [Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71))

In such cases, the owner will have copyrights violated and misses out on the royalties that are entitled legally. When a content media like a digital video disc (DVD) or Blu-ray is produced with a video content, it is considered to be secured with the watermarks embedded in it. But there are also many attacks available that can remove or tamper the watermark on the content. [Figure 11.3](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig3) shows different types of multimedia that are available on the Internet. Many of the audio services provide audio to the user at a monthly cost. But tampering with the audio that is broadcast over the Internet is not difficult with the technological advancements that are present at a current date. Digital rights management (DRM) is a major issue that many different areas of research are concentrating on. Watermarking the audio files, video files, images, and also text is a solution.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f03.jpg)

Figure 11.3 Multimedia music overview ([Mohanty, 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib66); [Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71))

#### 11.1.2 Copyright protection of multimedia—a brief history

There are several advantages to digital media over the analog world. Higher quality, ease of processing, and editing are some of them. The most common forms of digital media are compact disc (CD), DVD, TV broadcast, and computers. But there are also many disadvantages to the digital media. Digital media counterfeiting has been a very big problem lately. It can easily be duplicated, which has raised the need for more secure and effective DRM tools ([Devillier, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib25); [Kougianos *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib46); [Lah and Lewis, 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib48); [Ma, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib52); [Ma *et al*., 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib53)). Watermarking is one of the ways of securing the digital media such as audios, photographs, and videos. There are different kinds of watermarking like visible or invisible and can be inserted into different domains like spatial or frequency. There are various software implementations of digital watermarking but very few hardware implementations ([Liu *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib50); [Sarreshtedari *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib94); [Zhao *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib129)). When designing a hardware implementation of watermarking, various issues are to be considered such as low-power consumption, high-performance, ease of integration, and reliability.

Emil Hembrooke invented electronic watermarking in 1954 ([Cox and Miller, 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib19)). Since then there has been extensive research carried on by various experts from different domains, such as cryptography, computer science, communications, and signal processing. Digital watermarking was proposed to provide robust protection along with encryption and scrambling. Many of the following questions were raised by the community ([Cox and Miller, 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib19); [Zhao *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib128); [Yeung, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib124)):

1.  What is digital watermarking and what are its properties?
    
2.  What is the process of implementing digital watermarking?
    
3.  What are its disadvantages?
    

Digital watermarking is the process of embedding information into digital media and generating a watermarked media ([Liu *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib50); [Sarreshtedari *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib94); [Sequeira and Kundur, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib97); [Zhao *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib129)) which evolved from steganography techniques. A difference between steganography and cryptography is shown in [Figure 11.4](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig4). In the case of cryptography, a key is used to encrypt the message and convert into a cipher text and when it is decrypted, the original message will be exposed and will not be protected. In the case of steganography, the message is hidden in the plain text, and the Data is embedded with the original message ([Mathivanan and Ganesh, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib59); [Vijayan and Sreedivya, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib113)). The way and intent of using the method differs between steganography and digital watermarking. A watermark can be perceived as an attribute of the carrier (cover). The information that will be watermarked into the media can be anything, including, and not limited to, tracking, license, authorship, copyright, and so on.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f04.jpg)

Figure 11.4 (a) Steganography versus (b) cryptography ([Kahn, 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib39); [Pfitzmann, 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib87))

Digital watermarking has been around for a very long time and many applications are being developed that use the watermarking for security ([Cox and Miller, 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib19); [Kamaruddin *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib40); [Kirovski and Malvar, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib44); [Loan *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib51); [Memon and Wong, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60); [Mintzer *et al*., 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib61); [Barnett, 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib6)), such as fingerprinting, ownership evidence, and authentication. No single watermarking technique can be universally used for all the applications, which makes the research and development of new techniques in watermarking more difficult and challenging. The watermarking technique depends on various factors including the type of application and deployment ([Kamaruddin *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib40)). There are different attacks that can be launched on a media and its watermark, and the security resistance against such attacks and performance determines the success of watermarking scheme ([Vellaisamy and Ramesh, 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib112); [Wang *et al*., 2017b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib120); [Xiang *et al*., 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib123)). The two major conflicting factors of watermarking are the performance of the embedded watermark and fulfilling the desired characteristics. Various benchmarks are available for watermarking techniques ([Kaur *et al*., 2012](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib42); [Voloshynovskiy *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115)).

There are three different parts of a watermark ([Memon and Wong, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60); [Mohanty, 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib65)):

*   The encoder
    
*   The watermark
    
*   The decoder
    

Algorithm that is used for marking will embed the watermark into the media object and the verification algorithm will authenticate if the object is watermarked. Spatial or frequency domain can be used to embed a watermark into the media, which can be visible or invisible. A visible watermark will be a translucent mark that the original media is overlaid on and is visible only to the consumer on careful observation. An invisible watermark cannot be seen even with careful observation and needs to be retrieved from the pixels where it is embedded into. To increase the robustness, multiple watermarks can be embedded into a single media object ([Hua *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib36); [Mohanty *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib72)), which can be used for content authentication or copyright protection.

Before a watermarking scheme is used in a consumer market, different technical, legal, and social issues need to be addressed. Watermarking schemes have been already in use for a very long time. IBM visible watermarking techniques have been used in Vatican library project ([Mintzer *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib63)). In order to develop a robust watermarking scheme or an algorithm, various properties need to be met. For example, application-specific watermarking algorithms need to be developed, which will require a formal body to be involved (ASCAP, 2018; [Cox and Miller, 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib19); [Mintzer *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib62); Broadcast Music Inc., 2018; Motion Picture Licensing Corporation, 2018). Copy Protection Technical Working Group (CPTWG) is a group that focuses on sharing knowledge and information on copyright protection (CPTWG, 2018). There has been extensive research in this area and many algorithms were proposed for watermarking. Hardware integration of watermarking has also been explored for better robustness and performance. [Figure 11.5](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig5) shows a hardware watermarking chip integrated into a camera ([Mohanty, 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib66); [Mohanty *et al*., 2004, 2005b, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71)). The watermarks in the camera will be embedded in the spatial or DCT domain. The watermarking can be performed for either images or videos. An example of encoder in spatial and DCT domain modules for JPEG compression is presented in [Figure 11.6](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig6).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f05.jpg)

Figure 11.5 System architecture for a digital camera with DRM hardware components ([Mohanty, 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib66); [Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71))

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f06.jpg)

Figure 11.6 JPEG encoder with watermarking modules: (a) spatial domain and (b) DCT domain ([Mohanty et al., 2003](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib78))

#### 11.1.3 Hardware versus media protection

Many questions arise when it comes to the copyright protection. There is a major issue of counterfeiting which should be protected against. Many different agencies are trying to protect the copyrights of the owners. But there are always attackers who illegally claim ownership by attacking the watermark protection of the original image or tampering with it. There is media protection and hardware protection when it comes to the Copyright Safeguarding and DRMs. Compared to media, hardware watermarking schemes are better. This is because they can be optimized for a better performance with a low-power consumption. The chip area of the watermarking module can also be optimized so that the overall cost of production is lower. Media protection in some cases is protecting the media on which the copy of original content is reproduced on. For example, DVD will have an information on the discs such that they will not be able to play the content outside the region of distribution. A disc produced in an area and region locked cannot be played outside that region in another drive. The contents of the disc will not be visible for reading. The hardware watermarking can be used for copyright protection and ownership authentication of the owner.

### 11.2 General framework for copyright protection

Primary use of watermark is to embed it into a digital media using different algorithms and extract it at a later time for authentication of ownership and so on. The digital media can be an image, a video, or an audio. For example, a watermark on media can be considered as a “seal” that is on an image to identify the ownership, the quality of media, and in some cases, the identity of purchaser ([Wang *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib121)). [Figure 11.7](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig7) shows the big picture of encoding and decoding techniques which consists of various parts such as encoder, comparator, and decoder ([Memon and Wong, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60); [Mohanty, 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib65)). In case of a visible watermarking technique, the watermark used will be an image. But in case of an invisible watermarking technique, the watermark can be an image, a random, or a pseudo random number. The owner may have a unique watermark of his/her own and can also embed different watermarks in different media objects. When needed, the watermark can be extracted for authentication.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f07.jpg)

Figure 11.7 General framework for watermarking: (a) the encoder and (b) the decoder ([Craver et al., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib21); [Memon and Wong, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60); [Mohanty, 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib65))

#### 11.2.1 The encoder

[Figure 11.7(a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig7) shows the process of embedding a watermark into an original image. The block “E” in the figure represents an encoder. The original image (I) is fed to the encoder along with the watermark. The encoder is designed based on the watermark insertion algorithm that the owner wishes to use to secure the original image. Depending on the algorithm used, the original image is watermarked with the one that is given as an input to the encoder.

For example, let the original image input is denoted by *I* and watermark input is denoted by ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-1.gif). The output watermarked image is denoted by ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-2.gif). The encoder function is denoted by *E* and the inputs to the encoder for the original and watermark images are denoted as *I* and *W*, respectively. The output is given as:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn1.gif)

The input watermark image *W* depends on various factors like size of *I*, its features, and identity.

#### 11.2.2 The decoder

When the watermarked image is needed to be authenticated, it should sent through a decoder. [Figure 11.6](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig6) shows the big picture of the decoding process. The decoding process will depend on various factors, including the process of inserting a watermark into the original image and nature of watermarking algorithm. The watermark extraction process is where the entire watermark is extracted from the image. But in some cases, only a specific watermark signal can be detected in the media, and this process is called a watermark detection. Watermark extraction can prove the authenticity of ownership on the media, but only detection can verify the ownership. The input to the decoder *D* is an image, that is watermarked, nonwatermarked, or even corrupted, denoted as *J*, which needs to be challenged for ownership. The decoder will recover the watermark ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-3.gif). In this process, an additional image *I* can also be included, which is often the original and nonwatermarked version of *J*.

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn2.gif)

#### 11.2.3 The comparator

After the watermark is extracted, it needs to be compared to the original watermarked image. The extracted watermark image from the decoder is sent to the comparator. The comparator is also given the original watermark as the input as shown in [Figure 11.7(b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig7). The comparator compares the extracted watermark ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-4.gif)and the original watermark *W*. The output of the comparator will be in binary, “1” if both the ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-5.gif)and *W* match and “0” if they do not.

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn3.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-6.gif)is the correlation between the two signatures and ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-7.gif)is some threshold. Thus, the watermarking scheme can be treated as a triplet ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-8.gif).

### 11.3 Types of digital watermarks

As mentioned in the previous sections, the research of digital watermarking has evolved and newer innovations are coming out every day. [Figure 11.8](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig8) shows different types of watermarking techniques and their classification. This section describes different types of digital watermarking techniques classified based on different aspects of the media, watermark, and so on.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f08.jpg)

Figure 11.8 Types of watermarking techniques

#### 11.3.1 Spatial versus frequency domain watermarking

The digital watermark can be embedded in frequency or spatial domains ([Chen *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib13); [Mohanty *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71)). There are also some alternatives implemented other than the frequency and spatial domain watermarking, like DCT, FT, and wavelet transform (WT). In all of the watermarking techniques, the spatial techniques are much simpler to implement and are less power hungry. For the frequency domain watermarking techniques also, there are several advantages ([Cox *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib37)). Nonsalient components in the image or an audio file will be eliminated by the lossy compression. So if the watermark has to be preserved after a lossy compression, it should be embedded in a region of the data that is significant and will not be damaged in the lossy compression. Such processing is performed in the frequency domain. High-frequency components are subjected to more loss. So embedding the watermark in a low-frequency region is preferred while watermarking the media. In the case of spatial domain watermarking, cropping is a major issue that might affect the watermark. It is highly difficult to analyze the effects of distortion in spatial and frequency domains.

#### 11.3.2 Based on multimedia objects

There are four different types of watermarking techniques based on the type of media:

*   Image watermarking
    
*   Video watermarking
    
*   Audio watermarking
    
*   Text watermarking
    

Image watermarking is the most focused area of research for the past several decades. Developing a common type of watermarking technique for all the types of media is highly difficult. Secure Spread Spectrum algorithm was considered to be better for image, audio, and video media ([Cox *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib37)). But watermarking halftoned images has to be done in a different manner which was a contradiction to the previous claim ([Memon and Wong, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60)). In such cases, the binary image is embedded with another binary watermark using visual cryptography. Text watermarking is much different compared to the image, audio, or video watermarking techniques ([Kamaruddin *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib40)).

#### 11.3.3 Based on human perception

Digital watermarking techniques can be classified into two types based on the human perception ([Chen *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib13); [Mohanty *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71)):

*   Visible watermarking
    
*   Invisible watermarking
    

In the case of a visible watermark, an image is overlaid on the original image that can be seen but is very translucent. Such watermark can only be seen when the media is carefully observed. An invisible watermark is not visible to the eye. In such cases, the pixel values are altered and the watermark is embedded but the original image itself is not altered. But when the appropriate techniques and algorithms are run, the invisible watermark can be retrieved and authenticated. But this watermark should be embedded into the image so that it is not damaged or removed when the image itself is modified. There are also different watermarking techniques that are available for implementation ([Chen *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib13); [Hua *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib36); Mohanty *et al*., [1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib72), [2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71)). A dual watermark will implement both visible and invisible watermarking techniques. Invisible watermark techniques need the original image in order to detect the watermark when needed. But in the case of a visible watermarking technique, the original image is not needed for authentication. Invisible watermark can also be attacked by creating “counterfeit original” which is called invertible. A watermarking scheme ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-9.gif)is called quasi-invertible if, for any watermarked image ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-10.gif), there exists a function ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-11.gif)such that

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn4.gif)

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn5.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-12.gif)is a computationally feasible function, ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-13.gif)belongs to the set of allowable watermarks, and the images *I* and ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-14.gif)are perceptually similar.

#### 11.3.4 From applications point of view

The digital watermarking techniques can be classified into two types based on the application perspective ([Voyatzis and Pitas, 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib116)):

*   Source
    
*   Destination
    

In case of the source watermarking technique, the watermark which will identify the owner of the media will be embedded into all copies of the media. Authentication is the main aim of the source watermarking where the image received can be challenged to be real or tampered with. The technique where the watermark will identify the user but not the owner is called the destination watermarking technique. Here, each distributed copy embeds a unique watermark identifying a specific user. This type of watermark can be used to identify the media at the buyer side and will help reduce the counterfeiting.

#### 11.3.5 Based on embedding techniques

Digital watermarking techniques can be classified as additive, multiplicative, or quantization based on the embedding techniques ([Voloshynovskiy *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115)). In the case of an additive technique, there are very weak dependencies between the watermark and the image. But in the case of a multiplicative scheme, the original data samples are multiplied by an independent factor. In the quantization watermarking schemes, the watermark and the original media will have strong dependencies but are statistically independent.

#### 11.3.6 Hardware-based watermarking systems

There are many advantages to a hardware watermarking techniques. The module can be designed on an FPGA. Designing the module on an FPGA will give more room for optimization for performance and power consumption trade-off and also will be highly efficient ([Gafsi *et al*., 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib31); [Mohanty *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib81)). There are also cell-based ASIC designs that are available for the invisible and visible watermarking techniques. The choice between FPGA and cell-based IC is a trade-off between cost, power consumption, and performance ([Mohanty *et al*., 2004, 2005a, 2005b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib79)).

### 11.4 Applications of digital watermarks

This section discusses various applications of watermarking schemes, which include copyright protection, broadcast monitoring, misappropriation detection, ownership assertion, usage control, fingerprinting, information hiding, integrity verification, and so on ([Chan *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib12); [Cheng *et al*., 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib14); [Mohanty *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib81); [Zhang *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib127)).

#### 11.4.1 Copyright protection

There are cases where the media objects need to be uploaded to the Internet or publicly available. There are also the cases of research. In such cases, the media might be subject to illegal distribution where no royalties will be paid to the owner and the media is distributed or used commercially. There are also applications where the owner might have to distribute the preview of the media for public display before the content is released. In those cases, the owner might desire to have the ownership mark where it can save the media to be used or distributed illegally. A visible watermark can be used in such cases where a translucent image is spread across the significant portion of the original image or media.

#### 11.4.2 Ownership assertion

The owner might make the media available over the Internet or in a public domain and desire to publicly indicate the ownership of the content. Then the observer will be interested in patronizing the institute that owns the media or object. For example, the books in a library will have a small print of the printers. In case of ownership assertion, an invisible watermark can also be used. A watermark or a key will be generated by the owner and can be embedded into the original media. In such scenarios, an invisible-robust watermark which is a function of original image can be used and more suited.

#### 11.4.3 Authentication and integrity verification

For the authenticating and integrity verification purposes, an invisible-fragile watermark is used. When the media or object is used legally, for example, medical or news purposes, original image has to be verified that if it has been altered or tampered. If the image is captured and saved for a later use, it has to be verified that the image is not altered. For example, if an image is captured with a camera for news purposes, when it is being presented in an article, the image should be original and should not be altered. Similarly, the images of human fingerprints have been stored for various purposes, which has to be secure and authentic. In a library, invisible-fragile watermarking can be implemented to detect any alteration of images.

#### 11.4.4 Fingerprinting

When an image is distributed into the public domain, the owner might want to increase the security of the media by implementing a unique watermark of his/her own into the media, which is called “fingerprint.” After embedded into the media, a fingerprint can be retrieved and the origination of the image can be tracked. In this case, an invisible-robust watermark invulnerable to forgery, removal, and invalidation is most suitable.

#### 11.4.5 Usage control

In cases of physical media such as DVD or audio CD, proprietary hardware is to be used for copying and viewing. In such a scenario, invisible-robust watermark is used to determine if the media can be played or copied. A watermark can also be used to determine the number of times the media is copied. There is also a chance that the watermark is changed by the hardware to increase the robustness and to prevent the illegal use of the object.

#### 11.4.6 Broadcast monitoring

Broadcast monitoring is another application where watermarking can protect the content that is being distributed. Owner, broadcaster, and the user are the parties that are involved in this scenario. The owner and the protect rights can be identified using the invisible-robust watermarking in this case and the receiver end needs privacy monitoring stations. The monitoring station is responsible for watermark identification and not the owner in this case. Real-time detection also needs to be done without the original media content created being present in the scenario. A small visible watermark showing the ownership or TV broadcasting station logo can also be used.

#### 11.4.7 Content labeling

Most of the new digital cameras have GPS modules integrated in the camera that is used to stamp the photographs with the location. Time and date can also be stamped into the photograph automatically. During the management and retrieval of the data, this additional information is much helpful. A universal product code (UPC) can also be inserted by the watermarking scheme in the camera to identify the source of the media. Invisible or visible watermarking scheme can be used for this purpose. For successful operation of this scheme, the DSP of the camera has to be integrated with the watermarking blocks.

#### 11.4.8 Misappropriation detection

The misappropriate images and the identity of the person that has performed the act can be identified using the invisible-robust watermarks. The buyer of the shared content media, after buying the legit copy of the media, the mis-appropriator, may share the media for free, which can deprive the owner of legitimate licensing revenue. In this case, the watermark of the seller is retrieved and the availability of the seller’s objects are checked. The mis-appropriator might edit the original multimedia objects and distribute them without the payment of royalties. In this case, the owner needs to insert an invisible-robust watermark showing to whom has that object been sold.

#### 11.4.9 Anti-counterfeiting

Controlling the counterfeiting of media is another application of the watermarking techniques. Currency counterfeiting is a major issue that has to be addressed with high priority. With the availability of better performing scanners and printers, and open-source software, currency counterfeiting is becoming an issue every day. Inserting a digital watermark can save in such scenarios. The watermarking algorithms and schemes can be integrated into the printing hardware such that the currency can be saved from counterfeiting.

#### 11.4.10 UAV safety

UAVs have been around for a long time and are used for various applications including military. In some cases, UAVs are used for surveillance where it will have video recording capabilities. The video recorded by the UAV can be used for various purposes, but UAV itself is subject to different kinds of attacks including denial of service, spoofing, and so on. If the attacker gets access to the UAV, the data that is being recorded by the UAV can be tampered with, and the video recordings can be rendered useless. In such scenarios, watermarking the video can to some extent mitigate the threats and protect the integrity of the video recordings.

#### 11.4.11 Medical signals authentication

Medical field is a vast area and privacy protection is of the highest priority as it contains records of many patients. Many cases require confidential media such as videos, photos, or audio recordings, and also documents need to be stored where it may be subject to security threats. In such cases, invisible or visible watermark can be embedded into the media and can safeguard the media or documentation and mitigate the threats.

### 11.5 Desired characteristics of watermarks

This section discusses different characteristics of watermarks from a researcher point of view (Ahmaderaghi *et al*., 2018; [Bender *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib7); Bi *et al*., 2013; [Busch *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib10); [Kougianos *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib46); [Li *et al*., 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib49); [Makbol *et al*., 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib55); [Mohanty *et al*., 2004](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib68); [Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)). The general characteristics of digital watermarking—for example, cost, power consumption, tamper-resistance, perceptibility, orthogonality, robustness, unambiguity, universality, and so on—are discussed in this section. Trade-off between three different parameters is inevitable in the case of digital watermarking, data/information capacity, imperceptibility, and robustness. A single watermarking scheme cannot satisfy all three of these trade-off parameters simultaneously.

#### 11.5.1 Perceptibility

The viewer should not be able to see the invisible watermark and the embedded watermark should not degrade the quality of the image. The watermark should be imperceptible in ideal scenarios. But in case of the imperceptible signal, if it goes through a lossy signal, the watermark signal will be removed or lost. A just noticeable distortion (JND) is usually observed by comparing two signals: watermarked and original ([Cox and Miller, 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib18); Delaigle *et al*., [1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib23), [2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib22); [Kankanhalli *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib41)). In case of visible watermark also, the watermark image should not degrade the quality of the original image.

#### 11.5.2 Robustness

A watermark image that is embedded into the original image should be robust to different transformations, which include lossy compressions, digital and analog conversions, and signal distortions. In case of images and video watermarking, the watermark should be resistive to geometric distortions such as cropping, scaling, and translation. The robustness of watermark can be increased by embedding in a significant portion of a signal. But, to make the watermark imperceptible, it should be embedded in perceptually insignificant regions of an image. There are two trade-offs that conflict in designing the algorithm. Ownership establishment need not be the only goal of a robust watermark scheme in an image or a video unless they are implicated legally on the schemes ([Craver *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib21)).

#### 11.5.3 Tamper resistance

Signal distortions are not the only type of transformations that a watermarked image is subjected to but also attacks that intend to remove the watermark image from the original image ([Voloshynovskiy *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115); [Wang *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib121)). Hence, it is highly important that the invisible and visible watermarking schemes are resistant to such attacks. Detecting any attacks that are performed on the watermark should also be the quality of an invisible watermarking scheme. Using a private watermark, asymmetric encoder–decoder are some of the ways of protecting the image ([Bender *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib7); [Cox and Miller, 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib18)).

#### 11.5.4 Bit rate

Watermark bit rate is the amount of information of watermark image that can be encoded into an original image, which is an important aspect in case of public watermarking schemes ([Cox and Miller, 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib18)). Host signal modification and the quantity can vary depending on the application and its type. Some application will require more information to be embedded and in other cases, it requires large amount of data insertions. A watermark algorithm can embed huge data amounts or can be highly robust to different kinds of attacks but they are trade-offs ([Bender *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib7); [Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)).

#### 11.5.5 Modifiability, multiplicity, cascadability, and orthogonality

In some cases, after a digital watermark is embedded into a media object, it might have to be changed ([Cox and Miller, 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib18)), for example, to control the flow of usage so that the media is used at a limited rate. To achieve this, the original disc, once a copy of it is made, is rewritten with a new watermark on it so that copying it further becomes difficult. If any alteration to the original disc or copying has to be performed, the watermark can be removed first before doing so. Cascadability is the process of adding multiple watermarks to the media at different stages of production or reuse. Pseudo random numbers are used to create spread spectrum watermarking and such watermarks should be orthogonal to be detected individually.

#### 11.5.6 Scalability

It is known that the speeds of the computer double every 18 months ([Ross, 2003](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib90)). Therefore a watermarking algorithm that currently requires high computation power might not seem such computationally demanding in the near future with a better performing computers. For example, the decoders that are initially designed are computationally not demanding but are not as efficient as the new and better ones as the new decoders will have more computational powers to perform the computations.

#### 11.5.7 Unambiguity and universality

The owner of the media object can embed his/her own watermark, visible or invisible into the object for additional security. But the final goal of a watermark is to identify the owner of the media object. In detection process, the watermarking scheme should not have ambiguity and also should not lead to any deadlock situations ([Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)). In order to achieve that, the original media object should meet some conditions ([Craver *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib20)). There is a chance of watermarking an image that is already watermarked and claiming the ownership of the object. Also it can be desired that the same watermarking scheme be used for different purposes including images, videos, and audio media objects. This can be a lot helpful when all the media objects are implemented in a single application.

#### 11.5.8 Pixel alteration and human intervention

In some cases, the value of the artwork that is being watermarked will be very high. In such cases, the watermark should not meddle with the quality of the object. Introducing the watermark or embedding it should not degrade the quality of the original image or artwork. And when a watermark is embedded into the object, the human intervention should be reduced to as minimal as possible. The whole process of watermarking technique should be automated. This can be a lot helpful in reducing the cost of production and the time taken to get the final watermarked product.

#### 11.5.9 Reliability

A watermark, once it is embedded into the original media object, should be reliable in detecting and retrieving when necessary. This will pose some constraints on the capacity of the respective watermark used. There are three figures of merit (FoM) for measuring the reliability of the watermark. They are:

*   False positive error rate
    
*   False negative error rate
    
*   Bit error rate
    

False positive error rate is the probability of determining the watermark when an nonwatermarked image is given as an input to the detection system and the ideal value should be 0. False negative error rate is the rate at which the detector misses the watermark when watermarked image is presented to it. Bit error rate is the number of correct bits that are detected in the watermark image.

#### 11.5.10 Blindness

In the case of a blind watermark embedding scheme, the watermark pattern that is chosen to be embedded on the original media object is independent of the host. And while detecting such watermarks, the information regarding the original object will not be revealed or the knowledge of it will not be available. In some cases, the original media object will not be available when detecting the watermark for authentication or copyright purposes. In such cases, blind watermarking and detecting is highly useful and reliable. But there is a drawback or limitations to the amount of watermark data that can be embedded onto an object and retrieval can also be difficult ([Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)).

#### 11.5.11 Security

Securing the insertion phase of watermarking is of highest priority. To achieve more robustness and security with the watermarks, a secret key can be used such that the watermark that is embedded is dependent on the secret key. In such scenarios, the watermark will not be dependent on the algorithm but the secret key that is being used in the original image ([Busch *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib10); [Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)). This can be very helpful where even if the adversary gets to know the algorithm that is used for embedding and detection of watermarks, the integrity of the watermark will not be affected.

#### 11.5.12 Real-time operation

There are some applications where the watermarking is used for real-time applications. For example, there are many different TV broadcasting networks that do live TV shows or live sports events. In such cases, the watermarking of the media that is being shared should also be done real time. Such cases also demand the watermarking of audios, videos, and images to be watermarked in real time and broadcast to the public. The signal latency should also be as minimal as possible ([Busch *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib10); [Khan *et al*., 2010](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib43); [Marcinak and Mobasseri, 2005](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib56); [Wang *et al*., 2008](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib117)). The hardware that is used for watermarking should be designed with pipelining and parallel architectures for a better performance. The algorithm that is used for watermarking should also be designed to use parallel processing.

#### 11.5.13 Cost and complexity

Implementing a watermark onto an image has a lot of limitations, one of which is the complexity and cost. When designing a watermarking hardware, the cost of the entire module will be calculated in terms of chip area and memory that is required by the algorithm. In case of the blind watermarking, having the original image on hand is not necessary and hence the memory requirements are also comparatively low. With the reduction in cost of watermarking, the overall production cost will also be affected, which leads to a low-cost production.

#### 11.5.14 Energy consumption

With newer technologies being developed, power consumption bar is coming lower every day. This leads to the development of low-power consumption devices and applications. With the introduction of IoT and its applications, different devices require low-power consumption. Digital watermarking schemes also need to consume low-power consumption (Mohanty and Ranganathan, [2004](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib75), [2005](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib76)). The technique may be software or hardware watermarking scheme but the power consumption of the overall process should be kept as low as possible. Different devices have unique specifications of hardware like power sources and running on battery. So, power optimization is highly necessary in terms of watermarking.

#### 11.5.15 Integrability

Digital watermarking has come a very long way since its introduction. But so did the media community and devices that consume or distribute the content with watermarks with it. This has become a large system and watermarking algorithms should have integration capabilities into such huge systems. This is actually a high priority in case of hardware watermarking techniques where the compatibility of hardware module to be embedded in different applications should be increased. While implementing the watermarking chip, the target device, such as a DVD drive, digital camera, printer, and scanner, should be taken into consideration.

#### 11.5.16 Characteristics specific to a watermark

As discussed in Section 11.3, there are different types of watermarking techniques. With the discussion that we had until now in the current section, the characteristics of different types of watermarks can be formulated.

##### 11.5.16.1 Visible watermark

Visible watermarking technique is widely used in many applications and there are characteristics that need to be met for this type of watermark ([Mintzer *et al*., 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib61); Mohanty *et al*., [2000a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib73), [2000b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib75)). The color and the monochrome images, when used for visible watermark, should be more obvious when used. When the visible watermark is embedded into an image, a significant portion of the image should be selected for the insertion so that the watermark is not deleted by cropping. The watermark should be transparent and the original image details should be visible. Watermark should be difficult to remove and the removal process should be more intensive compared to purchasing the original image from the owner.

##### 11.5.16.2 Invisible-robust watermark

In the case of an invisible watermark, it should not be visible when embedded into the original image ([Mintzer *et al*., 1997](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib61)). When an invisible watermark is embedded into the media, the quality of the original media should not be affected and degraded. An invisible watermark should not be affected to any signal distortions and is also resistant to different kinds of attacks targeted to remove the watermark illegally. Identification of the owner should be unambiguous by retrieving the watermark. The decoder of the watermark scheme should be scalable and also be integrated into different generations of computers and systems. Pixel modification should be kept to a minimum when inserting the watermark into a high-quality artwork. The whole process of insertion of watermark should be autonomous with a little human intervention.

##### 11.5.16.3 Invisible-fragile watermark

Similar to the previously discussed invisible watermark, the invisible-fragile watermark should not be visible or noticeable and also should not degrade the quality of the original image. When the pixel values of the image are modified, the watermark should not be removed from the watermarked image and should be secure. This means that it is impossible to recover the changes, or regenerate the watermark after image alternations, even when the watermarking procedure and/or the watermark itself is known. In case of a high-quality image as an input to the insertion algorithm, the pixels that are modified must be kept to a minimum. In some applications, reversing the tampering of watermark might be necessary, which is called error correction.

##### 11.5.16.4 Video watermark

In case of a video watermark, the presence of the watermark in the video should not affect the viewing quality of the video or playback. Compression of the video should not affect the video and watermark and vice versa. Detection of watermark should be reliable and with less errors and false detection, it should be kept to a minimum, ideally zero. Attacks on the video watermarking may be intentional or unintentional like frame dropping and variable rate encoding. Detection algorithm hardware should be designed for low-cost implementations.

##### 11.5.16.5 Watermarking for broadcasting applications

Watermarking applications also include broadcasting applications ([Busch *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib10)). The watermark used in that applications should be resistant to the attacks and the codec encoder should not be overworked. When the watermark is embedded into the image, it should not be affected by the low bit rate of MPEG-2, VHS tape recordings, and TV transmissions. For broadcasting applications, the capacity of 64 bits in 10-second video is used. Multiple watermarking schemes should be able to handle that with false positive detection probability less than 10^(−12) and watermark should be more secure.

##### 11.5.16.6 Desired characteristics of hardware-based watermarking systems

Hardware watermarking chips are more secure and also can be optimized for better performance with low-power consumption ([Mathai *et al*., 2003a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib57); [Mohanty *et al*., 2005a, 2005b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib79)). In such cases, the chip area occupied by the chip should be low to reduce the cost of the entire component. The power consumption of the hardware watermarking chip should also be less so that the modules can be integrated in battery operated applications. The integration of the chip into other devices should not be an issue. The operational latency of the chip should be low so that it can be used for real-time applications. Blind watermarking schemes are preferred in such applications.

### 11.6 Technical challenges for watermarking

There are many technical issues when it comes to the implementation of watermarking. Security, robustness, and imperceptibility are the trade-offs of the digital watermarking and this is what makes the research in this area interesting. For an increased imperceptibility, the watermark must be added to a high-frequency component in the media object. But to attain high robustness, the low-frequency components should be used for watermarking. This becomes more difficult with added characteristics such that the watermark data should be resistant to different kinds of attacks on them. This section discusses different kinds of challenges faced during the watermarking algorithm design ([Delaigle *et al*., 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib22); [Frattolillo, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib29); [Kougianos *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib46); [Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib67); [Mohanty *et al*., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib72); [Peng *et al*., 2010](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib83); Singh *et al*., [2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib99), [2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib100); [Vo *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib114)).

#### 11.6.1 Properties of visual signals

The images and the videos are the visual signals. Behavior of such signals has to be studied and understood to develop more robust and secure watermarking schemes and hide them well in the signals. The visual signals are considered as the intensity versus space delays of image information, amplitude plots, and the intensity versus space and time displays. When these waves are studied more, the information regarding the properties of the signals will be revealed. Some of the properties are discussed in the following text.

##### 11.6.1.1 Nonstationarity

The nonstationary property is highly common to almost all of the signals. There is a huge amount of segments of flat or slowly changing intensity in the image and video signals. Besides these there will also be edges and textured regions in the image and video signals. The edges are the important regions that need to be protected to maintain the quality of the image or video and the textured regions should be used for storing additional information.

##### 11.6.1.2 Periodicity

There are frame-to-frame and line-to-line periodicities in the video and image signals. These are not precisely periodic in nature. There will be a little redundancy among the frames and the lines. In the case of the watermarking schemes, where additional content should be stored, this redundancy is taken as an advantage.

##### 11.6.1.3 Power spectral density

The visual signals mostly will have the low-pass frequency spectrum in the longtime average sense or a global sense. In the short-term frequency analysis of these signals in a local sense, when a certain region of the image or frame is selected, they tend to possess all-pass or high-pass frequency spectra. This can be highly useful in the watermark embedding for adding additional information.

##### 11.6.1.4 Properties of color signals

UV or IQ (chrominance) components of any kind of signal will have low energy with a lower bandwidth when compared with a luminance component Y. So when performing the data compression, a coarser quantization is used by subsampling them. This can be considered when developing algorithm for watermarking color and video signals.

#### 11.6.2 Properties of the human visual system

Any watermarking scheme can be called a success when the human visual system (HVS) is also considered and made a best use of it. Various properties of HVS should also be considered when developing watermarking schemes for the images and video ([Delaigle *et al*., 2002](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib22); [Kankanhalli *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib41); [Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105)).

##### 11.6.2.1 Brightness sensitivity

Low-intensity signals are easily perceived by the human eye when different background intensities are present. The surrounding intensity is increased, dark area intensity is reduced when the light areas intensity is increased. When the background is the mean of noise square, it tends to be more visible to the human eye. This is called the Weber’s law. At low intensities, eye has more sensitivity; in case of highest intensity, it has reduced sensitivity.

##### 11.6.2.2 Frequency sensitivity

When psychovisual studies were performed on the HVS it was discovered that it has a general bandpass characteristics with peak sensitivity of 3 or 4 cycles per degree and the reduced sensitivity at higher and lower spatial frequencies. Watermark intensity in the spatial frequency should be inversely proportional to the sensitivity of the corresponding frequencies.

##### 11.6.2.3 Texture sensitivity

Background texture will control the visibility of distortion. When the background is a strong texture, the visibility will be less distorted. When the image block is highly textured, the energy is more evenly distributed among the DCT coefficients. When the image has a flat featured portion, energy is more concentrated in low-frequency components.

##### 11.6.2.4 JND and minimally noticeable distortion

The visual signals are studied and the properties are then analyzed for a short time or spatiotemporally local analysis was performed on the input signals. When the properties are studied, it was observed that they can be used for deriving the perceptual distortion threshold. This is the function of time, space, or frequency. When the distortion by the watermarking algorithm is below the threshold value, signal quality will degrade. A critical distortion profile is expressed by the threshold as JND. Similarly, minimally noticeable distortion (MND) defines a supra-threshold generalization of it, which is not transparent, but still perceptually optimum.

#### 11.6.3 How much watermark signal to add and where?

Watermarking an object is a communication process where the watermark signal should be inserted reliably into the host, the media object ([Ramkumar, 2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib88); [Ramkumar and Akansu, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib89); [Servette *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib98); [Sugihara, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib104)). It was already proven that the communication is reliably possible theoretically but when the information rate does not go beyond the threshold. The threshold value in this scenario is called the channel capacity. The information theory can be used here to derive the rules which will be helpful in deciding the strength of the watermark used and the location on the original media object.

The watermark should be imperceptible and SNR is also highly limited. Communication will be reliable with the increase in bandwidth compensation mechanisms for a poor SNR. So when the watermarking process is being performed, a number of transform domain coefficients should be high and are easy to exploit for hiding information in the object media. An application for the spread spectrum communications can be considered to be digital watermarking. The Shannon limit may be considered by applying the error control codes. If necessary, more robust error correction methods may also be used here. This discusses how much watermark strength to be added to an image or media object. For an answer to the question, where to embed, the watermark should be embedded in a place where the local noise variance is small compared to the threshold value.

#### 11.6.4 Spread spectrum communications

From the discussion until now, it has become more clear that the watermark should not be embedded into a place that is perpetually insignificant region on the image. A watermark that is embedded into a high-frequency domain can be removed using a little degradation of the quality directly or indirectly. Then the problem here is how a watermark can be embedded into the most significant part of the image without noticeable alterations to the image quality. Small changes can be made and spectral coefficient can be altered but the small changes are susceptible to high amounts of noise.

To avoid this issue, the frequency domain of the media object is considered as a communication channel and the watermark is the signal that is transmitted through it. The signal distortions and the attacks are considered as noise that affects the signal. So in this way, a watermarking can be considered as an application for spread spectrum communication ([Sequeira and Kundur, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib97)). In this case of a spread spectrum communications, a narrow band signal is transmitted over a broad bandwidth so that the signal energy is imperceptible. In the same manner, a watermark is spread over a large image such that it is imperceptible. Location of the watermark is known to the watermark detection systems.

### 11.7 Hardware-based approaches for watermarking

The watermarking research has advanced in the past few decades and the maturity attained during this period has advanced the software-based digital watermarking schemes. But when it comes to hardware watermarking schemes, the development is not at an exponential rate compared to the software watermarking. There are already implementation of hardware modules for watermarking. But in designing the watermarking modules based on the hardware, there are a lot of limitations such as power consumption, chip area, latency, and so on ([Kougianos *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib46); [Krishnamurthy, 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib47); [Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib67), 2017; [Mohanty *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71); [Pexaras *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib86); [Roy *et al*., 2013](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib91); [Sengupta *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib95)). There are also many advantages of hardware modules for watermarking, such as low-power consumption, optimization, high reliability, real-time performance, and easy integrability. The watermarking schemes hardware implementation can be design of custom-made VLSI chips or can be designed on an FPGA or can be built around a DSP board. It will become a part of still or motion camera, digital TV, DVD player, or recorder and MP3 player or recorder. For example, an encryption based mechanism called “Signcryption” has been integrated for protection of data in smart cameras in IoT environment ([Figure 11.9](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig9)) ([Ullah *et al.*, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib130)). This section presents different hardware watermarking schemes and the designs. A comparative analysis of various designs of watermarking chips that are presented in this section is provided in [Table 11.1](#Chapter11.html#c11_tbl1) ([Kougianos *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib46)).

**Table 11.1** Watermarking chips proposed in the current literature

![image](OEBPS/images/tab11.1.jpg)

![image](OEBPS/images/tab11.1a.jpg)

#### 11.7.1 Image watermarking hardware systems

This section discusses the hardware-based watermarking schemes that are used for watermarking the images. This kind of hardware modules can be integrated into the still cameras and is useful in watermarking the images on the fly. The hardware modules embedded into the camera or other production systems will help a lot in reducing the extra production time of creating watermarked final products.

##### 11.7.1.1 Invisible-robust wavelet domain VLSI architecture

A progressive watermarking module is presented by Hsiao *et al*. ([2000a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib34), [2000b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib35)), which is a framework of image encoder. The design of encoder and decoder is used for high-speed image and video compression using the “embedded zero wavelet” (EZW) tree algorithm. The EZW encoder–decoder is embedded with a progressive digital watermarking algorithm which can increase the robustness of the entire design. Embedder is a part of the architecture of compressor encoder and the detector is part of the decompressor.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f09.jpg)

Figure 11.9 Signcryption

A progressive invisible robust algorithm is presented which is able to detect the watermark if the received data is partial but not complete. This algorithm embeds the pseudorandom numbers into the wavelet coefficient. Then the detector will compute the correlation between the original watermark sequence that is already present in the memory and the received image. The number generated for the watermark is embedded in the position next to the nonzero bit of each significant wavelet coefficient. A minimal hardware is required to implement this algorithm.

[Figure 11.10(a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig10) presents the insertion algorithm that is used in this design. This module consists of the LFSR, linear feedback shift register, which will generate the pseudo random number for the watermarking scheme. Comparator will then make sure that the watermark bit is embedded into the significant coefficients of the original image. [Figure 11.10(b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig10) presents the detection module for the watermarking scheme. The detection module consists of LFSR, comparator, top index register, and a threshold table. The total number of significant coefficients that is received by the detector is stored in the top index register. Then the threshold correlation value is stored in the threshold table and are compared during the detection process.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f10.jpg)

Figure 11.10 Watermarking embedder–detector modules: (a) embedder and (b) detector (Hsiao et al., [2000a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib34), [2000b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib35))

##### 11.7.1.2 Invisible-robust DCT domain chip

The image watermarking chip should be able to insert the invisible-robust watermarking in DCT domain and was presented by [Tsai and Lu (2001)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib110). This system will embed a pseudo random sequence into a previously selected set of DCT domain coefficients. When extracting the watermark, the original image is not needed. This can be a great advantage of the hardware watermarking scheme. The chip presented by [Tsai and Lu (2001)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib110) used a TSMC ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-35.gif)technology and occupies a die size of ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-36.gif)for 46,374 gates. The power consumption of the chip is ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-37.gif)and is operated at ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-38.gif)with a 3.3 V supply voltage. This is very memory efficient as the original image is not stored in the memory of the chip for extraction or detection.

A Gaussian random number generator is used for the watermark sequence and is represented as *N*(0,1). The length of the original DCT coefficients will be the length of the sequence of watermark. Three DCT coefficients are embedded with the watermark with each nonoverlapping ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-39.gif)block. The strength of watermark comes from the texture complexity and the average brightness. The image blocks are classified as:

*   Bright and strong texture
    
*   Dark and weak texture (strongest watermark)
    
*   Rest (weakest watermark)
    

If the watermark sequence is denoted by ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-40.gif), the DCT coefficient of the ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-41.gif)image block is represented by ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-42.gif), and the scaling factor is ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-43.gif), the watermarked DCT coefficients can be:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn6.gif)

The scaling factor ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-44.gif)is 2, 6, and 9 for class 1, class 2, and class 3 image blocks, respectively. Extraction of watermark can be dependent on the original watermark and the extracted watermark’s correlation.

The chip is designed to be integrated with the JPEG encoder which has the DCT/IDCT, hash, quantization, zigzag (ZZ) scan, and VLC encoder modules. [Figure 11.11](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig11) shows the architecture for watermarking functionality. The coefficients of DCT are stored in the register, watermark sequence in the ROM, and the comparison is carried out by the comparator. The FSM is used to implement the controller which gets the watermarking done using the data path.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f11.jpg)

Figure 11.11 Architecture for watermarking embedding module ([Tsai and Lu, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib110))

##### 11.7.1.3 Invisible-fragile spatial domain chip

A watermarking VLSI design for the implementation of watermark in the spatial design is presented by [Garimella *et al*. (2003)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib32). Here, the differential error is encrypted and along the first sample, it is interleaved. The digital watermark extraction can be done by the accumulation of consecutive LSBs of the pixels and then decrypting. The watermark that is extracted will then be compared with the original watermark for authentication purposes. This is designed with a ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-45.gif)technology. Chip area occupied by the module is ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-46.gif)and power consumption ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-47.gif)at an operating voltage of ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-48.gif). The critical path delay of the circuit is ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-49.gif). This design has an advantage of low-power consumption but only works for grayscale images.

The watermark used here is a text-based one that is converted into an ASCII code. This code will undergo an encryption process using a differential pulse code modulation (DPCM) technique for increased security. The final size of the watermark will be 2,048 bits. The LSB of the original image is replaced with the encrypted ASCII code. In the process of extraction, the LSBs of the image are accumulated and decrypted. This gives the original watermark from the image.

[Figure 11.12](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig12) presents the block diagram of the watermarking chip. Two CMOS clocked RAM modules, RAM 1 and RAM 2, are integrated, which are 40,000 and 2,018 bytes, respectively. The original and the watermarked images are handled in the RAMs. Watermark data is stored in the internal registers permanently. The extraction and insertion process is handled by the controller.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f12.jpg)

Figure 11.12 Functional block diagram of watermarking module ([Garimella et al., 2003](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib32))

Color image watermarking for the same scheme is presented by [Garimella *et al*. (2004)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib33). RGB-YUY and YUV-RGB converters are designed along with the watermark encryption, embedding, extracting, detection, and authentication modules. Similar to the previous design, the LSB of the pixels is integrated with the watermark and the pixel array of 8-bit grayscale image. The color image is initially transformed into the YUV color space and the encrypted watermark is inserted into it. After the embedding process, the YUV space is retransformed into the RGB color space. The luminance component Y is the watermarking channel where the RGB image transforms into the YUV color space. LSBs from the Y are used for the watermarking process in which the watermark is the encrypted stream of the ASCII code text file. Each bit is swapped with first LSB of Y and second LSB is the complemented bit of the first LSB. DPCM technique is used for the encryption process. During the detection process, the LSBs are accumulated and then decrypted to be compared with the original ASCII code text.

##### 11.7.1.4 Invisible-robust-fragile spatial domain chip

A hardware watermarking scheme that can embed both the invisible robust and invisible fragile watermarking is presented by [Mohanty *et al*. (2003)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib80). A ternary watermark is inserted into the original media object in case of an invisible-robust watermarking. This can be done with an encoding function with an addition of scaled gray value of the neighboring pixels. The watermark is a binary sequence of numbers which are pseudo random and are XORed with the original image bit plane. The chip is implemented using ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-50.gif)technology and consumes 2.0547 mW when operated at 3.3 V and 545 MHz frequency.

An invisible-fragile algorithm proposed by Mohanty *et al*. (1999) and invisible-robust algorithm proposed by [Tefas and Pitas (2001)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib106) are used in the chip presented above. This design can be implemented with a JPEG encoder. In the invisible-robust watermarking, *W*, the watermark is the ternary image of three pixel values that are generated with a key *K*. The original image pixels, *I*, are altered to obtain the watermarked image ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-51.gif)and are as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn7.gif)

Assuming ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-52.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-53.gif), the encoding functions ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-54.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-55.gif)are defined as follows:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn8.gif)

The neighborhood image pixel gray value ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-56.gif)is calculated as the average gray value of neighboring pixels of the original image as shown below:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn9.gif)

In the invisible-fragile insertion process, a pseudo random binary-sequence {0,1} is inserted in the ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-57.gif)bit plane of the original image using the XOR function:

![image](OEBPS/images/c11_eqn10.gif)

Finding of the candidate bit plane for watermark insertion is an iterative process, but the second ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-58.gif)bit plane is chosen as the candidate for watermark insertion (for LSB, ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-59.gif)). The watermarked image ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-60.gif)is obtained by merging all the bit planes.

The data path architecture is presented in [Figure 11.13](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig13). In this design, there are two RAM modules, watermark RAM and image RAM. They are used to temporarily store the image and watermark in them. Shift registers are used to generate the sequence of watermark. Address of the ram can be decoded using the address decoders. Main functional units are used for the adder/subtractor, adder, multipliers, and XOR. When a selection is needed, the multipliers are used. Data path that is designed as an FSM is used as a controller.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f13.jpg)

##### 11.7.1.5 Invisible-robust wavelet domain module

In case of a blind watermarking scheme, the original image is not needed. An FPGA implementation of the blind watermarking scheme is presented by [Seo and Kim (2003)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib96). In the two-dimensional discrete wavelet transform (2D-DWT), one or two image bit planes are replaced with the watermark. The hardware module is designed to be operated at 82 MHz, and 24% of logic array blocks and 3% of embedded system blocks are used of an Altera APEX20KC EP20K400CF672C7 device. JPEG 2000 CODEC was integrated with the watermarking scheme.

The watermark used in this scheme is created from the binary numbers. The candidate for the watermark embedding is the DC which makes it more robust to the attacks. The bit plane selected is done with more care such that the human eye cannot see the watermark because the DC subband has most important information regarding the image. During the embedding, the watermark is divided into 4-level 2D-DWT. Binary watermark is embedded in the second plane, the third plane from LSB plane. Selection of bit plane *p* is chosen from a set of *k* bit planes. Secret key is the initial value of the LFSR. Then, *k* parallel outputs of LFSR ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-61.gif)are chosen followed by computation of *p* as ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-62.gif). The same procedure is performed in reverse to extract the watermark from the image.

[Figure 11.14(a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig14) presents the encoder for JPEG 2000 architecture. Decoder is also similar to the encoder architecture. There are six functional units in the architecture:

*   Image-side controller to control the image input
    
*   Wavelet kernel
    
*   Quantizer/entropy encoder
    
*   Storage-side controller/buffer to control the output of the compressed data
    
*   Memory controller to control the data access with external memories
    
*   Global controller/scheduler to determine and control the whole processing
    

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f14.jpg)

Figure 11.14 (a) JPEG2000 encoder and (b) watermarking embedding module ([Seo and Kim, 2003](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib96))

Quantizer/entropy encoder modules consist of the watermarking scheme. [Figure 11.14(b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig14) shows the architecture of the watermarking module.

##### 11.7.1.6 Invisible-robust spatial domain module

Invisible-robust insertion algorithm is presented by [Mohanty *et al*. (2004)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib82). This algorithm was implemented on a Xilinx FGPA board and VIRTEX technology with XCV50-BG256-6 target device was synthesized.

[Figure 11.15](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig15) shows the functional diagram of the encoder chip. The encoder of this design consists of watermark generator, insertion, address decoder, controller, and registers. External storage is used to load the images. An LFSR is used for the watermark generation, which is the most important part of the design. LFSR should be avoided to power on randomly, which may become permanently stuck with some prohibited states. Insertion module consists of adder/subtractor, adders, subtractors, multipliers, and shifters. Controller is an eight-state FSM.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f15.jpg)

Figure 11.15 Invisible-robust spatial domain watermarking module ([Mohanty et al., 2004](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib68))

##### 11.7.1.8 Visible wavelet domain chip

A discrete WT-based watermarking design is proposed by [Fan *et al*. (2005)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib27). This reduces the operational and resource sharing which can increase the overall efficiency of the design. The watermark and the original image are transformed into three-level multiresolution structures. Original image is then divided into two different sequences of the same pattern length. A two-path parallel processing is used for calculating the processing time. De-multiplexers will then send the signal to different elements for processing. The watermark image is embedded by modifying the coefficients of the image.

##### 11.7.1.9 Low-power chip with DCT domain-invisible-robust and visible functionalities

A low-power watermarking chip is presented by [Mohanty *et al*. (2005a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib79). This is capable of both the invisible and visible watermarking techniques. The power consumption of this chip is significantly low and there is also the integration of dynamic frequency clocking and clock gating. A parallel architecture and three-stage pipelining is used to significantly improve the performance of the watermarking. TSMC ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-84.gif)technology was used for design and verification. The dual frequency of the chip is 280 and 70 MHz and operates at voltages of 2.5 and 1.5 V.
