#### 11.7.2 Video watermarking hardware systems

Until now, this section discussed the implementation of hardware-based watermarking schemes for the image files. But this part of the section presents different modules for the implementation of the watermarking schemes for video systems.

##### 11.7.2.1 Invisible-robust spatial domain module

A real-time embedder–detector modules are developed for the implementation in broadcasting in the framework of VLIW DSP processor and are presented by [Depovere *et al*. (1999)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib24), Strycker *et al*. ([1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib101), [2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib102)), and Termont *et al*. ([1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib107)). During the insertion of the watermark, the pseudorandom numbers are added to the received video stream and it is based on the luminance value of the frame. Detection of the watermark will depend on the correlation value calculations. Spatial and Fourier domains are used for watermark insertion and detection. Insertion process consists of adding pseudo random numbers to the stream. The initial sequence is a user key and then it is shifted and sum is calculated to generate *n* basic pseudo random patterns. Then one pattern out of those *n* is chosen thus creating a key. The size of this created number is ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-104.gif), which is same as that of the size of video frame. Depth of insertion will determine the imperceptibility and the robustness of the watermark. Larger values make the watermark more secure but are likely to be visible than the smaller numbers. The algorithm is designed to increase the security while reducing the visibility. The detection module will retrieve the key if a watermark is present. A group of *G* frames are selected and then folded. Sum of it is calculated with a buffer of size ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-105.gif)and correlated with each of *n* pseudo random numbers. This is equivalent to the 2D cyclic convolution which can be efficiently performed in the Fourier domain. If the correlation so obtained, known as decision variable, exceeds the predefined threshold, the video is declared as watermarked. [Figure 11.18(a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig18) shows the commercial TV broadcasting where two Trimedia processors are used. [Figure 11.18(b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig18) shows the setup of two PCs, each with a Trimedia PCI card inside.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f18.jpg)

Figure 11.18 Simulation of broadcast environment: (a) TV broadcast and (b) simulation ([Depovere et al., 1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib24); Strycker et al., [1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib101), [2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib102); Termont et al., [1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib107))

##### 11.7.2.2 Invisible-robust spatial domain chip

A millennium watermarking scheme system is presented by [Maes *et al*. (2000)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib56) for the implementation in DVD video system. The watermark detector location and the generation of copies of the DVD are discussed by [Maes *et al*. (2000)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib56). The insertion phase of the watermark in this algorithm consists of addition of scaled watermark to the original media object signal in the spatial domain. The detection phase consists of calculating the correlation in Fourier domain. The algorithms are presented by Strycker *et al*. ([1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib101), [2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib102)). The memory usage in this scheme for DVD video watermarking should be minimal.

A real-time detection module is designed and implemented using three different modules such as Trimedia processor board, high-end silicon graphics workstation, and an FPGA. FPGA platform implementation has been the most relevant implementation for the DVD watermarking ([Maes *et al*., 2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib54)). A random number generator is implemented which increases the robustness of the entire modules and the watermark.

Implementation of watermarking for the raw video encoding is presented by [Tsai and Wu (2003)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib111). A standard video encoder is used for implementing the watermarking algorithm like MPEG-1/2/4, H.26x, and Motion JPEG for a real-time IP protection. The insertion algorithm has three steps. Initially the watermark is read and the binary transformation is performed with a chaotic function. Then pseudo-noise is generated, which is of lengths 63 and 31, for both spatial and chaotic transformed domains. Then insertion is performed with a human visual characteristics that will dictate the weighting factor of ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-106.gif)for watermark insertion to be 16 for edge blocks and 4, otherwise.

In case of detection of the watermark, the correlation of the original pseudo-random noise is calculated. For implementing the algorithm, verilog was used for the watermark function. This has an advantage of using an MPEG encoder for the compression and increasing the robustness of the video. Watermark function has three parts, pseudo-noise generator, data path, and inserting component and watermarking information generator.

##### 11.7.2.3 Invisible-robust fractal domain module

A real-time video watermarking scheme was presented by [Petitjean *et al*. (2002)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib87). This actually embeds the watermark with the help of fractal approximation. Extraction of the watermark is done by performing the process in reverse to the insertion phase. C programming language was used for the implementation of the encoder and decoder. A general-purpose PC implementation of this algorithm will yield better results than that of the others.

For an increased security of the watermark, embedding exploits the affine transformation invariance properties of fractal coding. Embedding the watermark has three different phases:

*   Formatting and encryption
    
*   Cover generation
    
*   Embedding
    

During formatting and encryption, the message bits that are to be hidden will be oversampled and duplicated. This gives out the watermark of the size of object or host image video frame. Pseudo-random noise that is generated will be XORed to the watermark and is secured. The difference of original image and fractal approximation gives the cover signal. Watermark is then modulated to the cover which includes forcing some of the cover pixels to zero based on the watermark bit and sign. Modulated cover is added to the fractal approximation which gives the watermarked image. The process is reversed to extract the watermark from the frame.

##### 11.7.2.4 Invisible-robust wavelet domain chip

A hardware implementation of video watermarking algorithm is presented by [Mathai *et al*. (2003a, 2003b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib60). The algorithm is based on the implementation from [Depovere *et al*. (1999)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib24), Strycker *et al*. ([1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib101), [2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib102)), and Termont *et al*. ([1999](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib107)). In the paper, both the embedder and the detector are presented with a floating point data path architecture. For the implementation of algorithm, ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-107.gif)technology is used. The power consumption of the embedder module is 60 mW and detector is 100 mW at an operational voltage of 1.8 V.

The embedder consists of payload modulator, high-pass filter, and a watermark superposition unit. A video frame that is distorted without the degradation of quality is selected by the high-pass filter. The payload modulator modulates the pseudo random noise pattern using input payload to generate a base watermark which is then multiplied with the high-pass filter output to create the desired watermark. Then the raw images of the video will be added to the watermark that is created. Detection process contains the filter that is similar to the high-pass filter which is used for removing unnecessary components. The fold loop consisting of fold buffer and the adder components will accumulate the frames that are filtered. After accumulation, the input is stalled and detection will continue with the FFT computation. Then the pixel-wise multiplication is performed. The scan hardware is a set of registers used to keep track of highest correlation peaks.

##### 11.7.2.5 Visible watermarking hardware

A visible watermarking hardware for video copyright protection in compressed domain is shown in [Figure 11.19](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig19) ([Cai, 2006](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib11); [Mohanty and Kougianos, 2011](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib69); [Mohanty *et al*., 2009](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib70)). The watermark-embedding IBP embeds a watermark image into IBP video frame, where I is intra-frame and B and P are inter-frames. The watermark embedding I module embeds a watermark to intra-frame only. The “Frame Buffer” buffers the frames for every block procedure. Its size capacity is enough for one input group of picture (GOP), output motion vectors, and output stream. DCT module performs DCT. Motion estimate (ME) module performs motion estimation among the frames. The quantization module quantizes DCT coefficients. The ZZ module performs scanning procedure. The entropy module performs entropy coding procedure using a Huffman coding. The controller which is an FSM generates addressing and control signals with clock for each individual component module in the system to synchronize the system working functions. The IE module performs the inverse entropy coding or decoding. The inverse zigzag (IZZ) module performs IZZ scanning. The inverse quantization (IQuan) module performs inverse quantization. The motion compensation (MC) module performs motions compensation. A new frame is rebuilt which resembles the original one in terms of reference frame and motion vectors, prediction errors. If it is intra-frame, this block will be skipped. The input and output are buffered to frame buffer. The drifting compensation block has three processing branches as shown in the figure. In branch A, the watermark is embedded to all I, B, and P frames. In effect making two watermarks for inter-frames B and P, one is predicted from intra-frame, and one is embedded. In branch B, the watermark is inserted to intra-frame I only. However, inter-frames B and P have the same watermark by prediction. This watermark is the drift one and needs to be canceled in inter-frames B and P. In branch C, the frames are compressed without any watermark. So after decompressing, branch A has two watermarks, one is stable, another is drifting; branch B has one drifting watermark; branch C has no watermark. So, by subtracting branch B from branch C, the drifting watermark is extracted, and by subtracting branch A from the extracted drifting watermark, the drifting watermark effect in inter-frames is canceled. Overall a good visible watermark is inserted in the video frames. It may be noted that visible watermarking in compressed domain is bit tricky as compared to the watermarking in uncompressed domain. The host video frames are not independent as still images, but they are correlated frames with each other in temporal mode, that is, inter-frames (P or B) predicated from intra-frame. So, every object in base intra-frame is inherited by predicted inter-frames (P or B) such that the watermark in intra-frame appears in inter-frames (P or B) even though they are not embedded with the watermark. However, if it overlaps with any moving objects in the video scene, the watermark drifts around with the moving objects. The drift compensation is needed to cancel the side effect to obtain a stable watermark.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f19.jpg)

Figure 11.19 Copyright protection hardware DCT domain: (a) video watermarking architecture datapath and (b) video watermarking architecture Simulink design

#### 11.7.3 Secure better portable graphics (SBPG)

An SDC is a device that consists of all the features of a normal digital camera with additional onboard security features like watermarking. This can help in reducing the more time and resources that are used for watermarking the images taken with a normal camera. A hardware-based design also gives a low-power design with a high performance. Design of an Secure better portable graphics (SBPG) is presented by [Mohanty *et al*. (2018)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib73). When compared to a JPEG compression, BPG compression gives a better and low image size with a comparatively higher image quality. This makes BPG more suitable for implementations in the real-time bandwidth restricted applications. SDC with SBPG is usually implemented as a SoC. Encryption and watermarking are two different layers of protection that can be attained from this setup. Hence, it can help in safeguarding the DRM, ownership, and so on. This makes it suitable for the implementation in IoT applications and smart health care.

[Figure 11.20(a)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig20) shows the big picture and the architectures of secure BPG camera implementation. BPG encoding involves two different stages, the pre-encoding and the encoding. In the initial stage, the metadata like the bit-depth, color-space are read. The number of bits used for the indication of color are the bit depth: 8, 10, 12 are the commonly used bit depths. The bandwidth requirements for a higher bit rate images is higher and not all the displays are capable of displaying at higher bit rates. So, the bit depth of 8 is considered for BPG. During encoding, the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) reduces the spatial and temporal redundancies. This is performed by the inter- and intra-frame prediction. After that an ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-108.gif)block as the basic coding unit transforms the image data to the frequency domain, which uses the DCT or discrete sine transform (DST). The standard sizes that are used in this scenario are ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-109.gif), ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-110.gif), ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-111.gif), and ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-112.gif). The image that is transformed is then quantized and compressed additionally with the help of entropy coding. This is done to eliminate the redundancies that are not removed in the prediction mechanisms. Image is further compressed with the help of the entropy coding. [Figure 11.20(b)](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig20) shows the architecture of HEVC CODEC that is part of BPG.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f20.jpg)

Figure 11.20 Secure BPG–DRM hardware: (a) BPG big picture and (b) SBPG architecture

#### 11.7.4 Trust cam

[Figure 11.21](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig21) presents the design outline of a Trust Cam ([Winkler and Rinner, 2010](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib122)). This is a camera that is able to achieve the ROI detection when the raw images are taken by the sensor. Various privacy levels are present in the camera by performing edge detection for ROI. Then the ROI images are compressed to JPEG and a key is used to encrypt them with AES algorithm.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f21.jpg)

Figure 11.21 Trust cam

[Figure 11.22](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig22) shows the processing flow of the Trust Cam. Image from the sensor is obtained by the image acquisition block and is sent to the privacy block. The sensor is able to send RAW images or JPEG compressed. Then detection is performed on the ROI which are randomly computed every time. After selecting the ROI, they are extracted from the input images captured by the sensor. Then it is compressed using JPEG compression using libjpeg. The resultant image is then sent as an output which can be used to monitor the ROI.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f22.jpg)

Figure 11.22 Secure image sensor

[Figure 11.23](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig23) shows the designs of secure image sensors and the PUF-based image sensors. They are used to secure the images that are captured by the sensors. A PUF is a module that generates random numbers of cryptographic purposes. The PUF-based sensor attests the sensed data that is coming from the sensor for integrity and authenticity. Sensor controller will also undergo a secure boot to increase the robustness of the entire design.

### 11.8 Dynamic watermarking in smart car or UAV

IoT has become a major focus of research nowadays. With all the new technologies coming out everyday, designing new THINGS has been possible and sensor integration into various devices has become an important task in every applications. Smart transportation and UAV technology have developed significantly since their advent ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib67)). Autonomous vehicles and UAVs are being used for various purposes. Self-driving cars are not so far ahead in the future. With all these coming into picture, security is one of the main concerns that is bothering the research community. Both UAV and smart car will have video-recording capabilities. Watermarking that video will help in determining if the video that is recorded in the camera is tampered or not.

The video that is recorded in the vehicles is in some cases processed real time and in some cases, stored in the memory to be analyzed at a later time. Both these cases are important when it comes to a smart car and UAV. When the video is recorded, the cars and UAV might be subject to different kinds of attacks that let the attacker to tamper with the video surveillance footage of the vehicle. So, the watermark that is introduced in the vehicle should be tamper resistant ([Fallahpour *et al*., 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib26)). Many video editing software lets the user to tamper with the video and make the stream unreliable which defeats the purpose of the recording ([Su *et al*., 2011](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib103)). So, detection and distinguishing of the tampered video is also necessary in such scenarios.

Hence the watermark should be able to provide transparency, robustness, and higher capacity so that it can be embedded into different kinds of video footage. A fragile watermarking is used in most cases for detecting the tampering of a video ([Fridrich *et al*., 2000](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib30)). The attacker will try to change the watermarked video or object in the case of tampering but without touching the watermark itself. This poses a huge threat as distinguishing the original untampered video will become difficult. A fragile watermarking will be able to protect the footage against such tampering attacks. In case of a fragile watermarking algorithm, the video footage will become highly sensitive to the modifications and this will make it difficult to perform any kinds of modifications to the video like re-compression. A semi-fragile scheme was also proposed by [Sang and Alam (2008)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib93).

### 11.9 Medical signals authentication

As mentioned in the previous sections, the advancements of technology have allowed us to explore high-bandwidth communications which led to transmitting data globally ([Singh *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib100)). There has become no bounds for devices used for transmission, especially for medical use, such as the Internet, mobiles phones, wireless communications, and so on. There are different kinds of threats that are posed on the communication networks of such kind. The information that is being shared is also highly sensitive, which contains medical records of patients. This demands for higher levels of confidentiality and security. Medical image watermarking can provide a better service which can address these issues ([Acharya *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib1); [Coatrieux *et al*., 2006](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib15)). There have been few implementations of such security initiatives. For example, the use of watermarking in tele-medical applications in order to enhance the security of the transmitted sensitive medical data has been implemented. Tele-medicine watermarking will demand more care when the data is encrypted within the medical images as the information itself and its quality cannot be affected. The reliability, confidentiality, and availability are the major concerns of the security in the electronic patient record (EPR) exchange. Modern telecommunication infrastructure supports the possibility of delivering quality health care without the physical presence of medical experts. The integrity of biomedical signals being transmitted through communication channels must be established before their utilization. Investigations have been performed where digital watermarking techniques for signal integrity verification in an electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring application were performed.

A digital watermark which uses both the ECG and the patient demographic text as two-level watermarks was proposed by [Annadurai *et al*. (2012)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib5). In the insertion process, DWT is applied to the object, and it is decomposed into three sub-bands. After that the texture matrix will be calculated for each of the sub-bands. The wavelet coefficients are then selected for the watermarks which are used as threshold values. Authenticating the watermarked object is the main goal of this watermarking scheme. A wavelet spread-spectrum watermarking mechanism for both text and image is presented by [Singh *et al*. (2015)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib102). The watermark size is varied and the gain factor is obtained in this scenario for the experimental results. BCH codes are used for an increased robustness.

Researchers across the globe are using the hybrid watermarking schemes to improve the performance of the watermarking systems ([Fatima and Tuptewar, 2016](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib28); [Vo *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib114)). DCT and DWT can be used to embed the watermark into an image and the watermark can be selected at random. After a third level of decomposition, a DCT can be applied on them. A watermark with a zero mean and one variance is inserted in this process. The extraction process does not require the original image to be present in the memory.

Machine learning can also be used for the watermarking techniques. There are many variants of watermarking techniques that use machine learning and offer more imperceptibility and security compared to the other but demand high computational power. A blind watermarking technique which uses the multiwavelet and support vector machine (SVM) is presented by [Peng *et al*. (2010)](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib85). Initially the multiwavelet is performed on the each of the blocks of image. After this stage is complete, the lowest frequency sub-band is selected and the watermark is embedded into that using modulation. The watermark information contains a reference to the owner and the signature of binary logo image. The reference information of the owner will be helpful in training the SVM when extracting the watermark.

### 11.10 Side-channel information leakage attacks and countermeasures

Watermarking and cryptography hardware modules have an advantage of the low-power consumption along with a high performance and throughput. They can also be designed at a low cost per module and are integrated into different applications with ease. Besides these advantages, there are also some disadvantages to the hardware modules. They are made out of CMOS technology and are susceptible to various kinds of attacks such as side-channel attacks. The side-channel attacks collect the information from the hardware modules like the hardware watermarking chip directly unlike the software attacks.

During World War II, an engineer observed that the oscilloscope signal had a spike in it when a key was pressed in the secure typewriter Model 131-B2 at Bell Labs in 1943 ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib67)). Based on that the first publicly known side-channel attack was reported in 1965. Any attack that uses the physical implementation of cryptosystem and gains information is called a side-channel attack. There are two types of attacks that are possible on a crypto system: nondestructive and destructive. The target of the first type is analyzing the target module and gain information from it without destroying or tampering the device itself. Side-channel attacks are included in this category of attacks. Different side-channel attacks are presented in [Figure 11.24](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig24) (Parameswaran, 2018). This section discusses in detail the CPA and DPA attacks on the modules. There are also fault attacks, acoustic noise attacks, elapsed time attacks, EM radiation attacks, and so on, which exploit the advantages of different components of a device, like the time taken to complete a process, injecting faults into the device algorithms, and so on.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f24.jpg)

Figure 11.24 Different side-channel attacks (Parameswaran, 2018)

#### 11.10.1 An encryption hardware

[Figure 11.25](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig25) shows the process of AES encryption. AES is widely used for encryption and decryption in communication between two devices or nodes. It is considered to be the most secure cipher as the variable data block is supported by this standard with a variable key size ([Mohanty *et al*., 2018](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib71)). The key size and the block size can be chosen as any multiple of 32 and between 128 and 256. AES has no practical attacks against it and is more secure. Brute-forcing an AES encryption is highly difficult and requires high computational power. Fundamental algebraic transformations are present in AES like shift row, mix column, round key, and substitution. They are present for each of the standard round but there is an exception of the least standard round.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f25.jpg)

Figure 11.25 Advanced encryption standard (AES)

#### 11.10.2 Side-channel analysis attacks

Two major side-channel analysis attacks are considered in this section, CPA and DPA ([Jayasinghe *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib38)). CPA is the analysis of relationship between the cipher-text and the plain-text and it’s correlation as well as the instantaneous power consumption of the cryptographic device. When compared to DPA, CPA is a more effective attacking method. DPA uses the relation between the power and the data. Using that DPA will try to look at the difference of the category averages for all the keys. As it uses the averages, more power correlation data is needed for successfully launching this attack. So it consumes more time and is less efficient compared to the CPA. [Figure 11.26](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig26) presents a big picture of DPA and CPA ([Zhang and Shi, 2011](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib125)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f26.jpg)

Figure 11.26 DPA and CPA on HMAC: (a) oscilloscope and (b) detector ([Zhang and Shi, 2011](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib125))

A DPA attack is a side-channel attack which statistically analyzes the consumed power by the respective module in a cryptosystem. The module can be a watermarking chip or a cryptographic processor which performs encryption and decryption. [Figure 11.27](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig27) shows the overall process of DPA (Parameswaran, 2018). The biases varying power consumption is taken. Here, the microcontroller is monitored and the power analysis is performed when various operations are performed on the chip, which involve the secret keys. Signal processing and error correction properties are necessary for performing DPA, which are used for the extraction of secrets from the power consumption measurements. There is also noise that comes with the measurements so it must be filtered before the analysis is performed. A secret key can be obtained by the attacker by analyzing the power from the cryptographic operations on the chip using DPA.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f27.jpg)

Figure 11.27 Differential power analysis: (a) differential power analysis big picture and (b) differential power analysis attack overview (Parameswaran, 2018)

A CPA uses the relation between the data and the power as mentioned before. [Figure 11.28](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig28) shows the overall picture of the CPA (Parameswaran, 2018). This uses a correlation between the guesses of the keys. Hence, low power is required compared to the DPA. CPA is used to find a key that is stored in memory of the victim device. Launching a CPA attack involves the following four steps.

*   The power consumption model of the victim device should be noted.
    
*   The victim should encrypt different files of plain text.
    
*   Record the trace of the power consumption on the victim device.
    
*   Attack the small parts of the secret key from the observed power analysis.
    

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f28.jpg)

Figure 11.28 Correlation power analysis: (a) correlation power analysis big picture and (b) correlation power analysis attack overview (Parameswaran, 2018)

Every possible combination for the subkey should be considered. When each guess is performed, it is compared to the power that is analyzed on the main board. Repeating this process will give a guess of the subkey which will equal to the main key and power of the key used on the plain text will match the power observed from the module.

#### 11.10.3 Side-channel attack countermeasures

Side-channel attacks are highly efficient in stealing information from the microcontroller or memory. The attacker can use various kinds of attacks such as CPA, DPA, timing analysis, and so on on the hardware to get the information stored on it. Many techniques are available to mitigate the issues of power analysis attacks ([Ambrose *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib3); [Jayasinghe *et al*., 2015](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib38)). There are many ways to avoid the side-channel attacks on the hardware modules. Figures [11.29](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig29) and [11.30](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig30) show different ways of safeguarding the hardware modules from CPA and DPA attacks.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f29.jpg)

Figure 11.29 Differential power analysis attacks countermeasures

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f30.jpg)

Figure 11.30 Correlation power analysis attacks countermeasures

One of the main drawbacks of the power analysis attacks is that the hardware should be powered on during the time of the attacks in most of the cases. So, if the power supply to the module is turned off, the attacker cannot perform the attack anymore. Introducing some interrupts to the power can also mitigate the security threats to some extent. Power supply to the module can be detached when unused but this will only apply when the module is not solely in the hands of the attacker. During the execution process, there can be a nondeterministic execution which will not give out the exact power statistics of the device during the processing of secret keys. These are some of the hardware solutions that can be implemented. De-synchronization, software balancing, random masking, and so on are the software countermeasures to the DPA attacks on the security modules.

### 11.11 Attacks on watermarks and watermarking systems

When a watermark is embedded into a media object, there is a great chance that it might be subjected to manipulative attacks before the media reaches the receiver. Some of the manipulations are analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversions, resampling, quantization, dithering, low-pass and high-pass filtering, and so on. The media can be printed and rescanned in some cases intended to remove the watermark from the media. Any processing of the watermarked image that is intended to remove or tamper the watermark and fail the detection process is an attack on the watermark ([Cox and Linnartz, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib17); [Mintzer *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib62); [Sequeira and Kundur, 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib97); [Swanson *et al*., 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib105); [Voloshynovskiy *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115)). The characteristics of the watermark and its performance against the attacks which are mutually conflicting FoM. Comparing metrics for different algorithms is needed to come to a decision in selecting a suitable watermarking scheme for a particular application. Benchmarks of the watermark are different attacks in a unified framework which allow the owner to check the scheme for applicability.

This section discusses different attacks that are possible on a watermarked image. There are different types of attacks on a watermarked image to remove the watermark. They are classified into four different types ([Liu *et al*., 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib50); [Pereira *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib84); [Vellaisamy and Ramesh, 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib112); [Voloshynovskiy *et al*., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115); Wang *et al*., [2017a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib119), [2017b](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib120); [Xiang *et al*., 2014](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib123)) as shown in [Figure 11.31](#Chapter11.html#c11_fig31):

*   Geometric attacks
    
*   Removal and interference attacks
    
*   Cryptographic attacks
    
*   Protocol attacks
    

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-11-f31.jpg)

Figure 11.31 Attacks on watermarks ([Pereira et al., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib84); [Voloshynovskiy et al., 2001](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib115))

#### 11.11.1 Removal and interference attacks

Removal attack on the watermark is targeted to remove the watermark from the object. A watermark is the noise that is added to the original image and this is taken as an advantage by the attacker to remove the watermark. Interference attacks target the watermark by adding more noise to the watermarked image. Quantization, lossy compression, collusion, remodulation, denoise, averaging, and noise storm are the examples of such kinds of attacks. JPEG, MPEG, and so on are the lossy compression styles that can degrade the quality of watermark that is embedded in the media object. When many legit owners of the watermarked copy of the media come together to create a nonwatermarked image, it is called a collude attack. This can be achieved by averaging different objects in the media that is already watermarked.

#### 11.11.2 Geometric attacks

The geometric attacks are more targeted toward the watermarked images and videos. These kinds of attacks do not remove the watermark present in the media but will manipulate the watermarked media so that the detector will not be able to extract or retrieve the watermark. Affine transformations such as translation, rotation, and scaling are used to successfully launch this attack. Line removal, wrapping, and cropping can also be done to remove the watermark from the media object. Mosaic attack is another example of this category ([Koubaa *et al*., 2007](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib45)). In such attacks, the media object is divided into different parts and again rearranged into one using HTML, which makes the watermark difficult to be detected by the detector.

#### 11.11.3 Cryptographic attacks

The two attacks that are discussed above will not be able to breach the algorithm security. A cryptographic attack is the one that precisely attacks the security of the watermarking algorithm and cracks it. When the watermark is secured with a secret key, as discussed in the previous sections, a brute-force attack can be performed and broken, which can be considered as a cryptographic attack. Oracle attack is another kind of cryptographic attack which uses a public watermark detector to create a nonwatermarked media object.

#### 11.11.4 Protocol attacks

This kind of attacks takes advantage of the loopholes that are present in the watermarking algorithm ([Craver *et al*., 1996, 1998](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib21); Wang, 2009; [Zhang and Liu, 2017](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib126)). This kind of attack is also known as inversion, deadlock, or fake–original attack. One or many new watermarks are introduced on an already watermarked media which makes it difficult to detect the original watermark and the owner. Some kinds of attacks will produce a fake original media object with a watermark so that the detector will detect it as an original watermarked legit copy. Watermark from an already watermarked object is detected and transferred to another media object which is called copy attack, which is also very popular.

### 11.12 Limitations of watermarks and watermarking

Limitations of the watermarking schemes are discussed in this section. When a watermark is inserted into the original media object, it should be detected with ease if not tampered with. Even in the case of attacks, the watermark should be resistant. In this chapter, we discussed a lot about different kinds of watermarks and the characteristics. With the hardware watermarking coming into picture, the IoT integration is becoming easy. Different hardware modules that were discussed above can be integrated into IoT applications. But IoT devices need to be connected to the Internet all the time and some of them will be battery operated. So, the latency and the power consumption of the watermarking modules is a great challenge.

When it comes to the visible watermarking schemes, the copyright is clearly mentioned and need not be worried ([Mintzer *et al*., 1996](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib63); Mohanty *et al*., [2000a](#Chapter11.html#c11_bib73)). The watermark should occupy a significant portion of the original media object. Besides that the quality of the image should not be degraded. When removing the watermark it costs same as a new media object. This kind of security is sufficient for use in different applications. This also has some drawbacks where the watermark should be enforced with laws.

Invisible watermarking, unlike the visible watermarking techniques, is imperceptible and is more complicated for that reason. Robustness of the watermark is considered the highest characteristic that a watermarking algorithm has to meet. But this is not true in case of an invisible watermarking. Because, every watermark can be attacked using various techniques and invisible watermark is also not left out from that category. Any media can be subject to counterfeit production by attacking the watermark. So, invertible or quasi-invertible invisible watermark schemes are not able to resolve the rightful ownership. Without a standardized watermarking scheme, anyone can claim ownership.

Due to the advancements in the technology scaling and development of high-performance devices, signal manipulations are being introduced into various artworks and the indistinguishable noises are added to the media object. This makes it difficult to differentiate the manipulations and prove original ownership of the object. The additional data in the object is not known to occur due to the watermark or any new noise. In such scenarios, extracting watermark and authenticating the ownership of the object is a challenge. With the use of highly sophisticated DSP, this problem is further deteriorating. A watermarked image that is not protected properly cannot be used for authentication and hence cannot be used in a court of law. To avoid this situation, watermark can be embedded into the object during the acquisition phase directly using hardware modules.

For a satisfactory robustness of watermark image, in case of a *c* traitors out of *N*, the length of the codewords to be inserted into the watermark is given as: ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-113.gif), where the probability of error is denoted by ![image](OEBPS/images/c11-Eqn-in-114.gif). The discussed amount of added noise embedded into the image will surely degrade the quality of the image which in turn reduces the commercial value of the object. Digital watermarking will not be able to prevent illegal activity but can only provide evidence that such an activity has been performed by a party. But cryptographic techniques can protect the data from such attacks. So digital watermarking should be used as a secondary protection layer.

### 11.13 Conclusion

This chapter discusses the watermarking schemes, some issues with watermarking and its limitations, and attacks and solutions on different watermarking algorithms. A big picture of watermarking from basics to deployment is presented in this chapter. Different hardware watermarking schemes along with some very-low-power chips which can be integrated into battery operated devices were discussed. With the introduction of a new watermarking scheme or a new cryptographic algorithms, the attackers are soon coming up with ways to attack them and breach the security. There are many counterfeit devices being produced and media content being shared without proper legalities being met. This has become a major issue that has to be addressed designing of high sophisticated and low-power security modules in both cryptography and watermarking.

## *Chapter 12*  
**Physical unclonable functions (PUFs)**

It has been the practice to store information under lock and key for safeguarding it. Even today, we use cryptographic primitives to store information securely under lock and key, encryption, and decryption. For the process of cryptography, keys are necessary for any operation. But these keys should be stored in the memory so that they can be used whenever necessary. When a key is stored in the memory, it can be stolen by the adversary using various methods. Therefore, storing it in a non-volatile memory is not an option in this age of security threats. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are the promising security primitives used for generating the keys instead of storing them in the memory. These modules use the naturally occurring manufacturing variations in the fabrication process for generating the keys for cryptographic purposes. This chapter discusses different types of PUFs. Section 12.1 gives a brief introduction of PUFs. Section 12.2 discusses working principles of PUFs. Section 12.3 discusses different characteristics of a PUF design. Section 12.4 presents different classifications of PUFs. Various designs of PUF based on ring oscillators (ROs) are presented in Section 12.5, based on multiplexers and reconfigurability are presented in Section 12.6. Static random access memory (SRAM)-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.7, memristor-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.8, and diode-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.9. There are also non-silicon-based PUF designs, such as carbon PUFs, presented in Section 12.10. Microprocessors can also be used for implementing the PUF designs which are presented in Section 12.11. Magnetic material-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.12 and the FPGA implementations of PUF and security measures for FPGA are presented in Section 12.13. Some case study applications are presented in Section 12.14. Further the issues and challenges faced during the design of PUF modules are presented in Section 12.15. The conclusion and future directions are presented in Section 12.16.

### 12.1 Introduction

The first transistor was invented in 1948. With the introduction of the transistor, vacuum tubes occupying huge space disappeared and led to the invention of the IC in 1958 (Kilby, [1976](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib28)). Along came the Moore’s Law which states that the number of transistors on an IC will double every two years. This came true until recently and the number of transistors on a single chip has exponentially increased since its first introduction. With the introduction of the new 10 nm technology, each square millimeter of an IC can be packed with 100 million transistors ([Courtland, 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib11)). With technology improving at such a drastic pace, it has penetrated into almost every sphere of human life. Day-to-day activities such as communications, business, financial transactions, and so on depend on technology. Digital footprint of human being has become an inevitable and unavoidable parameter ([Gencoglu *et al*., 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib16)). IoT has become an integral part of our lives. In an IoT environment, every device is connected to the network and will have a unique IP address ([Mohanty *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib54)). Smart cities, smart grid, smart healthcare, and so on are various forms of IoT.

With so many devices connected to each other, there are security concerns that are raised. The data that is being collected by various applications, sensors, and other devices should be stored securely. There are many attacks reported recently where security needs to be given the highest importance (Charette, [2018a](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib6), [2018b](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib7)). To secure the data that is being generated, cryptography is used. It has been around for a very long time. Cryptography is the process of concealing a message or information by converting it into unreadable text and only the end user will be able to extract the original information from the text. It was found that in the year 1900 BC Egyptians used techniques such as [steganography (2001)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib67). Various algorithms are available currently for encryption and decryption which can transfer the data securely. The National Bureau of Standards proposed DES algorithm which lasted for 20 years. Then came AES algorithm which is very popular now but there have been reports of AES being successfully broken ([Mangard *et al*., 2005](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib47)). An amount of $7.5 billion is estimated to be lost by the US semiconductor industry because of IC counterfeiting ([Rose *et al*., 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib59)). In addition to all of this, in the case of many devices, sensors, or applications, the device itself will not be monitored all the time. It will be in a remote location transmitting and receiving necessary data to the cloud or a remote server. In such cases, the current practice of encryption and decryption is to store the necessary keys in a nonvolatile memory and use it ([Herder *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib21)) when required. The memory is subject to side-channel attacks where the attacker can get access to the physical device and retrieve data from it.

A *PUF* is a new primitive that is being introduced into various applications. Without storing a key in nonvolatile memory, it can provide keys for encryption and decryption (as shown in [Figure 12.1](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig1)) ([Yanambaka *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib77)). The cryptography key will be generated by PUF whenever necessary, based on the imperfections that are introduced into an IC while fabrication. There are various advantages to PUF. Fabrication of PUF components is much easier compared to the memory modules necessary to store the key. This also means the reduction in cost and chip area necessary for the memory modules like EEPROM. Side-channel attacks on the device itself will become more difficult. With some types of PUF, expensive cryptographic processors can be avoided. The number of keys generated by the PUF increases exponentially with the complexity of the architecture and design used. The same keys generated by a PUF module can also be used for IP protection where the input and output pair of PUF can be used to authenticate the ownership of a device. PUF uses the manufacturing variability of the IC to generate the output keys. Hence, the output keys generated by a PUF module should also be unique. The concept of PUF is shown in [Figure 12.2](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig2). For the same PUF module, different inputs yield different outputs as shown in [Figure 12.1](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig1). For different instantiations of a PUF circuit (logically same) on different chips, the same input yields different outputs as shown in [Figure 12.1](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig1).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f01.jpg)

Figure 12.1 The concept of a PUF over traditional key stored in a nonvolatile memory

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f02.jpg)

Figure 12.2 Concept of PUF

### 12.2 PUF: Principle

When an IC is fabricated, there is a process that will be followed from the beginning to the end. From the time silicon becomes an ingot to the final IC, these series deals with various fabrication steps such as masking, ion implantation, photolithography, chemical diffusion, polishing, electrolysis, and so on ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). During this process of fabrication, the devices that are being fabricated on the wafer will be affected due to various factors. [Figure 12.3](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig3) shows the manufacturing variability of devices. The geometry of the devices such as length, gate oxide thickness, doping concentration, and so on will also be affected. Due to these variations, no two devices that are fabricated will look the same.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f03.jpg)

Figure 12.3 Working characteristics of the PUF

Even when the devices are fabricated on the same die, there will be variations in their geometry that will make them distinct from the others on the same wafer. A PUF will take advantage of these variations to generate the keys. The manufacturing variations that are introduced into the IC are unpredictable and unavoidable. A naturally occurring phenomenon will introduce unwanted changes in the geometry of the device. When two different transistors on the same die have variations in their geometry, the output of the two will also be different. The output from two different devices will be compared with each other to generate a single bit key of PUF.

The design of a simple PUF is shown in [Figure 12.4](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig4). The input to a PUF is called the “Challenge” and the output from a PUF is called the “Response.” The pair of input and output of a PUF is called “Challenge Response Pair” (CRP). [Figure 12.4](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig4) shows the design of arbiter PUF ([Lee *et al*., 2004](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib36)). As shown in the figure, the PUF uses two sets of multiplexers connected in series. The output from each set is connected to the D-input and clock signal of a D-flip-flop. The select lines of the multiplexers are the challenge input the user gives to PUF. Based on the challenge input, the multiplexers through which the input signal traverses will change. Once the input signal is given to the module, based on the challenge input, the delay will be added before it reaches the D-flip-flop. The output from the flip-flop will depend on the amount of delay added to the input signal by the devices it passes through. In this scenario, due to manufacturing variations, each transistor in the multiplexers will add various amounts of delay. This delay added is unpredictable. Thus, the PUF key generated is also unique to the module and secure. However, predicting the CRPs in the arbiter PUF is also not difficult. To avoid this, much complex designs of PUF are designed, which are introduced in the later sections.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f04.jpg)

Figure 12.4 Arbiter-based simple PUF

### 12.3 Properties or characteristics of PUFs

A PUF is used to generate keys for cryptographic purposes. Various properties should be satisfied by the outputs of PUF to be used for various applications. [Figure 12.5](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig5) shows the different characteristics of PUF that should be satisfied for it to be ideal ([Böhm, 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib4); [Chang *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib5); [Maiti *et al*., 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib45); [Yanambaka *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib77)) ([Table 12.1](#Chapter12.html#c12_tbl1)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f05.jpg)

Figure 12.5 Properties of PUFs

#### 12.3.1 Uniqueness

A PUF module generates an *N*\-bit key which should be unique. PUF uses the manufacturing variations on an IC to generate the output key. Hence, the same PUF key should not be generated by the same module for a different challenge input. The uniqueness can be considered to be calculated over different chips. Let us consider a pair of chips, *i* and *j*, where *i* is not same as *j*. The responses generated be ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-1.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-2.gif). Then the uniqueness can be given as ([Chatterjee *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib9); [Maiti and Schaumont, 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib42)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_1.gif)

**Table 12.1** Comparison of various publications

![image](OEBPS/images/tab12.1.jpg)

HD is the hamming distance of the two response bits and *n* is the length of the response. The number of different elements that two strings of the same length have is called the HD. Initially, XOR is performed on the two strings and the result is added to get the HD. For example, consider the two strings “11001100” and “11100111.” The XOR of the string will be “00101011” and adding all bits will get us 4, which is the HD ([Böhm, 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib4)). HD is also represented in percentage, where the result is divided by the length of the string and multiplied by 100. In the previous example, it is ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-3.gif)is 50%. The ideal HD for a PUF to be securely used for cryptographic purposes is 50%.

#### 12.3.2 Reliability (correctness)

When necessary PUF will generate the keys for various purposes. But once it is implemented, for a single challenge input, the output response should not change. Various factors such as aging, voltage fluctuations, noise, and other factors should not affect the output of a PUF. This is the reliability or correctness characteristic of PUF where it will be able to generate the same key for a given challenge input. The reliability of a PUF can also be calculated using the HD. If the same key is given to a single PUF over a long period of time, the ideal HD should be 0%. No errors in the output bits should occur. As no design is ideal, various techniques were employed to avoid them, especially to avoid the aging effects of a design.

Let us consider a chip *i* from which an “*n*” bit response ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-4.gif)is extracted for reference at optimal conditions of environment. Now the same *n*\-bit response is extracted from the same chip *i* at different environmental conditions, such as supply voltage and power supply, and let the value be ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-5.gif), where *x* different samples are taken from the same *i* at different conditions. The reliability can be given as ([Maiti and Schaumont, 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib42)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_2.gif)

#### 12.3.3 Randomness (uniformity)

For the output of a PUF to be random, the key should contain equal number of 1’s and 0’s. This ensures that the output of a PUF is random and secure to be deployed in an application. Apart from the HD, the randomness parameter validates the keys generated by the PUF. In some cases, it is also useful in determining the error rate in the output.

#### 12.3.4 Correlation (bit aliasing)

The correlation characteristics of a PUF are of two different types: (1) bit and (2) chip. There should be no correlation between any of the bits generated by the PUF module. If a different challenge is given to the PUF, the response should be different. And various chips on the same wafer should not affect the working of a PUF module and generate the same keys. In some cases, the manufacturing variations will be uniform across the wafer. In such cases, there is a chance that with the CRPs of one PUF chip, the other can be predicted.

#### 12.3.5 Power consumption

A PUF is designed to be deployed in devices like RFID tags which consume very low power. In an IoT environment, there is a chance that the devices are battery operated and need to work with low power consumption. PUF is also being deployed in various smart devices which require a low-power operation. Hence designing the PUF with low-power consumption is vital.

#### 12.3.6 Speed

There are various IoT environments depending on the place they are deployed and the application tasks they are supposed to perform. Based on the various tasks, there is a need that the environment has to send and receive the data in real time. In such cases, there is a need for security but the same cannot be a bottleneck to the processing speed or increase the transfer latency. Hence the speed with which the keys are generated is also going to play a major role in where the respective design is going to be deployed.

### 12.4 Classification of PUFs

PUFs can be classified based on the fabrication method and security strength as shown in [Figure 12.6 (](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig6)[Chang *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib5); [Joshi *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib26); [Škorić *et al*., 2005](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib66)). In a broad sense, there are two categories of PUFs. They are categorized based on the types of devices used to design the PUF and the other category is based on the level of security provided by the module itself. Further, each of the categories has different types of PUFs. Various researchers around the world have proposed different types of PUF: these are silicon-based, non-silicon-based, electronic, and non electronic. Based on the level of security provided, there are three types of PUFs, strong, controlled, and weak.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f06.jpg)

Figure 12.6 Different types of PUFs

#### 12.4.1 Device-based PUFs

Various devices are used by researchers to manufacture PUF. A PUF uses the manufacturing variability present in the devices to generate the outputs. Not all the devices in the world are ideal. Therefore, different varieties of devices can be implemented at the core of design to generate the PUF keys.

##### 12.4.1.1 Silicon-based PUFs

Almost all the ICs are made from silicon and other materials. This category of PUFs is made on the silicon and fabricated on the same die as part of the IC. Various designs of PUF are proposed by researchers around the world depending on the implementation and the area of deployment. Examples of this type of PUFs are SRAM ([Schrijen and Leest, 2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib65)), butterfly ([Kumar *et al*., 2008](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib33)), arbiter ([Lao and Parhi, 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib34)), RO ([Rahman *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib56)), and lightweight secure ([Majzoobi *et al*., 2008](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib46)). These PUFs will be extracting the manufacturing variations on the IC which can generate the keys for cryptographic purposes.

##### 12.4.1.2 Non-silicon PUFs

PUFs that are not classified as silicon PUFs are referred as non-silicon PUFs. They are fabricated in silicon systems but require special fabrication techniques which are not part of a generic CMOS fabrication technology. The response is generated from the challenge set obtained from the random physical variation in the physical system rather than the ICs. Such types of PUFs are optical, acoustic, magnetic, radio frequency (RF), coating, etc.

#### 12.4.2 Security-based PUFs

Once a PUF is fabricated, the design itself cannot be modified. Hence, various designs of PUFs will generate different number of CRPs. The CRPs will decide where the particular design of PUF can be deployed and used. Based on the category, PUF is of three types: strong, controlled, and weak.

##### 12.4.2.1 Strong PUF

The strong PUF is the types of designs that will be able to generate more number of CRPs. The CRPs can also be not easily extracted from the device. A protection is provided through a complex input–output relations and an exponential number of CRPs. This type of PUF operates in the range of few MHz, so even a short duration of eavesdropping can collect many CRPs. However, all known strong PUFs are vulnerable to one or more types of attacks. This type of PUFs is frequently used for device authentication purposes. Some common example of circuits belonging to this class are arbiter, feed-forward arbiter, XOR arbiter, lightweight secure, and optical PUFs. This class of PUFs is also frequently referred to as super-high information content (SHIC) ([Lugli *et al*., 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib39); [Ruhrmair *et al*., 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib62)).

##### 12.4.2.2 Weak PUF

This category of PUFs will not be able to generate more number of CRPs. The least number of CRPs that can be generated is “1” in a worst-case scenario. Therefore, this design can be easily vulnerable to attacks. This is the reason that the design of this PUFs cannot be revealed publicly. These are mainly used to derive a secret key in cryptographic algorithms and are the least susceptible to modeling attacks. Some common examples of circuits belonging to this class are SRAM, coating, and butterfly PUFs. These are also known as physically obfuscated keys (POKs).

##### 12.4.2.3 Controlled PUFs

This class of PUFs has a strong PUF as an underlying core additionally protected by control logic. Since the challenges are preprocessed first before passing to the strong PUF and the responses are preprocessed before coming out of the strong PUF, the CRPs of the strong PUF are never accessed directly. This preprocessing of challenges and responses significantly improves the security of controlled PUFs. A controlled PUF ([Yu and Devadas, 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib82)) is only accessed via an algorithm which is fabricated in the same chip as the PUF such that the PUF and the algorithm are inseparable. This implies that the actual PUF outputs are never given to the outside world directly and the outputs that are given to the outside world are the processed outputs from the algorithm.

### 12.5 Ring oscillator–based PUFs

The design of a ring oscillator PUF is shown in [Figure 12.7](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig7) ([Suh and Devadas, 2007](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib69)). There are two different sets of ROs that are connected to two multiplexers “Mux1” and “Mux2.” The two multiplexers are connected to two counters which are connected to a comparator, which gives the final output. The multiplexers will select different combinations of ROs and feed the oscillations to the counters. The number of oscillations over a selected period of time are given to the input and clock of the comparator. The comparator compares the two input values and gives out “1” or “0.” The input to the multiplexers is the challenge input given to PUF and the output from the comparators is the response of the PUF.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f07.jpg)

Figure 12.7 Ring oscillator PUF

Due to the manufacturing variations in the IC, all the ROs will not oscillate at the same frequency. This causes the counters to give out different number of oscillations for a same period of time. When different inputs are selected by the multiplexers, different ROs will give distinct oscillation frequencies, which generate different bits at the output of the comparator. Thus the keys generated by the RO PUF will be unique. If there are *N* different ROs, only *N* × (*N* − 1)/2 different comparisons will be possible. The main component in the RO PUF design is the inverter. Due to the manufacturing variations in the inverter, the delay added is different for each inverter. The delay of an inverter can be calculated as ([Wang and Tehranipoor, 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib73)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_3.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-6.gif)is the supply voltage, ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-7.gif)is the load capacitance, *W* and *L* are the effective width and effective length of the channel, respectively, *μ* is the mobility of carriers, ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-8.gif)is the saturation source to drain voltage, ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-9.gif)is the oxide thickness, ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-10.gif)is the oxide dielectric permittivity, and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-11.gif)is the threshold voltage. The oscillation frequency of the ROs with *N* inverters is given as:

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_4.gif)

There are some advantages to the implementation of ring oscillator PUFs. They are easier to build, evaluate, highly reliable, and relaxed layout and routing constraints in the design. There are some disadvantages also to the design. It is comparatively slow; to increase the number of bits, the chip area needs to be increase, which results in consumption of more power. In addition, aging is also one of the main issues that can affect the reliability of the ring oscillator PUF. Various factors like positive bias temperature instability (PBTI), negative bias temperature instability (NBTI), time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB), hot carrier injection (HCI), electro-migration (EM), and thermal cycling (TC) also affect PUF. Due to the aging effect, the change in the output oscillations of the ROs will affect the output bits of PUF module itself. This can become a major issue when implemented in the cryptographic applications. In a PMOS transistor, when a negative voltage is applied at gate-to-source terminal, an interface trap is generated at Si–SiO[2] interface. Over a period of time, this results in the change of transistor parameters like transconductance, drain current, and threshold voltage. This effect is called NBTI. The HCI occurs due to the switching activity of the transistor ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). NBTI and HCI will depend on various factors, including workload of the transistor and technology.

TDDB is occurred due to the rapid scaling of the device. The high operating voltages at the gate terminal of the transistor will lead to the structural degradation of the device, like the gate oxide and its interface. With the continuity, the dielectric layer will lose the property to insulate and as a result, a conduction path will form between the gate oxide and the substrate. This effect has been addressed and reduced significantly with the implementation of high-κ material. Other parameters that affect the performance of the device are the temperature and supply voltage. With the variations in the supply and temperature, the output oscillations of the ROs will change. When the temperature of the chip increases, the threshold voltage of the device is reduced. The increase in temperature can also decrease the drain saturation current and the carrier mobility. But the operating temperatures of the chip and the supply voltages can be regulated and maintained. If the temperature increases, it can be decreased using various methods. But the effects caused by aging cannot be reversed and have a permanent damage on the device and hence the chip itself. This affects the performance and reliability of the chip over time.

To avoid these, aging-resistance designs are introduced. [Figure 12.8](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig8) shows the design of an aging-resistant PUF ([Rahman *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib56)). The NBTI effect is decreased by introducing an NMOS transistor to connect two inverters in the RO as shown in the figure. The supply voltage ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-12.gif)is connected to the ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-13.gif)transistors which are activated using the ENABLE signal. These are introduced to avoid the logical “0” at the input of the inverter’s PMOS transistor. When the RO is not active, there is a chance that a “0” might be at the input of PMOS in the inverter and can cause power consumption. This design of PUF will reduce the NBTI effect in the off state. Various other designs of aging-resistant RO PUF designs were also introduced ([Chowdhury *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib10); Rahman *et al*., [2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib57), [2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib58)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f08.jpg)

Figure 12.8 Aging-resistant RO PUF

There are various designs of PUF that are implemented for different applications ([Yanambaka *et al*., 2017, 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib78)). One of the properties of PUF is the speed of key generation as discussed in Section 12.3. A PUF can be deployed in various applications, including network switches and routers. The speed with which the key is generated by the PUF is important in such cases. [Figure 12.9](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig9) shows the design of hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF intended to be deployed in applications where the speed of key generation is pivotal. As shown in the figure, there are two sets of ROs in the design. Unlike the conventional ROs, multiplexers, counters, and the comparator are replaced with the D-flip-flops. The D-input and the clock input of D-flip-flops are connected with two ROs, one from each set as shown in the figure. Due to the manufacturing variations in the inverters of ROs, the delay added in each of the oscillator will be different and so will be the oscillation frequency. Based on the oscillation frequency of the ROs, the output bit from the flip-flop changes. Bits ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-14.gif)to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-15.gif)give the key generated by the PUF.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f09.jpg)

Figure 12.9 Speed-optimized hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF

### 12.6 Reconfigurable or dynamic PUFs

The previous section presented a ring oscillator PUF and different designs which can be implemented in various applications. Some of the designs that are presented in the previous section are reconfigurable but the others generate a constant set of CRPs and the design itself is not reconfigurable. This section concentrates on the reconfigurability of the PUF design. Reconfigurability is an important aspect of PUF design. There is a chance that if the attacker gets hold of the device and perform attacks such as machine learning, emulation, man-in-the-middle and RE, he/she will be able to regenerate the CRPs. The reconfigurable or dynamic PUFs are introduced in order to increase the security of PUF against these attacks and to be able to generate new set of CRPs when necessary. A feed-forward structure is introduced in the arbiter PUF to avoid the attacks using linear modeling. This introduces some nonlinearity in the design and increases the security and robustness of the design trading-off the design complexity. This can also be achieved using other techniques like preprocessing the challenge input before feeding it to the PUF, postprocessing the output response from the PUF, and adding some components to the output of module which can be used for reconfiguring the response bits. The preprocessing challenge bits can be done by introducing an additional circuitry which can implement linear feedback shift register (LFSR) or by introducing some hashing. The postprocessing of response bits can mean the introduction of hashing to the bits. [Figure 12.10](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig10) shows the design of arbiter PUF with an LFSR at the input. The challenge inputs given to the PUF are not directly fed to the arbiter PUF. Initially they are passed through the LSFR, preprocessed and then they are given as input to the PUF, “Real Challenge” as shown in [Figure 12.10](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig10) ([Lao and Parhi, 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib34)). With the introduction of the input-reconfigurable circuitry, the robustness of the overall design and also the reconfigurability can be increased.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f10.jpg)

Figure 12.10 Arbiter PUF with LFSR at input

To avoid various attacks on the arbiter PUF, different configurations of the design are implemented (Lao and Parhi, [2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib35)):

1.  Feed-forward MUX PUF overlap structure (FFO): Design of FFO is shown in [Figure 12.11](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig11). In this design, there is an overlap between the two feed-forward connections.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f11.jpg)
    
    Figure 12.11 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based overlap structure PUF
    
2.  Feed-forward MUX PUF cascade structure (FFC): Design of FFC is shown in [Figure 12.12](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig12). In this design, the stage which got the input from feed-forward path will be the start of a new feed-forward path.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f12.jpg)
    
    Figure 12.12 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based cascade structure PUF
    
3.  Feed-forward MUX PUF separate structure (FFS): Design of FFS is shown in [Figure 12.13](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig13). In this design, there will be no overlap between the feed-forward paths of the multiplexers.
    
    ![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f13.jpg)
    
    Figure 12.13 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based separate structure PUF
    

[Figure 12.14](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig14) shows the design of a lightweight PUF. The design is presented by [Majzoobi *et al*. (2008)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib46) with an improved robustness and increased security. In this PUF design, there are two networks at the input and the output, “Input Network,” which takes in the challenge inputs, and “Output Network,” which gives out the response outputs. The module itself will contain a number of parallel PUF structures which are run by the input and the output networks. For connecting the challenge inputs to a number of parallel PUF structures, an interconnect network is implemented. A single PUF will be satisfying the strict avalanche criterion (SAC). Any cryptographic primitive is said to satisfy the SAC if a complement in the single input bit induces a change in each of the output bits with a 50% probability. But when the overall parallel network of the design is considered, the SAC is not satisfied.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f14.jpg)

Figure 12.14 Lightweight PUF

[Figure 12.15](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig15) shows a design of hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF which uses RO as a main component in the module and can also be reconfigured ([Yanambaka *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib78)). As shown in the figure, there are two different sets of ROs which are connected to two multiplexers “Mux 1” and “Mux 2.” The ROs will generate the oscillations which are fed to the multiplexers. Challenge input given to the PUF module acts as the select lines to the multiplexers. Based on the challenge input given, the multiplexers select different ROs. The output from Mux 1 is given as D-input to the D-flip-flop and output from Mux 2 is given as clock signal to the D-flip-flop. Due to the variations in the ROs, the oscillations produced will not be of the same frequency. Therefore, the output of D-flip-flop will change based on the input challenge. Different configurations of inputs can be achieved by changing the select line inputs. The robustness and security offered by the design can be increased by increasing the number of ROs in the design, but it also increases the complexity and chip are occupied.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f15.jpg)

Figure 12.15 Power-optimized hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF

### 12.7 SRAM-based PUF

Many devices and development board have SRAM which can be used to design a PUF. [Figure 12.16](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig16) shows the circuit design of a 6T SRAM cell ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). The start-up value of the SRAM cell is used by the PUF to generate the output bits. When compared to the other designs of PUF, the reliability and uniqueness of the SRAM PUF are less. As shown in [Figure 12.16](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig16), an SRAM cell can be designed using cross-coupled inverters and will be able to store a single bit of binary data, “1” or “0.” When the SRAM cell is powered up, its initial condition is taken as the advantage by the PUF to generate the unique output. But there are issues with the behavior of SRAM cells at the start-up. Different SRAM memory modules were compared and analyzed by [Schrijen and Leest (2012)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib65), operating at different temperatures and supply voltages. The analysis was performed by calculating the reference bits at the starting, at various temperatures of 20 °C, −40 °C, and 80 °C by [Schrijen and Leest (2012),](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib65) which showed the stability of SRAM. The supply voltage of the SRAM was also varied by 10%. This does not affect the performance of the PUF as claimed ([Schrijen and Leest, 2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib65)) because the start-up conditions are attained during the initial few nanoseconds.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f16.jpg)

Figure 12.16 6T SRAM cell

In the case of an SRAM memory, one of the important challenges is to get a sufficient entropy into a key that is of a fixed length. In the case of an SRAM PUF, the generated keys will have noise and the entropy will be lost during the generation of helper data and the error correction ([Koeberl *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib30); [Maes *et al*., 2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib41)). In some cases, the loss of entropy during the helper data will be considered where it is uniformly distributed. The entropy and the length of output are equal when the entropy density is multiplied by the error correction. In that scenario, the entropy of the raw PUF outputs, even when low, can be used for generation of keys. The entropy of the output of PUF is usually unknown and so the estimation of entropy should be performed using a more rigorous method in worst-case scenarios. In the syndrome constructions and the code-offset, when a binary linear code *C*(*n*, *k*, *t*), where the length of the dimension of code is represented by *n* and *k* and the maximum number of errors that can be corrected is represented by *t*, is considered. When a worst-case scenario is taken into account, the entropy lost can be calculated as ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-16.gif)bits which can be considered satisfactory ([Maes *et al*., 2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib41)). When the original bit entropy is less than ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-17.gif)/bit, entropy will not be present in the output in case of a worst-case condition. Therefore, PUFs are not suited for generating the keys under a worst-case condition. For calculating the min-entropy, NIST specification 800-90 ([Barker and Kelsey, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib3)) is usually used. Let *p*[0] and *p*[1] be the probabilities of binary source of outputs where ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-18.gif), the maximum probability of *p*[0] and *p*[1] which can be used for the calculation of min-entropy is as follows ([Liu *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib38)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_5.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-19.gif).

For increasing the entropy of the source bit, Von Neumann extractor is used to compress the bits ([Leest *et al*., 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib37)). In the case of Von Neumann extractor, the process is as follows: a sample of the pattern is considered and is divided into successive nonoverlapping bits. When the pair of bits differ from each other, the second bit that is considered is discarded. If both the bits are equal, both of them are discarded. After the completion of processing all the bits, the remaining bit will be in order. A bias to “1” is considered for simplicity. Pair of bits A and B having a maximum probabilities of ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-20.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-21.gif)are the probabilities due to the bit “1” occurrence, with the probabilities ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-22.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-23.gif), respectively. The ratio between the lengths of the output and input of extractor is called “Extraction Rate.” This can be given as ([Liu *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib38)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_6.gif)

### 12.8 Memristor-based PUFs

Technology scaling has led to designing high-performance, low-power chips and SoCs ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). Transistor sizes have reached 12 nm ([AMD, 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib1)) and are going low still. There are speculations of 7 nm chips being released commercially.
