But there is a threshold that can be reached and alternatives to the transistors are being explored to replace them. Scaling has also led to many issues, including power consumption, fabrication, and switching speeds. High switching speeds and low power consumption have been achieved using the RRAM, resistive random access memory technology, and 3D arrays ([Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). These RRAMs are also called “Memristors.” It is a two-terminal device, whose resistance depends on the amount of voltage and the direction of current that passes through it. So taking this property of a memristive device as an advantage, multiple resistive levels can be achieved. A continuous variable resistance can also be achieved by switching states from one resistive to other states. The resistance change will also be dependent on the state that it is already in, that is, the voltage/current that has already passed through the device in the previous iteration. This proves that a Memristor has the properties of a “Resistor” and “Memory.” Hence the name “Memristor” (Memory + Resistor). The memristance of the memristor is given as ([Rose *et al*., 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib59)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_7.gif)

where the maximum resistance (![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-24.gif)) offered is represented as ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-25.gif), the difference between the maximum and minimum memristance offered is represented as ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-26.gif), and applied voltage polarity is represented by ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-27.gif). ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-28.gif)is the mobility and *D* represents the device thickness.

In case of an analog model, the memristance offered by the device will change gradually from minimum to maximum and takes place from varying *W* and *D*. [Figure 12.17](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig17) shows the device structure and working of a memristor. The doped and undoped regions of the device will change based on the direction and amount of current that is passing through it. The memristor contains two titanium dioxide layers, one of which contains excess amount of oxygens sandwiched between two metal electrodes. When a current is applied in the forward direction, the oxygen ions will be distributed all over the device, which increases the doped region as shown in [Figure 12.17](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig17). Then the resistance offered by the device will reduce. Similarly, when current is applied in the opposite direction, the oxygen atoms will be concentrated at one place, which reduces the doped region as shown in [Figure 12.17](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig17). Then resistance offered by the device will increase significantly. Thus, the memristance can be varied in case of a memristor.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f17.jpg)

Figure 12.17 A memrister device

The memristor-based PUFs use the variation of resistance in the device, which depends on the thickness of device, “D.” Due to the manufacturing variations, the device thickness will vary which will affect the read and write times of the device in a memory cell. In case of the memristor, a logical “1” can be written to it when it is set from high resistive state (HRS) (![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-29.gif)) to a low resistive state (LRS) (![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-30.gif)) for a write time above a minimum threshold of time ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-31.gif); else, a logical “0” will be written. *T* is called the SET time and when it is close to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-32.gif), the probability of having a “1” in the cell will be equal to that of a “0.” This uncertainty will make memristor much suitable for the design of PUF. Also, in this case of a binary memristor, where two states are considered, “1” and “0,” transition from one state to the other will take place very abruptly. In such cases, the tamper resistance of memristor-based PUFs will be very high. For the initialization process, a high voltage should be applied so that it will be in a SET state and then switching should be performed between the HRS and LRS at a lower voltage. Below this SET voltage threshold, the device will be operating as a normal resistor. This property can be used as a tamper resistive mechanism. [Figure 12.18](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig18) shows a 1-bit memristor memory-based PUF (McDonald *et al*., [2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib49), [2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib50)). This uses the write time variability of the devices for design of a PUF.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f18.jpg)

Figure 12.18 A 1-bit memristive memory-based PUF

As shown in [Figure 12.18](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig18), there are two control signals in the design, where (![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-33.gif)) is used to determine the write/read operation of the device and the NEG is used to determine the polarity of the writing operation. When a RESET operation should be performed on the device, ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-34.gif)and NEG should be supplied with a “1.” Memristor will go into an HRS with the ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-35.gif)signal. After this, SET signal can be applied for writing a “1” or a “0” by supplying “1” to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-36.gif)and “0” to NEG. Reading can be done by supplying a “0” to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-37.gif). An XOR operation is performed on the output with the challenge input resultant of which will be the output of PUF.

In case of a lateral switching PUF cell designed using memristor (McDonald *et al*., [2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib49), [2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib50)), forming step is highly important for the operations. During the forming step, the conductive filament of the device is supplied with a large voltage in the dielectric sheet. This gives an advantage of values being hidden even during the fabrication state in the foundry. Therefore, if a filament is not present in the dielectric of the device, then it can be assumed that the device has not been tampered with and is secure. In the case of a lateral switching configuration, when the device is SET, during the RESET operation, only one device can go to HRS while other will stay in LRS. Which devices stays in LRS and which goes to HRS is completely random.

[Figure 12.19](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig19) shows the design of a lateral switching filament-based memristor PUF. Like the previous design, there are control signals that are used for various operations and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-38.gif)is used for selecting formation step or operation modes of memristor devices, M1 or M2. When the signal “0” is applied to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-39.gif), either RESET ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-40.gif)or SET ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-41.gif)is applied to the devices, during which the nodes between them are floating. When a “1” is applied to ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-42.gif), both the devices are driven with ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-43.gif)and memristors are loaded. The RESET operation will be done when the filament is formed and one of the memristors will go to HRS. Select signals of MUX will be given the challenge bit and response is read. Noise immunity of a binary memristor PUF is high compared to the others as it is forced either to LRS or HRS. Noise margin is high provided the states are far from the thresholds. But the operation of the memristor is near the threshold voltages which reduces the noise margin.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f19.jpg)

Figure 12.19 A 1-bit filament-based memristive PUF

[Figure 12.20](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig20) shows the design of a hybrid memristor CMOS PUF ([Chatterjee *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib8)). As shown in the figure, the memristor array is connected to an arbiter at the end from which the response is collected. The delay produced by the memristors will decide the output bit that comes from the arbiter where a D-flip-flop can be implemented. Both the memristor arrays are given the same input at the same time. The signal that is present at the input of the arbiter at time of response collection will decide the output bit of PUF.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f20.jpg)

Figure 12.20 Hybrid memristor CMOS PUF

### 12.9 Diode-based PUF

There are various advantages to a crossbar array compared to other circuit designs which make them more suitable to be used in a PUF design. [Figure 12.21](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig21) shows the design of a memristor crossbar array. Regular structure, low energy consumption, high packing density, and simple implementation of the designs are some of the advantages. Besides these, there are also some disadvantages to this design, like sneak current path and crosstalk. The sneak current is dependent on the reverse junction current.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f21.jpg)

Figure 12.21 Memristor crossbar array

There are two sets of wires in the crossbar array, horizontal and vertical, as shown in [Figure 12.21](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig21). The intersection of the wires is separated by a thin material or by a molecular compound. The compound will be resistive to any voltage variations among the wires. Therefore, achieving different resistive states can be done using the intersection which is used for storing the data. Horizontal wires are the word lines and vertical are the bit lines with the voltages “*V*[word]” and “*V*[bit]”. The voltage applied for reading is high compared to that of the reading.

When the memristors in the figure are replaced with diodes, it becomes a diode-based crossbar array. In this case, there are three schemes: in floating schemes, the bit and word lines that are not accessed are kept floating. In the single-supply biasing scheme, the word and bit lines that are not accessed are kept at a voltage ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-46.gif). When it is “0,” it is considered grounded scheme. In case of a double supply biasing scheme, the word lines that are not accessed are biased at a voltage ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-47.gif)and bit lines at ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-48.gif). When they are equal, it will be in a single-supply scheme and when they are opposite polarity, they are called reverse biasing scheme. A crossbar array cell is a bistable element consists of two resistive states ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-49.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-50.gif), which are used to store “1” and “0.” The noise margin in this design can be calculated as ([Ruhrmair *et al*., 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib62)):

![image](OEBPS/images/c12_eqn12_8.gif)

where ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-51.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-52.gif)are the junction currents.

In the case of a memristor-based crossbar array, the forward voltage applied will reduce the resistance offered by the device and the input voltage in opposite direction will increase the resistance of the device ([Lugli *et al*., 2013](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib39)) thus writing a “1” or “0” to the array. Another design of PUF is a super-high information content PUF (SHIC-PUF), which can be characterized by slow readout time and high information content ([Ruhrmair *et al*., 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib62)). For storing information, a crossbar array is used in this case. But for using this, there are some requirements that should be met: the readout time should be low and this will be controlled by the construction of memory cell or slow-process modules. For higher security, the slow readout times should be due to the intrinsic construction of memory cell. Another requirement is that the circuit should be characterized completely and should be very large. The bits of information that are stored on the memory should also be random. Characterization time for a ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-53.gif)bits (~10 GB) and *k* = 100 bits/s circuit is ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-54.gif). This array should also be able to fit in the small area which reduces the occupied chip area.

The bit and word lines are used for the addressing of bits at the intersection of vertical and horizontal lines. This is where the current will flow through the crossing. The word and bit lines will be biased at ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-55.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-56.gif)and during this period, and the word and bit lines that are not accessed will be biased at ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-57.gif)and ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-58.gif)voltages. So, the junctions that are at the accessed word and bit lines are only made to go into forward bias and others are reverse biased in case of a diode-based crossbar array. Word lines are connected with a sense resistor and depending on the voltage at the word line, there are two states that are shown, high or low resistance. In this case, the information in the bits is random and is also important to see that the structural features are irregular. To achieve this, aluminum-induced layer exchange is considered. This gives an advantage of randomizing the distribution of conductivity which will result in an inhomogeneous conductivity. This can be taken as an advantage in case of PUF. When the array size is increased, reverse bias junction current will increase, which in turn will increase the power dissipation of the module. But the parasitic paths will avoid the accessed bit and word line. This reduces the noise margin and makes it suitable for PUF design. And large generator resistance values are required for readout cycles to be slow and for limiting the capacitive peak current. As an alternative, high-*κ* material can be used.

A crossbar array can also be used and a weak PUF and SHIC PUF can be implemented as presented by [Lugli *et al*. (2013)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib39). In this case, rewriting and erasing the PUF response can be performed without the other responses changed. This is only possible in case of a crossbar array but not in the case of other PUF designs. An increased crossbar array will be a huge issue as the sneak current path becomes a problem and this also decreases the noise margin and degrades power dissipation. A rectifying element can be implemented for reducing the crosstalk and leakage between the accessed and unaccessed cells. The design of a crossbar can also contain a memristor in series with a diode which can reduce the noise margin and power dissipation. There is a compatibility issue in case of a traditional silicon process and transitional metal oxide memristors ([Kim *et al*., 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib29)).

When the floating biased scheme was implemented, the size of the array was reduced and noise margin was also reduced because of the increase in sneak current. This is also same in case of power dissipation. Due to this, the size of memory is limited to a few megabits. External resistance effect is minimal on the noise margin and reverse-biased scheme is suitable for the noise margin and power dissipation. But when compared to the floating point scheme, the power dissipation is high due to the higher off currents. It can be inferred that the memory size can be increased if power consumption is not a problem, which also decreases the noise margin. Scaling also helps in reducing the diode current and wire resistance.

In case of an ALILE, the diodes that come from a weak-doped wafer will have high rectification ratio and high randomness. But noise margin is low when compared to a ZnO junction because of low rectification of about 10⁸ at ±2 V.

An ALILE diodes of small size is suited for use in case of a weak PUF when compared to a ZnO Schottky diodes, as the randomness is high ([Ruhrmair *et al*., 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib61)). The stability of ALILE diodes is also high over a long period and resistive to invasive readouts. Temperature dependency of the diode’s performance is high, which can be improved with the use of differential measurement techniques.

### 12.10 Carbon-based PUFs

In the current research trend, silicon devices are used widely for the development of PUF designs and are more focusing on the randomness, reliability, and robustness. But the power consumption of the devices is not being monitored or focused. Scaling of devices has led to a place where low-power consuming devices are more required and low-voltage operational devices are required, which becomes a challenge to the PUF design. Scaling of devices also makes it difficult to control the gate and charge carriers in the channel. This makes it necessary to explore post silicon device which can be used for scaling. Carbon derivative options such as the carbon nanotube (CNT) and graphene are promising candidates.

#### 12.10.1 CNT-based PUF

CNT FET-based PUFs can be implemented for various advantages such as low-power consumption, high reliability, and low energy ([Konigsmark *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib31)). In case of a CNTFET, a CNT is used as a channel in the transistor. The configuration of a CNTFET changes depending on various properties of the CNT, such as diameter, chirality, growth density, misalignment, and doping concentration. Chirality is used for the generation of secret bits. The direction in which the graphene sheet is rolled decides the chirality of a CNT which decides the metallic or semiconductor nature of the device. [Figure 12.22](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig22) shows the design of a CNPUF, which contains the CNTFETs connected in series. The parallel elements of the transistors, CNPUF-PEs, share a common gate voltage. In this case, there can be a large number of semiconducting CNTs and a small number of metallic CNTs. The ratio in which they are used is 10%–30% where the semiconducting current will dominate the metallic current. Each parallel element consists of a distinct state for high- and low-input gate voltages. Due to the process variation, this states will vary, which affects the output. The improvement of area can be achieved by 300% when compared to design of silicon-based arbiter PUF ([Konigsmark *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib31)). The interchip HD of 49.67% has been presented by [Konigsmark *et al*. (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib31). When the simulation was performed in different conditions, by giving random values to the temperature and the supply voltage of the devices, the performance of CNPUF-PE has been more reliable and stable compared to that of an RO PUF, current-based PUF, and SRAM PUF. For a higher security, a trade-off between security and power consumption should be made. An extended CNPUF adds an area overhead but is comparable to the Si PUF with higher security.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f22.jpg)

Figure 12.22 CNT-based PUF design

Even though the CNTFET has various advantages over the silicon transistors and allows more scalability, fabricating the CNTFET gives high difficulties. The planar geometry of the graphene makes it easier compared to the CNTs during fabrication and is also comparatively cheaper to silicon devices. Graphene is also compatible with the CMOS technology, which gives additional advantage of scaling and performance. Therefore, high-density SoC and higher performance can be achieved by combining the CMOS fabrication technologies with the graphene’s unique properties.

#### 12.10.2 Graphene-based PUF

[Figure 12.23](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig23) shows the design of a graphene nanoribbon transistor. Graphene has high electron mobility which has an added advantage to be used as a channel in case of FETs ([Khan *et al*., 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib27)). It is a two-dimensional carbon atom network which is arranged like a honeycomb lattice. Graphene is a single layer of graphite structure which is interconnected in a lattice structure. It is highly strong in all the directions. A CNT structure can be formed by rolling a graphene nanoribbon and one with 12 pentagon defects will give a fullerene structure. Properties of graphene which makes it more suitable than silicon for future technology are two-dimensional one atom crystal, light and thin material with high flexibility and strength. It is transparent and nonflammable and highly conductive.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f23.jpg)

Figure 12.23 Graphene transistor

Besides these advantages, there are also some challenges in this graphene technology: it is highly sensitive to environmental changes and does not work easily with discrete electronic signals as there is a no band gap in the semiconducting graphene structure. Unlike a silicon transistor, the graphene-based transistor cannot be turned off as the bandgap is low. But the high bandgap makes it more suitable for use in RF applications, which controls the gate current in digital logic environment. Off-state leakage currents are high, which results in smaller I[ON]/I[OFF] ratio. Saturation of drain voltage current is not readily available.

A measurement circuit is usually present in a PUF-based security modules. This can be used for measurement of the property of graphene devices such as resistance, capacitance, and voltages for deriving the output of PUF which can be used for cryptographic applications ([Dimitrakopoulos *et al*., 2012](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib12)). There are some points that should be used for graphene-based PUF designs:

1.  Properties of graphene-based PUFs should be stable over a wide range of time, temperature, and other environmental variables.
    
2.  During the fabrication process under extremely controlled conditions, there will be variations in the properties of the devices because of chemical processing, the presence of terrace edges, and growth process during growth of graphene. This results in device-to-device variations on the wafer. For the introduction of additional variations, different methods can be employed:
    
    *   (a) Molecular doping, hydrogen inhalation, width/length scaling, contact treatments, and contact metal variation.
        
    *   (b) Laser annealing can be introduced during the fabrication where beam width, energy, pulse duration, and wavelength can be varied.
        
    *   (c) Contact treatment and contact metal variations.
        
    *   (d) Different ambient conditions such as varied dopant quantities and types, oxygen levels, and so on can also introduce variations.
        
    *   (d) For increasing the variability, a single graphene device can be packed with more layers. Which will vary the electrical properties of device.
        
3.  For an improved stability, passivation layers can be employed, which also does not affect the security of the device during attacks based on scanning electron microscopy (SEM). A higher yield can be achieved using the passivated graphene. Resistance is inversely related to temperature in case of an unpassivated graphene device, which can reduce the resistance with the increase in temperature.
    
4.  Array of devices that can be used for the implementation of PUF has a very low variability range almost close to threshold values of the core device used. In this case, reliability decreases with time and so will the temperature variation. This can cause to read errors while reading the output bits from the PUF module. There are also various solutions that can be implemented in this case. Some of them are:
    
    *   (a) Error correction schemes can be employed but by sacrificing security.
        
    *   (b) Average values of device in the array can be considered for setting the threshold value for digital fingerprint.
        
    *   (c) Temperature-compensating algorithms can be used along with the temperature sensors for mitigating the temperature variance issues.
        
5.  Robustness against attacks can be increased by implementing the following:
    
    *   (a) The device location in a large array can be changed randomly which makes it difficult for the attacker to correctly give the challenge input to get an appropriate response.
        
    *   (b) A measurement circuit can be employed on the circuitry to make it difficult for the attacker to use probes for accessing the devices.
        
    *   (c) Delayering the measurement circuits can also be implemented, which makes the circuit more robust. This makes it difficult for the attacker to convert the read values to digital outputs. Attempting to remove the delayering will render the device useless.
        

### 12.11 Microprocessor-based PUF

Until now, this chapter discussed different PUF circuits that were designed for security and need to be fabricated. This section discusses different components such as microprocessor, power rail, and so on for designing PUF circuits. [Figure 12.24](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig24) shows the design of a microprocessor-based PUF ([Kumar *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib32)). Two 32-bit multiplexers and two PUF counters are used for designing the module. The output of the multiplier is connected to MUX as shown in the figure. The MUX will choose which PUF module will be driven by the bits of the multiplier. PUF counter is 32-bit long and the general-purpose registers of the microprocessor will store the 9th bit to 24th bit output from PUF counters. A 32-bit long output is generated from the two different PUF counters as shown in the figure ([Kumar *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib32)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f24.jpg)

Figure 12.24 Microprocessor-based PUF

There are five select lines for each of the MUX for selecting the output of the multiplier. Part of the challenge input to the PUF module will be the select lines that go into the MUX. Different paths of the multiplier are selected using the assembly program, which becomes the later part of the challenge input to the PUF module. Response from the counters gets stored in the registers of the microprocessor. For an efficient CRP generation, the assembly program development is an important task. The interconnects will add delays with the manufacturing variations introduced during the fabrication stage.

In the design presented by [Kumar *et al*. (2017)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib32), the openmsp430 design has been modified into two different modes of operation, normal and PUF. I/O pins of the microprocessor are given the 10 select lines and “En” pin. Multiplier output has been modified for generating the addition of multiplexer and PUF counter. Additional circuitry in the module will become active when the PUF mode is selected and during the normal operation, they will be separated from the microprocessor.

### 12.12 Magnetic PUF

Sections 12.10 and 12.8 presented two different types of non-silicon material-based PUF designs. This section presents another type of non-silicon-based PUF designs, magnetic PUFs. There are various devices which use magnetic properties of materials for performing operations ([Gao *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib14)).

Spin transfer torque magnetic random access memory (STT-MRAM) devices are one of them. [Figure 12.25](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig25) shows the design of an STT-MRAM (Huai, [2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib22)). When current passes through the fixed layer, a spin-polarized current is produced. If the current that is produced is directed toward the free layer, the angular momentum can be transferred to the layer which can change the orientation of the magnet. When the two layers are parallel (P) to each other, the resistance is low. When the two layers are anti-parallel (AP) to each other, the resistance is high.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f25.jpg)

Figure 12.25 Spin transfer torque magnetic random access memory PUF

A magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ)-based PUF was proposed by [Marukame *et al*. (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib48) which can extract the fingerprint of the spin transfer-switching properties. The characterized STS characteristics were measured experimentally by [Marukame *et al*. (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib48) and a method to extract the PUF signature was also presented. It was also observed that different programming voltages for AP to P state and P to AP state transitions were required by the MTJ. Extrinsic properties such as the process damage and junction resistance lead to the MTJ. Due to these variations, an operation sequence for the extraction of bits from PUF-based 4×4 array was implemented. Initially, the reset voltage is applied to initialize them into a state of parallelism. Then the precalibrated voltage ![image](OEBPS/images/c12-Eqn-in-59.gif)is applied for inducing the switching with a probability of 50% for majority of the MTJs. The switching will result in a random distribution of the devices in an array in various states, AP and P. Signature extraction circuit will take care of the information resistance. After extracting the information, the entire array is set into P state. For increasing the reliability, the operation sequence is repeated for extraction of the bits.

[Figure 12.26](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig26) shows a phase change material (PCM) which is similar to the previous one and takes advantage of the magnetic properties for designing the PUF. A PCM has amorphous and crystalline natures in the PCM. The difference in the resistance offered by the two states is largely different. To change the material to amorphous state, a pulse with high amplitude and fast fall time is supplied to heater to initially melt it and then quench it rapidly. So a region of high resistive amorphous material is formed in the PCM. A long fall time moderate amplitude pulse is supplied to the cell for converting it into a crystalline state which will anneal the active region at a temperature between crystallization and melting temperature which forms a crystalline material in the cell which offers low resistance. [Figure 12.27](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig27) shows the structure of a PCM array. During the reading operation, the resistance of the cell is read by sending a small current to it. This pulse will not be disturbing the state of the cell ([Wong *et al*., 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib75)). The resistance offered by the PCM cell can also be controlled by passing a small amount of current, a programming pulse with intermediate amplitude rise/fall time.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f26.jpg)

Figure 12.26 Phase change material

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f27.jpg)

Figure 12.27 Phase change material memory array PUF

### 12.13 Practical implementation of PUF

Designing a PUF module can be half the problem but the implementation and deploying the same in an environment can pose additional challenges. Any design to be validated has to be implemented in a real-time scenario where it is subject to different real-time conditions. FPGA implementations of PUF are being explored by researchers for validation of the design and implementation of their proposed designs into different applications. Deploying the design on an FPGA opens up a lot of opportunities to the PUF design and adds more to the list of applications ([Chowdhury *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib10); [Ikezaki *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib23); [Johnson *et al*., 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib25)).

The FPGAs are also evolving day-by-day and adding more features for better integration into the IoT world ([Johnson *et al*., 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib25)). One such capability is the dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) or runtime partial reconfiguration (RPR). With these features of an FPGA, the circuit design that is on the FPGA can be configured partially during the runtime. This ability is called “Partial Reconfiguration.” The power consumption of the FPGA can be reduced by using the DPR which makes them ideal for use in IoT applications. But these DPR-enabled FPGAs are subjected to various attacks by the adversary which can get the entire network of devices into jeopardy. A protection technique that can be used for protecting the DPR-enabled FPGAs was proposed by [Johnson *et al*. (2015)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib25). An XoR PUF was employed in the paper for securing the protocol. Because of the complex nature of the PUF that is deployed in the application, modeling an attack by the attacker will be difficult as there will be no access to the PUF responses. If that access is gained by the adversary, attacking the PUF with a modeling attack will become easy and successful in some cases.

There are also many different aging-resistant PUFs designs that are implemented on the FPGAs ([Chowdhury *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib10)). The aging effects on the FPGA are presented by [Maiti and Schaumont (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib43). It was also presented that a change in the location of the output response bits and the devices that are affected by the aging are also random. There are also many designs of PUF that are implemented based on SRAM on the FPGA that use the aging effects on the design to an advantage. An aging resistant RO PUF is proposed for reliable key generation in ([Rahman *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib58)). With the FPGA lacking the ability to change the circuit architecture, implementing this idea becomes more difficult.

### 12.14 PUF: case study applications

All the above sections discussed different designs of PUFs. This section discusses different applications of PUF in various domains. There are many applications and domains where PUF can be used and implemented. One such major issue that is becoming a problem is counterfeiting. [Figure 12.28](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig28) shows a big picture of counterfeiting in the case of an IC. When an IC is designed by a manufacturer, there can be many clones designed by various third parties to be sold in the market ([Chang *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib5); [Mohanty, 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib53)). But this is a major issue economically and also in terms of security. The ICs that are created by the counterfeiting party can be malicious and might contain trojans. A PUF can be implemented in the IC design so that it can be used for authenticating the original device ([Yan *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib76)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f28.jpg)

Figure 12.28 Securing against IPR PUFs

A PUF module that contains on-chip hash function can increase the cost of the entire chip but can also increase the robustness of the entire design. An index-based syndrome encoding has been shown to be implemented with RO PUF for a better reliability ([Yu and Devadas, 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib82)). There are also variations in the output bits that get flipped due to the environmental and operational conditions. So error correction mechanisms can also be implemented with a PUF so that the output can be read without errors. But error correction mechanism can increase the chip area and hence the total cost of the chip. There is also a power trade-off that has to be considered while adding additional circuitry. A comparison of built-in hash functions and their effects is shown in [Table 12.2](#Chapter12.html#c12_tbl2).

**Table 12.2** Comparison of different types of hash functions in terms of chip area and clock ([Majzoobi *et al*., 2008](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib46))

![image](OEBPS/images/tab12.2.jpg)

Man-in-the-middle attacks can be controlled by implementing PUF modules in various applications like distributed computing ([Gassend *et al*., 2002](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib15)). Different steps involved in such an attack are as follows:

*   “A” should interact with the PUF module by using the CRPs shared between A and PUF.
    
*   “B” is an attacker who has access to the PUF module. Therefore, B will be able to gather the responses from the module by giving the challenge inputs that are chosen by B. B wants to use it with the identity of “A” and impersonates with fake results.
    
*   A gives out PUF challenges from CRP list and compares responses that come from the output of PUF module with a private list.
    
*   B has access to the challenges and PUF, so gets the response from PUF for that specific challenge.
    
*   B will be able to fool A by pretending that A has PUF access and can impersonate the PUF as if it is A.
    

The applications of PUF are very broad as shown in [Figure 12.29](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig29). They can also be used in applications or devices where randomness is needed. PUF modules are elegant solutions in various applications such as RFID tags, random number generation, secret key generation, device authentication, and so on ([Gunlu and Iscan, 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib18); [O’Donnell *et al*., 2004](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib55); [Suh and Devadas, 2007](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib69); [Suh *et al*., 2005](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib70)). PUF has also been used in consumer electronic devices where authentication is needed at a low cost ([http://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/mit-spinoff-verayo-developed-srini-devadas-gains-increased-use-commercial](http://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/mit-spinoff-verayo-developed-srini-devadas-gains-increased-use-commercial)).

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f29.jpg)

Figure 12.29 Typical applications of PUFs

In case of the cryptographic and security applications, the random number generation can be used for generating the encryption and decryption keys, initial seed values, and in some cases, where required, introduce some randomness to the padding schemes and protocols. Pseudo-random number generation (PRNG) is not truly random and in that case, the pattern will repeat after a certain number of iterations. Each of the number generated by the PRNG has to go through a very complex algorithm. Initial seed value should be kept highly secret in case of PRNG. Due to all these different issues with the PRNG, hardware random number generation (HRNG) has been implemented in various cases ([O’Donnell *et al*., 2004](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib55)). In case of an HRNG, an initial seed is not required for generating a truly random number. A delay-based PUF circuit will have the rising edge of the input signal and challenge bits as select lines to the multiplexers. Input will propagate through the series of multiplexers and depending on the delay offered by each of them, a D-flip-flop will generate the output bit “1” or “0.” An unbiased output response will be given by a meta-stable PUF. A Von Neumann correction gives a 32-bit output response from an *N*\-bit input. Similarly, there are various designs of PUF which can be implemented based on the requirements of application. [Figure 12.30](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig30) shows a key generation system using PUF modules.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f30.jpg)

Figure 12.30 Secure key generation system using PUFs

For using the authentication schemes of PUF on a chip, a trusted party or the manufacturer should store the CRPs which are exponential in number in a secure database which can be matched for authentication ([Suh and Devadas, 2007](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib69)). For an input challenge, the output of PUF is the same, in that case, the device that has been challenged will be authentic. But when using the challenge inputs, the man-in-the-middle attack should be avoided by discarding the challenge once used.

A controlled PUF module can also be used for certified execution. It is a process of executing or running a program on a remote server where the client can rely on the results produced by the server ([Gassend *et al*., 2002](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib15)). [Figure 12.31](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig31) shows the process of authenticating a person over the network using PUF. In this case, the PUF device will generate a challenge input and has the response respectively. When authentication is needed, the response is sent to the server where it confirms the identity of the client. This can help avoid identity fraud and rendering the results of the client useless. This can also avoid an attacker from generating different malicious results and sending it to the user. This scenario is often seen in case of a distributed computing where one processor cannot handle the workflow. This type of PUF modules can also be used to restrict the usage of a specific software to a respective amount of processors.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f31.jpg)

Figure 12.31 Authentication of user using PUFs

[Figure 12.32](#Chapter12.html#c12_fig32) shows the design of a secure digital camera which has a PUF module that is built into it ([Haider *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib19)). Secure boot of sensor controller of the camera is used to ensure the integrity of the platform at booting. PUF-based secure key generation and storage module provides key for sensed data attestation to ensure integrity and authenticity. In system architecture of the secure camera, the PUF-based key generation and storage module has two cascaded components, a PUF source and a helper data algorithm (HDA). The choice of the HDA depends on the selection of the PUF source. The HDA is used to obtain: (1) a perfectly reproducible PUF response under a range of environmental and operating conditions, in other words, the HD between any two responses from the same PUF is zero, and (2) an almost uniformly distributed PUF response.

![image](OEBPS/images/PBCS0600-12-f32.jpg)

Figure 12.32 Secure camera using PUFs

IoT applications have become more necessary nowadays. Many situations are arising where the devices have to be deployed in places where they cannot be monitored or have human interaction. Such cases are more often prone to attacks by the attacker who has access to the device without security. PUF can be used to stop attacks in such situations where the entire network of devices can be secured ([Mohanty *et al*., 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib54); [Yanambaka *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib77)).

### 12.15 PUF: issues

The understanding of this chapter so far is that a PUF provides better security and robustness to the entire application. But there are many issues and challenges that have to be addressed while designing and implementing the PUF in an application ([Chang *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib5); [Wan *et al*., 2015](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib72); [Wen and Lao, 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib74); Ye *et al*., [2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib79), [2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib80)). There are various attempts for providing better security and robustness by implementation of PUF, but some of the common attacks are:

*   There is a chance that the attacker can create a large number of chips with the similar design to the PUF module used in a respective application for obtaining the response. In cases where the design of PUF is simple, this can be very successful.
    
*   It is also possible to predict the response of the PUF or calculate it using mathematical modeling techniques ([Ma *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib40); [Mispan *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib52); [Tanaka *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib71)). Adding a nonlinearity to the PUF design can avoid these kinds of attacks.
    
*   There are different types of attacks, invasive or semi-invasive, which can determine the time delay and power of the devices. Tamper-resisting packaging can avoid these attacks.
    
*   Introducing errors into the module can also be performed by the attacker to tamper with it and render it useless.
    

These attacks are common and there are many different kinds of solutions that are suggested. Improvements can also be made to the PUF designs to make them difficult to attack by the attacker.

*   A hash function can also be implemented before or after the PUF module which can prevent the attacker from gaining knowledge of the CRPs. This can prevent the modeling attacks on the modules.
    
*   Error correction mechanisms can be implemented in the PUF modules which can make them more reliable and avoid bit-flips due to environmental variations and operational disturbances.
    
*   Control of PUF response is often desired by the client who is using the module. Additional secret keys for the input of the modules can be implemented, which is totally in hands of the user or client.
    
*   Tamper-resistant packaging should be used for the ICs and PUF modules. This will increase the cost of the entire application and will increase the robustness also.
    

Attacking the PUF modules is a kind of attack that has to be performed by an adversary with an ill intent. But there are also other challenges faced during the design of PUF modules ([Ganta and Nazhandali, 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13); [Sahoo *et al*., 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib64); [Wang and Tehranipoor, 2010](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib73); [Yanambaka *et al*., 2017, 2018](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib78)). Some of the challenges include crosstalk, noise in the signals, noise in power supply, and so on. Noise sources can also originate from an unusual input pattern which varies with a different input. Such a noise can be taken as an advantage by the user in designing different input challenges which will increase the robustness of the module against the attackers.

When a large switching activity is triggered due to the input pattern, a power supply noise can occur. The dynamic power is increased due to this and will be responsible for a voltage drop in the power line and an increase in voltage at the ground. Such changes in the supply voltages can cause the change in gate voltages and induce unusual delays in the circuitry. Then the entire circuit operation changes which affect the output response inducing more errors into it. Parasitics should also be taken into consideration during the design of a PUF module.

Aging is another issue that is present in the PUF designs. With the aging effects, the integrity of the circuit degrades over time and renders it useless. Over a period of time, the circuit health degrades and the output responses of a set of challenges can also be affected due to these changes ([Chowdhury *et al*., 2017](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib10); [Ganta and Nazhandali, 2014](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13); [Meguerdichian and Potkonja, 2011](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib51); [Rahman *et al*., 2015, 2016](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib58)). The aging effects on the PUF module depending on the frequency of turning the device on have been presented by [Ganta and Nazhandali (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13). An RO PUF was subjected to the study and some of the observations presented by [Ganta and Nazhandali (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13) are:

*   The bit error rate (BER) in the case of PUF, which is always on is the highest. But when the device is turned on during the day only once, the BER is 2%. A 35% reduction in BER can be achieved by turning on the device once a day.
    
*   The manufacturing variations of the devices are modeled during the simulation as threshold voltage variations. A mismatch was observed by [Ganta and Nazhandali (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13) in identical circuit elements, and when the process variation is high, the PUF is stable.
    
*   For the effects of temperature and the aging of the modules, and their effects on the stability of design, the PUFs were operated at various temperatures and ages. The effect of aging on the PUF design was not observed to be significant on the stability of the device due to the differential nature. The correlation on stability is shown as 70% of the aging effect and the temperature.
    
*   Supply voltage and the noise in the supply voltage are also the challenges in the designs. The PUFs’ performance is measured in the presence of these issues and aging by [Ganta and Nazhandali (2014)](#Chapter12.html#c12_bib13). The effect of supply noise is less than 0.2% in the presence of aging. But the BER of the PUF that is operating at a subthreshold voltage with aging is high.
    
*   The stability of the PUF depends on the ring oscillation configuration highly where with an increase in the stages, there is also an increase in the susceptibility to the environmental changes.
    

### 12.16 Conclusion

This concept of a PUF was initially proposed in 2001 as physical one-way function. Since then, there are various concepts of PUF that were designed using different architectures, devices, and materials. Many of the PUFs are highly robust and others are not secure which can be easily broken with the implementation of a simple machine learning algorithm.

Research is being conducted for designing more robust and secure designs of PUFs for better security. But with the high implementations of IoT architectures, there is more necessity and scope for the development of low-power designs of PUF. There are low-power-consuming designs being implemented and proposed by many researchers around the world but the main focus of research has been the increase in the robustness and resistance to attacks. As a future research, low-power design of PUF can also be implemented for better wide range of implementation and integration.

There are also the threats and attacks on the PUF that are yet to be addressed. With the introduction of new applications every day, it is necessary to secure them against attacks that come with it. Side-channel resilient PUF designs are yet to be more saturated and better designs are yet to come into the consumer-level market. PUFs are being implemented in many enterprise domain applications like servers, but commercial market is still open to the implementations of PUF. This can also be considered as a future research of the PUFs.
